All providers behind model.BaseChatModel / model.ToolCallingChatModel interfaces. Adapters in eino-ext for 11+ providers (OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Gemini, Ark (ByteDance Volcengine), Qwen, DeepSeek, Ollama, OpenRouter, Qianfan); trivial to add your own.

First-party plugins: googlegenai (Google AI), vertexai, anthropic, compat_oai (OpenAI-compatible), ollama, modelgarden. Fallback middleware handles outages. Strong multi-provider but Firebase/Google is the brand-level tilt.

None — pluggable LLM abstraction with 104 implementations. 104 directories under llama-index-integrations/llms/ (Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, Cohere, Mistral, Groq, Together, vLLM, Ollama, etc.). Each integration is a separately versioned PyPI package.

Low LLM-provider lock-in. MultiProvider supports openai/..., litellm/..., any-llm/... prefixes natively. LiteLLM covers 100+ providers, Any-LLM adds OpenRouter and others. The Responses API gets first-class treatment but Chat Completions also works.

Low LLM-provider lock-in. ~14 providers + FallbackModel chain + pydantic-ai-litellm direction. Custom models implementable via the Model abstract base. Per-provider extras (openai, anthropic, google, mistral, groq, cohere, bedrock, huggingface, xai).

Low LLM provider lock-in. Bedrock is the default but the Model base class is provider-agnostic, with shipped adapters for Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI (Chat + Responses), Google, and a VercelModel shim wrapping the Vercel AI SDK provider interface.

Low LLM-provider lock-in. 50+ provider adapters (packages/<provider>/), all behind the LanguageModel interface. Swap providers in one line. Includes openai, anthropic, google, amazon-bedrock, google-vertex, azure, gateway, and many more.

note: 3 — runs anywhere Go runs; heavy GCP pull
details: Runs anywhere Go runs but README and launchers explicitly mention Cloud Run; Agent Engine session backend is GCP-only. SDK works against any LLM behind model.LLM but content types are google.golang.org/genai, and recommended deploy target is Cloud Run + Agent Engine + Vertex AI. Not GCP-locked, but heavily GCP-pulled.

note: 5 — pure Python uvicorn process, no platform lock-in
details: Hosting-platform lock-in: minimal — it's just a Python process running uvicorn. Self-hosted; managed os.agno.com control plane points at your runtime (no data handoff). Runs anywhere Python runs.
Hosting platform lock-in: none — runs anywhere Rust runs. No mandatory database, no Redis, no Postgres. Embeddable in any Rust binary (axum, actix, custom). Optional WASM target.

Hosting: none — pure library, deploys anywhere Python + the bundled claude binary run. But each query() spawns a new claude subprocess with platform-specific binary; cold-start cost (issue #333: 20-30s). Memory baseline ~200-500MB per active session.

note: 3 — Low self-host; high if claude.ai bridge
details: Low lock-in for self-host, High for claude.ai bridge. Self-hostable with your own Anthropic API key. bridge.mjs is opt-in alpha for claude.ai-anchored workers. Per-platform binaries (~200-233 MB) ship via optionalDependencies; multi-arch Docker images add up.
OSS hosting lock-in: None — anywhere Python runs. AMP (Enterprise) hosting lock-in: Heavy — AMP-only deploys, AMP-managed automations and triggers. The OSS path itself has no hosting lock-in.

note: 5 — library only; deploy wherever Go runs
details: Hosting platform lock-in: None — library only. Deploy wherever Go runs. CloudWeGo/ByteDance owns the project and their internal use case drives the roadmap (Volcengine Ark, APMPlus), so non-Chinese language coverage trails Chinese, but no hosting tie-in.

note: 4 — slight GCP tilt; samples target Cloud Run
details: Slight GCP tilt. Samples target Cloud Run. Telemetry plugin is GCP-only (googlecloud). Sessions persistence ships only Firestore adapter. But nothing GCP-required: you can run on any Kubernetes, AWS, on-prem.

note: 3 — OSS-only requires BYO HTTP+queue+auth; Platform paid
details: Medium hosting lock-in. The HTTP server, auth, run queue, multitask coordination, and /mcp routes ship only via LangGraph Platform (closed-source). Going pure-OSS means BYO HTTP + queue + auth. Self-host of Platform via Docker compose / K8s Helm chart but still on the Platform code.
Hosting lock-in: None for the OSS framework. llama_deploy is OSS too; LlamaCloud is for parse/ingest, not serving. Library runs anywhere Python runs.

Low hosting lock-in. Deployers for all major edge platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers); the Hono server runs anywhere. Mastra Cloud exists but is optional. Storage lock-in low — 15+ adapters.

note: 4 — Azure first-class but no hard dependency
details: Microsoft Azure stack is clearly first-class (Foundry, Azure Functions, Cosmos, AI Search), but core packages have no hard dependency on Azure. ASP.NET Core hosting works against any LLM. Multiple hosting options (Aspire, Azure Functions, DurableTask, Foundry Hosted) but ASP.NET Core deploys anywhere.
Hosting-platform lock-in: none. Run anywhere Python 3.10+ runs (any container, any cloud, any laptop). Library-only; no vendor opinion on topology.
Hosting: low. Library-only. Runs anywhere Node.js / Deno / Bun runs; Cloudflare Workers experimental with nodejs_compat.
Hosting lock-in: none — library runs anywhere Python runs. Optional durable execution via Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate. Logfire is one OTel backend among many.

note: 5 — library only; runs anywhere Rust runs
details: Hosting-platform lock-in: none. Rust library; embed in your binary (typically axum + tokio). No vendor binary downloaded; no Node sidecar. WASM-compatible.

Hosting lock-in: low (pure Python). Bedrock is the default model provider but Strands is genuinely multi-provider. Apache-2.0; you self-host. Sister A2A FastAPI server is optional. AWS ecosystem backs it but no hard hosting requirement.
Hosting: none — pure library. Optional A2AExpressServer adapter exists but is a JSON-RPC adapter, not a chat HTTP server. Node 20+, browser-tested via esbuild check. No mandatory Postgres/Redis.

note: 5 — library only; runs anywhere Node runs
details: Hosting platform lock-in: low. Library-only — runs anywhere Node runs. Vercel hosting and AI Gateway are conveniences, not requirements. No SDK-provided server; you mount on Next.js/Hono/Express/Fastify/Nest/Nuxt yourself.

ADK Go's loop runs entirely in your Go process via runner.Runner.Run → llminternal.Flow.Run with no subprocess, sidecar, or vendor bridge. The same module also ships an optional first-party HTTP/SSE/WebSocket/A2A server that embeds the loop in the same OS process. This is the simplest deployment shape of any benchmarked stack.

Agno's loop is a single Python _run/_arun function in agno.agent._run executed inside your Python (FastAPI) process. AgentOS mounts 50+ routes against the same in-process agent — no subprocess, no vendor cloud required. Background memory/learning work runs as threads or asyncio tasks in the same process.

AutoAgents runs the loop in the caller's tokio runtime: BaseAgent::run → AgentExecutor::execute → TurnEngine::run_turn, all inside the host Rust process. There is no daemon, subprocess, or vendor cloud. An optional ractor-based actor runtime is in-process pub/sub only.

The actual agent loop (turn boundaries, tool dispatch, planner, hook firing, compaction) runs in the bundled Claude Code Node.js CLI spawned via subprocess over a JSON control protocol. The Python side is a transport + typed-message parser + hook callback router. You cannot fork the loop without forking Claude Code.

note: 3 — TS shim over native CLI binary
details: Despite the TypeScript SDK branding, the agent loop executes in a spawned native Claude Code binary (~200MB per platform), not in your Node process. The TS code is a transport + control-protocol shim over stdio JSON-RPC. Architectural ceiling is identical to the Python SDK — you cannot escape the Claude Code subprocess.

CrewAI runs the loop in your Python process: Crew.kickoff → AgentExecutor (a Flow subclass with planning, todo list, asyncio.gather parallel step execution). No subprocess, no separate runtime, no vendor binary — the library is the loop. LLM HTTP calls go directly from the same process to the provider.

Eino's loop runs in your Go binary in a goroutine spawned by ChatModelAgent.Run, driving a compiled compose.Graph internally. Workflow agents fan out via real sync.WaitGroup goroutines. No subprocess, no vendor daemon, no hosted service — purely in-process import-and-call.

Genkit Go's loop is a single in-process Go function — ai.GenerateWithRequest — that recursively calls the model, runs tool calls, and feeds results back until done. No subprocess, no IPC, no remote agent runner. The genkit-tools JS CLI talks to your process only in dev mode via a Reflection HTTP server.

The graph runtime runs inside PregelLoop.tick() in your Python process — tools, checkpointer I/O, and LLM calls all execute in-process. The closed-source langgraph_api HTTP server wraps the same in-process loop but adds queue + persistence + auth on top; that's a paid platform layer, not where the loop lives.

LlamaIndex's agent layer runs as an asyncio coroutine inside your Python process. FunctionAgent.run resolves into Workflow.run which schedules @step methods on the running event loop. No bundled binary, no subprocess, no vendor cloud round-trip.

Mastra's loop runs entirely in your Node/Bun/Edge process: the loop is itself a Mastra workflow (then(llmExecutionStep).foreach(toolCallStep)…). No subprocess, no vendor binary. The Hono-based @mastra/server embeds the agent in the same process.

MAF runs the loop in-process: Python BaseChatClient.get_response and .NET FunctionInvokingChatClient middleware both execute the LLM round-trip and tool-call loop in the host process. No subprocesses, no bundled CLIs. Optional hosted runtimes (Azure Functions, DurableTask, Foundry) externalize orchestration when chosen.

openai-agents runs Runner.run as a single-threaded async loop on your asyncio event loop. The entire ReAct loop — including streaming, tool dispatch, guardrail evaluation, hook firing, and session persistence — happens inside your Python process. No bundled CLI, no Node sidecar, no sister-repo server.

Runner.run is a TypeScript while(true) loop inside your Node/Deno/Bun process that calls a Model instance over HTTP/SSE/WebSocket directly. No subprocess, no vendor binary, no first-party server. The OpenAI in the name is provider-agnostic loop + first-party OpenAI provider.

Agent.run opens a pydantic_graph GraphRun walking UserPromptNode → ModelRequestNode → CallToolsNode → End in your Python process. Every model call is model.request(...) executed by the host — no bundled binary, no subprocess, no vendor cloud. HTTP exposure is opt-in via agent.to_web() or UI adapters.

Rig is a Rust library: the agent loop lives in the caller's Tokio runtime as plain async functions in crates/rig-core/src/agent/prompt_request/. No bundled server, no sidecar process, no vendor cloud — pure Cargo crates you pull into your binary.

Strands runs the loop in your Python process as a pure-Python async generator (event_loop_cycle in src/strands/event_loop/event_loop.py). No subprocess, no bundled binary, no vendor cloud. Closer to LangGraph/Vercel AI SDK style than to Claude Agent SDK Python.

Agent.stream() is an async function* generator running entirely inside the host Node.js (or browser) process on the V8 event loop. No bundled server, no subprocess, no vendor runtime. An optional A2A Express adapter exposes any agent as a JSON-RPC endpoint without changing where the loop runs.

The agent loop runs inside generateText / streamText as a do/while loop in your Node.js process. ToolLoopAgent is a thin wrapper around that — not a long-running process. No vendor cloud, no subprocess, no daemon — only LLM provider HTTPS calls leave the process.

Go 1.25 binary with pure-Go modules (google.golang.org/genai, gorilla/mux, gorm). No bundled binaries, no native libs, no mandatory Postgres or Redis, no mandatory Vertex — runs on Gemini API key alone. Optional GORM driver of your choice (Postgres/Spanner/SQLite); Vertex/GCS only if you choose those backends.

Python 3.7+; for the AgentOS server: fastapi[standard] + uvicorn + sqlalchemy + PyJWT + opentelemetry-sdk + openinference-instrumentation-agno + croniter + pytz. Optional DB driver of your choice. Moderate footprint — pydantic v2 + 100+ tool modules + 49 model adapters baked in.

Rust 1.75+ with tokio runtime; ractor for actor runtime. No mandatory database, no Redis, no Postgres, no LangSmith. Every LLM provider, vector store, sandbox (wasmtime/Deno/rquickjs), and MCP client is gated behind a Cargo feature so you only pay for what you use.

Python 3.10+ wheel ships a Claude Code Node.js binary under src/claude_agent_sdk/_bundled/claude (platform-specific). Requires anyio, sniffio, mcp>=1.23, and an Anthropic API key for the subprocess. The bundled artifact makes the wheel chunky and platform-specific.

Node ≥18 (or Bun/Deno), plus mandatory optionalDependency on a per-platform Claude Code binary of 207–233 MB. Multi-arch Docker images install all matching binaries (~460 MB for linux-x64 + linux-arm64 under npm). Also requires @anthropic-ai/sdk + @modelcontextprotocol/sdk + zod as peer deps and optional bubblewrap for sandboxing.

Python 3.10–3.13. Hard deps: crewai-core, crewai-cli, pydantic>=2.11, openai>=2.30, instructor, pdfplumber, regex, opentelemetry-api/sdk, chromadb. Optional: provider SDKs, mcp, e2b/daytona, lancedb, aiosqlite. No bundled binaries; LanceDB writes to ./.memory/ and checkpoints to ./.checkpoints by default.

Go 1.25; small set of direct deps (sonic JSON, kin-openapi, gonja templates, testify). No bundled binaries, no native libs, no required external process. Provider adapters (LLMs, vector stores, tracing) ship as separate eino-ext Go modules so you import only what you need.

note: 4 — Go modules; optional JS CLI for dev
details: Go ≥1.25 with no bundled binaries — everything is pure-Go modules. Optional Node.js + genkit CLI for the dev UI/eval (not in your production binary). Optional GCP credentials, OTel exporter, or Postgres/Firestore depending on plugins chosen.

Python ≥3.10. Core: langchain-core, langgraph-checkpoint, langgraph-sdk, langgraph-prebuilt, xxhash, pydantic. Optional storage backends via separate packages (langgraph-checkpoint-postgres, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite). LLM providers BYO via langchain-* packages. HTTP server requires closed-source langgraph-runtime-inmem/postgres.

Python 3.10+. Core pulls SQLAlchemy[asyncio], httpx, pydantic>=2.8, tiktoken, aiohttp, nltk, tenacity, wrapt, banks, aiosqlite, llama-index-workflows. No bundled binaries; tokenizer is tiktoken. Each LLM/store/tool integration adds its own provider SDK dependency from ~300 separately-versioned packages.

Node.js ≥18 (or Bun/Cloudflare Workers/Vercel Edge), pnpm for dev. Default in-memory store must be replaced for production with @mastra/store-libsql/-pg/etc. Optional vector store, Redis pubsub, OTel/Datadog. The package itself is heavy (>200 source files, packages/core/src/agent/agent.ts is ~7k lines).

Python: pydantic, mcp, opentelemetry-*, httpx, python-dotenv + provider extras (openai/anthropic/azure-identity). .NET: Microsoft.Extensions.AI, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, OpenTelemetry.* + provider SDKs. Optional backing stores via agent-framework-redis, agent-framework-azure-cosmos, Azure AI Search.

Python 3.10+. Core deps: openai>=2.26, pydantic>=2.12, griffelib, typing-extensions, requests, websockets, mcp. No bundled binaries, no native libs beyond pydantic-core wheels. Optional extras for litellm, redis, dapr, mongodb, docker, sandbox providers, etc.

Node.js 22+ (Deno/Bun also supported; Cloudflare Workers experimental). Direct deps: openai SDK, debug, optional zod, optional @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No bundled DB. For default tracing: outbound HTTPS to platform.openai.com.

Required: Python 3.10+, pydantic/pydantic-core/pydantic-graph, genai-prices, opentelemetry-*, anyio. Per-provider SDKs are optional extras (openai/anthropic/google/mistral/groq/cohere/bedrock/xai/huggingface). No required databases or queues; durable execution opts in via temporal/dbos/prefect/restate extras.

Rust edition 2024 with Tokio runtime. HTTP client configurable (defaults reqwest). 26 native provider crates plus 10+ vector-store companion crates, each gated by Cargo features. WASM-compatible (`wasm_compat.rs`). No mandatory DB.

Python ≥3.10. Mandatory: boto3, botocore, docstring_parser, jsonschema, mcp, pydantic, pyyaml, watchdog, opentelemetry-api/sdk/instrumentation-threading. Bedrock default. Optional extras for anthropic, gemini, litellm, llamaapi, mistral, ollama, openai, writer, sagemaker, a2a, bidi.

Node ≥20. Required: @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime, uuid, yaml, @types/json-schema (only Bedrock client is non-trivial). All other providers (Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/Vercel/MCP/Express/A2A/S3/OTel) are optional peer-deps you install if you use them. Browser-bundle tested in CI.

Node v18/20/22 (v22 recommended). pnpm v10+ for dev. No native libs required, no database required by the SDK. Optional LLM provider account and/or Vercel AI Gateway. Frontend adapters for React/Vue/Svelte/Angular/RSC are separate first-party packages.

note: 4 — Cloud Run, one process per app
details: README explicitly recommends containerization and Cloud Run; cmd/launcher/full composes Web UI + REST + A2A + agent-engine emulator into a single Go binary. Pattern is one binary per app deployed as Cloud Run service or GKE deployment, with sessions in Cloud SQL or Vertex Agent Engine. Multi-tenant achieved by namespacing on (AppName, UserID, SessionID).

Canonical pattern is agent_os.serve(app=run:app) which calls uvicorn.run with one process serving many concurrent sessions and many agents. Auth, RBAC, scheduling, tracing are all handled inside this single process. AgentOS provides 50+ endpoints, JWT scopes, RBAC scopes, scheduler, traces, knowledge — production-shaped out of the box.

Docs describe direct vs actor agent shapes but do not prescribe container-per-tenant vs shared process. You embed AutoAgents in whatever Rust binary you build — Axum/Actix/custom. README's Performance section says scalable via multi-agent coordination but refers to in-process actor runtime, not multi-process deployment.

Not stated in the SDK repo. Implicit: every query()/ClaudeSDKClient spawns a new claude subprocess; natural shape is container-per-tenant or one-Python-process-many-CLI-subprocesses-but-one-CLI-per-active-conversation. Repo ships Dockerfile.test for CI but no production Dockerfile or hosted runtime.

Vendor hosting doc recommends one CLI subprocess per session mediated by your HTTP server. attachBridgeSession and runAssistantWorker (alpha) document a worker-per-session pattern with userIdleMs despawn. For pure server-side multi-tenant the practical topology is N session workers per pod each owning one CLI subprocess. No first-party queue or scheduler.

OSS docs assume one Python process running a Crew per request. AMP (Enterprise) recommends GitHub-or-ZIP deploy to their managed runtime where containers spin per crew per automation. No vendor guidance on container-per-tenant vs one-process-many-tenants for the OSS path because OSS has no tenant primitive. production-architecture page discusses crew design patterns, not horizontal scaling.

No vendor-recommended topology document — this is a library, not a platform. CloudWeGo docs implicitly assume one-process-many-tenants with horizontal Pod scaling and BYO ingress; multi-tenancy guidance is minimal. Used inside ByteDance with each Pod owning persistence; equivalent guidance externally lives in user-side platforms.

Go SDK and samples all show one Go binary serving N HTTP routes, each a genkit.Handler(action). samples/cloud_run_deploy.sh targets Google Cloud Run as the canonical hosting model — stateless container instances behind a load balancer. Sessions and conversation state explicitly punted to your DB; tenant identity flows via headers → ContextProvider → core.WithActionContext.

LangGraph Platform docs recommend one-process-many-tenants with horizontal scaling: a fleet of API pods sharing Postgres for state + Redis for pub/sub between API and worker pods. Self-host follows the same pattern (langgraph up Docker compose, K8s Helm chart). Pure-OSS deployments without Platform are BYO HTTP layer.

Not opinionated. The official deployment tutorial at docs/src/content/docs/framework/understanding/deployment/deployment.md literally says TODO. The vendor's recommended path for production multi-agent serving is the separate llama_deploy project (microservice / message-queue runtime around Workflow), which is out of scope of the core repo.

Recommended pattern is one-process-many-tenants: single Mastra instance with all agents/workflows/tools registered at boot; @mastra/server is stateless across requests with state in the storage backend. Deployers under deployers/ package this for Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers, plus deployers/cloud for Mastra Cloud. Resumable streams make session affinity unnecessary.

Vendor documents multiple options with explicit samples: one-process-many-tenants via Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting (AddAIAgent + AgentSessionStore + AIHostAgent for ASP.NET Core / Worker Service); container-per-agent via Foundry Hosted Agents; worker pool / durable orchestration via Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask and Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.AzureFunctions. .NET hosting story maps cleanly onto multi-tenant servers.

note: 2 — uniform one-process examples, no vendor opinion
details: SDK has no vendor opinion on topology. Examples uniformly assume one Python process per host hosting many sessions via asyncio. For horizontal scaling: run N stateless worker processes with a shared store (Postgres via SQLAlchemySession, Redis via RedisSession, MongoDB via MongoDBSession). Each worker can serve any session as long as it can reach the store.

Docs do not prescribe a topology. examples/nextjs reference shows one-process-many-requests embedded in a Next.js Route Handler. Each run() call is request-scoped. Many concurrent runs share one Node process but each owns its own RunState. No built-in worker pool, queue, or cluster mode. Cloudflare Workers documented as experimental.

Not explicitly opinionated; docs treat Agent like a FastAPI app: "Agents are designed for reuse, like FastAPI Apps". UI adapter docs assume one agent instance per ASGI app and one HTTP route per agent endpoint. Production durable patterns are documented for Temporal/DBOS/Prefect via durable_execution extras.

Not opinionated. Rig is a library; the docs offer no production deployment guidance. You ship a Rust binary (typically axum + tokio) and embed Rig inside it. Container-per-tenant vs. one-process-many-tenants is your call.

Not prescribed by the SDK itself but there is an official strandsagents.com docs page for operating agents in production. The hard _invocation_lock that refuses concurrent invocations on a single Agent effectively pushes you toward one Agent instance per active session. No queue/worker primitives in-tree.

Not prescribed in the repo. README and examples treat the SDK as a normal Node library. A host typically would put new Agent(...) instances behind an HTTP layer (Express/Hono/Fastify) — there is no shipped agent runtime daemon. Optional A2A Express server is for inter-agent comms, not user-facing chat.

SDK doesn't ship hosting recipes but Vercel docs and examples/next-agent recommend mounting createAgentUIStreamResponse inside a Next.js API route — one process per Node instance, many tenants per process. For multi-region you scale Next.js horizontally, but all session state lives in your external DB (no in-process session map).

note: 5 — Go binary, sub-second start, tens of MB
details: Sub-second from main() to first r.Run(...) (Go binary linking + genai.NewClient HTTPS handshake). RAM baseline tens of MB; disk ~20–40 MB depending on whether you embed the Web UI. No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK's 20–30s startup. Fastest cold-start of any benchmarked stack.

Cold start = Python interpreter import + FastAPI app + AgentOS init (db lifespan initialises sync and async databases). With Postgres-backed BaseDb this includes SQLAlchemy engine creation and optional table creation/migration. Exact RAM/disk not measured but moderate footprint from pydantic v2 + 100+ tool modules + 49 model adapters.

Release binary cold start is essentially process startup time (typically <100 ms). Memory baseline is small with no embedded vector store and no LLM weights unless you opt into llama.cpp/mistral-rs features. Compile time is the real cost — full workspace builds with all features are significant.

Each connect() runs _check_claude_version (2s timeout), anyio.open_process for the CLI binary, then an initialize control-protocol roundtrip (default 60s timeout, configurable). Empirically a few seconds to ready; cold-start latency is dominated by Node startup. Issue #333 reports 20–30s cold start for some configurations. ~200–500 MB RAM per active session.

Binary footprint 207–233 MB per platform in node_modules. Cold start per subprocess estimated 5–20s warm-process resolve + initialize handshake; the startup()/WarmQuery API exists to amortize this. Per-session RAM baseline ~1 GB resident (issue #268 reports listSessions() alone using 900 MB+). Heaviest of all benchmarked stacks by bytes-on-disk.

Fresh import crewai + Crew.kickoff() is dominated by openai + LiteLLM imports (~0.5–1 s on cold disk) and LanceDB index initialization (~100 ms). No 20–30s startup penalty like Claude Agent SDK. RAM baseline ~150 MB Python interpreter + framework, growing with memory store size.

Startup latency is negligible (Runner construction is struct allocation, adk/runner.go:63-69) — no model warm-up, no checkpoint hydration, no plugin loading. Per-session memory is dominated by runSession.Events accumulating during a run. Disk baseline zero (no on-disk cache, no JSONL persistence, no skill cache unless you build one). Massive cold-start advantage for serverless deployments.

Init cost dominated by plugin Init(ctx) calls (googlegenai.Init is sync HTTP/credential check, typically <1s with cached ADC). Go binaries cold-boot ≪1 s after image pull on Cloud Run. RAM baseline ~30 MB for a minimal binary, growing with model SDKs (Vertex AI client + gRPC adds ~50 MB on first call). No 20–30s startup ceremony.

Pure-OSS embedding has a few hundred ms to import the package and RAM baseline a few tens of MB beyond your model client. LangGraph Platform / self-host: Starlette+Uvicorn worker pods with multi-tenant Postgres connection pool dominating RAM (closed-source server, exact numbers not visible).

Pure-Python import overhead — llama-index-core pulls in SQLAlchemy, pydantic, tiktoken, nltk, banks, httpx, aiohttp (non-trivial). No published baseline RAM figure. Cold start is dominated by your LLM SDK warm-up, not the framework itself.

No public benchmark in-repo. Processor pipeline and registry are lazy-instantiated, but @mastra/core is heavy (>200 source files). Realistic baseline for a 5-agent app: tens of MB RAM, sub-second cold start on Node, longer (~1–2 s) on Cloudflare Workers due to bundle size.

Not advertised explicitly. The framework is a thin .NET assembly / Python package — startup is dominated by provider SDK initialization (AzureCliCredential, OpenAIClient) and any context-provider loading (e.g. scanning skill directories). DevUI lists ports 8080/8090; not for production.

Cold start is low — import agents triggers a chain of openai SDK + pydantic imports; lazy SQLiteSession import. No 20–30s startup like Claude Agent SDK. RAM baseline modest (~100–150 MB for Python interpreter + pydantic + openai SDK). Disk baseline tens of MB; SQLiteSession defaults to :memory: (zero disk) unless pointed at a file.

No bundled binary — the SDK is pure JS/TS so startup is whatever your Node process takes (~200–400 ms typical). RAM baseline minimal beyond Node baseline; sessions live in memory by default (MemorySession). No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK issue #333 (slow bootstrap).

Pure-Python import — sub-second once Python interpreter is warm. No bundled binaries, no LLM subprocess. RAM baseline = whatever pydantic + the chosen provider SDK brings. Cold start dominated by Python and provider SDK imports, not by pydantic-ai itself.

Ships first-party REST server (`server/adkrest/`) with `POST /run_sse` (SSE) for streaming and `GET /run_live` (WebSocket via gorilla/websocket) for bidirectional live, plus a one-shot `POST /run`. Library-only, no bundled server. Separate `AutoAgents-CLI` repo wraps it but is out of scope. `run_stream` returns an in-process iterator; serialization to SSE/WS is host work.
SDK is library-only over a stdin/stdout CLI subprocess. No FastAPI/Starlette adapter shipped. Users wrap `query()`/`ClaudeSDKClient` in their own SSE endpoint.
Library-only. Browser sub-export accepts `websocket: { url }` but the WS server is the user's responsibility. The `bridge.mjs` path targets claude.ai's hosted endpoint, not a server you run yourself.
OSS framework ships no HTTP server. AMP (closed/managed) provides `POST /kickoff` with webhook-based event push (not SSE/WS chat). Self-hosters wrap `Crew(stream=True)` themselves.
No `net/http` serving in core eino; no shipped server. In-process runtime uses `*AsyncIterator[*AgentEvent]` channel; you write the SSE handler yourself.
`genkit.Handler` returns an `http.HandlerFunc` with SSE via `?stream=true` or `Accept: text/event-stream`. No WebSocket support, no HTTP/2 push. Each flow is mounted manually on your `http.ServeMux`.

`langgraph-api` (closed-source / source-available paid platform) exposes SSE over `POST /threads/{tid}/runs/stream` and `GET .../stream` for resume. OSS repo ships only the runtime, checkpointers, client SDK and CLI shell — not the server.
`llama-index-core` is library-only. Recommended path is FastAPI + SSE over `handler.stream_events()`. Companion `llama_deploy` is a separate project.

Several optional servers: DevUI (FastAPI, OpenAI Responses-compatible, beta `sample app, not for production`), AG-UI (rc, SSE), A2A (beta), Foundry hosting, Azure Functions, ASP.NET Core building blocks. SSE is standard. No single canonical multi-tenant production HTTP surface yet.
Library only; `Runner.run_streamed` yields a Python async iterator. Realtime sibling speaks WebSocket to OpenAI's hosted realtime API, not to your clients. No stock SSE adapter.

No first-party HTTP server. The `@openai/agents-extensions/ai-sdk-ui` package adapts a `StreamedRunResult` to Vercel AI SDK's SSE format, so SSE is achievable as an extension wrapper. No bundled server framework.

Two first-party surfaces: `agent.to_web()` returns a Starlette app and `UIAdapter.dispatch_request` plugs into Starlette/FastAPI. Both stream SSE via `_event_stream.py`. `to_web()` is positioned for local dev; UIAdapter is the production composable.
Rig is library-only. `Stream<MultiTurnStreamItem<R>>` is in-process; SSE/WebSocket framing is the user's job. No SSE adapter shipped.
Default is library-only. Optional `A2AServer` (FastAPI) wraps an Agent as Google A2A endpoint for agent-to-agent comms, plus experimental bidi voice. No first-party REST/SSE chat server.

`createAgentUIStreamResponse` / `pipeAgentUIStreamToResponse` return SSE-shaped `Response`/pipe a `ServerResponse`. `JsonToSseTransformStream` is the canonical wire format with `x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v2` header. SSE only; user mounts in Next.js/Express/Hono.

Wire is `data: <json Event>\n\n` for every `models.Event`, covering user/model messages, function calls, function responses, partials, errors. Linked to `FunctionCall.ID` for tool tracking. No explicit start/end SSE frame types but the iterator's lifecycle is observable.

SSE frames carry typed events: `RunStarted`, `ToolCallStarted`, `ToolCallCompleted`, `RunCompleted` (with metrics), `RunPausedEvent`, etc. Each is `event: <name>\ndata: <json>` shaped. Tool calls keyed by `tool_call_id`.

Rich `Event` enum (`ToolCallRequested`, `ToolCallCompleted`, `StreamChunk::ToolUseInputDelta`, etc.) all `Serialize/Deserialize`, but only available in-process via `Environment::subscribe_events`. Host writes the wire format.
In-process `Message` dataclasses (Assistant/User/Tool/Stream/Task events) are rich and stable; partial messages available via `include_partial_messages=True`. Wire encoding to SSE is consumer-side.

Iterator yields fully typed `SDKMessage`s including `SDKAssistantMessage`, tool progress, partial messages, system init. Wire framing left to user; recommended pattern is one SDKMessage per SSE `data:` frame.

AMP webhook delivers batched typed events (151 `BaseEvent` subclasses including `llm_call_started`, `tool_usage_finished`). Doc explicitly notes order is not guaranteed and recommends `realtime=true` at cost. In-process `StreamChunk` available for self-hosted but no SSE framing shipped.
`*AsyncIterator[*AgentEvent]` provides rich typed events in-process; serialization is host code. No first-party wire format.

Multiple stream modes (`values`, `updates`, `messages`, `messages/partial`, `messages/complete`, `checkpoints`, `tasks`, `tasks/result`, `custom`, `debug`, `error`, `metadata`, `end`, `feedback`) selectable per call. Events keyed for resume by `last_event_id`.
`handler.stream_events()` yields typed Pydantic `Event` models including `AgentStream`, tool events, `InputRequiredEvent`. Wire framing to SSE is BYO.

DevUI wire format is OpenAI Responses-compatible (`response.created`, `response.output_item.added`, `response.completed`, function_call_arguments.delta, function_approval events). AG-UI uses typed AG-UI protocol events.
`stream_events()` yields `RawResponsesStreamEvent`, `RunItemStreamEvent`, `AgentUpdatedStreamEvent`, etc. — rich and typed but serialization to SSE is host code.
`StreamedRunResult` iterates `RunStreamEvent` including `raw_model_stream_event` deltas. `ai-sdk-ui` extension converts to Vercel UI Message stream. No built-in wire framing.

`UIAdapter` emits Vercel AI Data Stream or AG-UI typed events: `start`, `text-delta`, `tool-call`, `tool-result`, `finish` with usage. Underlying loop yields typed `PartDeltaEvent`/`ToolCallPartDelta`.
`MultiTurnStreamItem` and `StreamedAssistantContent` are `Serialize+Deserialize` (serde `tag=type`) so usable on the wire, but Rig itself ships no serializer/handler.
`agent.stream_async` yields typed events (`init_event_loop`, `tool_use_stream`, `message`, `result`, etc.) with `toolUseId` linkage. Wire framing is host code.

`agent.stream()` yields `BeforeInvocationEvent`, `ContentBlockEvent`, `ToolStreamUpdateEvent`, `AfterToolCallEvent`, `InterruptEvent`, `AgentResultEvent`. Each event class has `toJSON()` for wire serialization. SDK does not enforce a wire format.

Canonical wire format `x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v2` with `start`, `start-step`, `text-delta`, `tool-input-start`, `tool-input-delta`, `tool-input-available`, `tool-output-available`, `tool-approval-request/response`, `finish-step`, `finish`, `[DONE]`. Client `useChat` consumes this natively.

Default OSS REST router registers no auth middleware (`handler.go:37-60`). An example `AuthInterceptor` exists for the A2A path but hardcodes the user. Tenant scoping flows through user-supplied `stateDelta` and `context.Context` middleware you wrap yourself.

No HTTP boundary to terminate auth at.

OSS: BYO entirely. AMP provides bearer-token-per-automation but no first-party JWT/RBAC at request boundary.
No HTTP layer means no auth boundary; you wire your own.

`langgraph-api` invokes `@auth.authenticate` on every request and `@auth.on.*` per-resource handlers apply filters. Identity flows into `runtime.context` / `ctx.user.identity`. Fully terminates at the API boundary.
No HTTP layer; auth is the host's responsibility.

DevUI ships bearer-token auth on by default with `DEVUI_AUTH_TOKEN`; `--no-auth` only for loopback. AG-UI / A2A / Foundry / Functions rely on host framework middleware. No first-party JWT-validation/tenant-scoping in production-positioned surfaces.
No SDK-level auth surface; host middleware validates and feeds identity into `RunContextWrapper.context`.
No auth handling in SDK; host middleware does JWT/API-key validation before calling `run()`.
Docs explicitly say `Treat the adapter endpoint as an internal backend service, running it inside your own authenticated route handler`. The adapter intentionally is not an auth boundary.
No HTTP surface; auth is the host's middleware.
No first-party auth boundary; A2A and BYO HTTP both delegate to the host.
`A2AExpressServerConfig.userBuilder` integrates with `@a2a-js/sdk`'s `UserBuilder` for per-request user resolution on the A2A path only. BYO HTTP path delegates entirely.
SDK does not parse `Authorization` headers; host framework (Next.js middleware, Hono auth, etc.) terminates auth before calling `createAgentUIStreamResponse`.

`GET .../sessions/{session_id}` returns full event list for client replay. No dedicated `/resume` endpoint — resumption is implicit by reusing the same `sessionId` on `/run_sse`. Live (bidi) path uses Gemini's `SessionResumptionConfig`.

`POST /agents/{agent_id}/runs/{run_id}/resume` reconnects to in-flight `asyncio.Task` and replays buffered SSE then continues live. `GET .../runs/{run_id}` returns persisted run, and `GET .../sessions/{session_id}/runs` lists runs per session.
No HTTP surface; in-process there is no resume primitive either.
`ClaudeAgentOptions.resume=<session_id>` re-opens a session on disk (or via SessionStore). There is no resume endpoint — it is a parameter when spawning a new client.
`query({ options: { resume: sessionId } })` and `resumeSessionAt: messageUuid` are SDK options; you build the endpoint. SDK provides logic, not the route.
OSS: `Crew.from_checkpoint(config)` is the in-process resume API; you wire `POST /sessions/:id/resume` yourself. AMP: redeploy and re-kickoff; replay via Studio UI.
`Runner.Resume(ctx, checkPointID)` exists at the Go API level; HTTP exposure is your job.

`X-Genkit-Stream-Id` request header re-subscribes to a durable stream via `StreamManager` (in-memory or Firestore-backed). First call writes the stream id; subsequent calls replay from durable store. No general session-reopen endpoint.

`GET /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/stream?last_event_id=...` resumes the SSE stream from last delivered event id (when created with `stream_resumable: true`). Plus state endpoints `GET /threads/{tid}/state`, historical `state/{checkpoint_id}`, and HITL resume via `command: {resume: ...}`.
Pattern is to serialize `Context` to your store keyed by `session_id` and pass `ctx=` to `workflow.run(...)`. No endpoint shipped.

`GET /agents/:id/observe-stream` attaches mid-stream as observer (resumable, multi-client). `POST /agents/:id/resume-stream` resumes suspended runs (generic tool.suspend). `GET /agents/:id/subscribe-thread` SSE subscribes a thread's runs.

DevUI: resending same `conversation` id pulls thread history automatically. AG-UI propagates `availableInterrupts` and `resume` metadata via `AGUIChatClient`. No dedicated replay/re-attach to an in-flight stream.
`RunResult.to_state().to_json()` + `RunState.from_json(agent, json)` is the primitive. No endpoint shipped; host builds `POST /runs/{id}/resume`.
`RunState.toString()` + `RunState.fromString(agent, str)` round-trips state for HITL/resume; the endpoint and persistence are BYO (next.js example only).

No dedicated resume endpoint; clients send full `messages` history on every request (Vercel AI / AG-UI design). For server-authoritative history persist by `conversation_id` and pass `message_history` to the adapter.
With `ConversationMemory`, calling `agent.prompt(...).conversation(\user-123\")` again resumes. No HTTP endpoint shipped."
`session_manager=FileSessionManager(session_id=...)` restores prior messages. `Agent.take_snapshot` / `load_snapshot` are building blocks. No endpoint.

`SessionManager.restoreSnapshot({ target: agent })` hydrates an Agent from `snapshot_latest`. Resume an interrupted run via `agent.invoke([interruptResponseBlock])`. Replay of past events is not a primitive.

Recipe in `examples/next/app/api/chat/[id]/stream/route.ts` uses third-party `resumable-stream` + Redis with `createResumableStreamContext`. Re-attaches via `GET /api/chat/[id]/stream`. Not part of `ai` proper but documented and supported.

SSE handler reads `req.Context()` so the client closing the SSE connection cancels the context and propagates into `Runner.Run`. No explicit `DELETE /run/{id}` endpoint; no AbortSignal framing inside SSE.

`POST /agents/{agent_id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel?session_id=...` calls `agent.acancel_run` which sets a cancellation flag observed by `raise_if_cancelled` checkpoints inside the run loop (multiple safe points).
`Environment::shutdown` drains the whole runtime; per-task cancel is BYO via a `CancellationToken` you check in a hook. No HTTP cancel endpoint.

`ClaudeSDKClient.interrupt()` sends a `control_request: interrupt` to the CLI which handles mid-LLM-call / mid-tool-call cancellation. `stop_task(task_id)` cancels a specific sub-agent. No HTTP endpoint, but a stable primitive.

`Query.interrupt()` and `Query.close()` over the JSON control protocol (`SDKControlInterruptRequest`); also `Options.abortController.abort()`. HTTP cancel endpoint is BYO mapping `DELETE` to `q.interrupt()`.

OSS: no in-process cancel API at all. `Crew.kickoff()` runs to completion; the bus surfaces `SigTermEvent`/`SigIntEvent` but no `Crew.cancel()`. AMP has no documented mid-flight cancel endpoint either. Real gap for long-running agent runs.
No first-class cancel API; cancellation is via `context.CancelFunc` propagating through Go ctx. No abort-run endpoint shipped.

Standard HTTP request cancellation propagates via Go `context.Context` for non-durable runs. Durable streaming detaches with `context.WithoutCancel`, so closing the connection does NOT cancel the underlying flow. Dev UI reflection API has cancel for traced actions but is dev-mode.

`POST /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/cancel?action=interrupt|rollback&wait=0|1` halts and persists an interrupt marker or rolls back state. `on_disconnect: cancel` option auto-cancels on SSE disconnect at creation time.
`WorkflowHandler.cancel_run()` is the in-process API; HTTP endpoint exposure is BYO.

`AbortSignal` is wired from HTTP layer into `agent.stream(..., { abortSignal })`; dropping the connection cancels. No explicit `DELETE /runs/:id`. `POST /agents/:id/signals` can carry an application-defined stop signal if the agent's signal schema includes one.
DevUI exposes `POST /v1/responses/{response_id}/cancel`. Also auto-cancels on client disconnect. AG-UI / A2A / Foundry rely on host conventions.
`RunResultStreaming._cancel_mode` (`none`|`immediate`|`after_turn`) and `result.cancel()` from the handler are the primitives. HTTP endpoint is BYO.
`options.signal: AbortSignal` propagates into model and tool calls. Pattern: attach `request.signal` to `options.signal`. No DELETE/cancel endpoint.
`StreamedRunResult.cancel()` interrupts streaming. HTTP-side cancellation works via Starlette closing the connection. No explicit DELETE endpoint.
In-process cancel by dropping the Stream or via `AbortHandle`/`Abortable` from `streaming.rs`. No HTTP cancel endpoint.
`Agent.cancel()` flips a `threading.Event` checked at safe points (during model streaming, before tool execution); returns `stop_reason='cancelled'`. HTTP endpoint exposure is BYO.

`agent.cancel()` flips internal AbortController; `InvokeOptions.cancelSignal: AbortSignal` composes external signals (bind to `req.signal`); cooperative cancellation inside tools via `context.agent.cancelSignal.aborted`. Endpoint is BYO.

Same-server: `chat.stop()` aborts local fetch, mapping to `request.signal` which propagates to `streamText({ abortSignal })`. Multi-server: documented pattern `DELETE /api/chat/:id/stream` writes `canceledAt` to DB; running POST polls via throttled `onChunk` and aborts. Recipe shown in next.js example.

Forwards Gemini's `Partial == true` events on `FunctionCall.Args` as the same `models.Event` frame with `partial:true` and the in-progress args map. Downstream frames complete the args. No dedicated `tool-input-start/delta/end` event taxonomy.

`ToolCallStartedEvent` carries the complete tool call at the moment it is parsed; partial-JSON streaming depends on the model adapter (OpenAI/Anthropic provider-side feature). Agno surfaces the final `tool_args` on `ToolCallStarted`.
`StreamChunk::ToolUseInputDelta { index, partial_json }` emitted in-process while LLM streams tool args. Provider-dependent (Anthropic, OpenAI tool-streaming). Wire framing BYO.
`StreamEvent` carries raw Anthropic SSE events including `input_json_delta`, enabling progressive `Bash command: ls -l /var/` style UIs. Bug-fixed in 0.1.48 for env-var wiring.
Emits `SDKPartialAssistantMessage` wrapping raw `BetaRawMessageStreamEvent` (sdk.d.ts:3226). `input_json_delta` events progressively reveal tool input JSON character-by-character.

`LLMStreamChunkEvent` carries `tool_call: ToolCall | None` with `function.arguments: str` accumulated incrementally. `StreamChunk(chunk_type=TOOL_CALL, tool_call=ToolCallChunk(arguments=...))`. AMP webhook `llm_stream_chunk` carries the same shape.

Tool-call deltas come through streamed `*schema.Message` chunks with `ToolCalls.Index` for merging via `schema.ConcatMessages`. No separate `tool-arg-fragment` event type; you extract from message chunks yourself.

`ToolRequest.Partial bool` flag flows through `ModelResponseChunk` for providers that stream tool args (Gemini supported). No dedicated tool-input-start/delta/end sub-event taxonomy. Plugin-level support varies.
`AIMessageChunk` events on `stream_mode='messages'` carry `tool_call_chunks` field with progressive tool args; final validated args appear on assembled `AIMessage.tool_calls[*].args`.
The LLM's streamed delta of a tool call surfaces via `AgentStream.tool_calls` as the model emits it. Granularity depends on underlying LLM integration.

Three chunk types: `tool-call-input-streaming-start { toolCallId, toolName }`, `tool-call-delta { toolCallId, argsTextDelta }`, `tool-call-input-streaming-end { toolCallId }`. UI can render partial args in real time.
DevUI streams `response.function_call_arguments.delta` (OpenAI Responses convention). AG-UI behaves the same.
OpenAI Responses API emits `response.function_call_arguments.delta` events; they flow through `RawResponsesStreamEvent` directly. End-to-end example at `examples/basic/stream_function_call_args.py`.

Raw model events surface as `RunRawModelStreamEvent` with underlying provider event under `event.data.event` — partial tool args visible if provider streams them. SDK does not normalize into a typed `tool-call-delta` event.
`ToolCallPartDelta` emits incremental `args_delta` strings/dicts via `PartDeltaEvent`. UI adapters (Vercel AI / AG-UI) surface them in their respective dialects.
`StreamedAssistantContent::ToolCallDelta { id, internal_call_id, content }` where content is `Name(String)` or `Delta(String)`. Wire serialization BYO.
`ToolUseStreamEvent` yields `{type: 'tool_use_stream', delta: {...}, current_tool_use: {toolUseId, name, input}}` as the model builds tool arguments. Wire framing is BYO.

Model providers yield `ModelContentBlockDeltaEvent` with `delta: { type: 'toolUseInputDelta', input: '<partial json>' }`. Wrapped as `ModelStreamUpdateEvent`; full `ToolUseBlock` yielded later as `ContentBlockEvent`.

Canonical wire chunks `tool-input-start`, `tool-input-delta` (with `inputTextDelta`), `tool-input-available`. Client `useChat` automatically updates `ToolUIPart.state` from `input-streaming` to `input-available`.

Tool calls `ctx.RequestConfirmation(hint, payload)`; framework emits a `FunctionCall` with name `adk_request_confirmation`. Client decodes, asks user, replies via `/run_sse` with a `functionResponse` matching the original call id. Runner re-runs the tool with the verdict. No separate `/approve` endpoint and no observable pause status (client infers from `LongRunningToolIDs`).

`@tool(requires_confirmation=True | requires_user_input=True | external_execution=True)` pauses the loop and emits `RunPausedEvent` with `status=RunStatus.paused`. Client inspects `run_response.active_requirements`, sends `requirement.confirm/reject`, then `POST /agents/{aid}/runs/{rid}/continue` resumes. Also admin-approvals track under `/approvals/...`.
`AgentHooks::on_tool_call` returning `HookOutcome::Abort` skips the call but there is no pause-and-wait-for-external-approval state — the run cannot be persisted and resumed.

Intra-process: `can_use_tool` callback resolves via `control_response`; for cross-request HITL the client must stay alive in process. `PreToolUse` hook can return `permissionDecision: 'defer'` so `ResultMessage.deferred_tool_use` lets a different process inspect what was deferred.

`canUseTool` is the HITL primitive: SDK awaits a Promise from your callback (correlated by `toolUseID`); for client-visible pause your handler emits a custom SSE frame and resolves the inner Promise on `/approve`. No separate pause-state observable to the client.

Best-in-class design at the Flow layer: `@human_feedback` with `HumanFeedbackProvider`; custom async providers raise `HumanFeedbackPending` which auto-persists state and returns the pending status. External system later calls `flow.resume(feedback=...)`. Tool-level `request_human_input` is console-only. AMP ships a Flow HITL Management UI.

Tools call `adk.Interrupt(ctx, info)` or `adk.StatefulInterrupt`; runner saves checkpoint and emits `InterruptedAgentEvent`. Caller resumes via `runner.ResumeWithParams(ctx, checkpointID, &ResumeParams{Targets: ...})`. No shipped HITL HTTP route.

Two-call protocol: first call yields a model response with `metadata.interrupt` and `finishReason='interrupted'`; second call resumes via `transferTool.RespondWith(part, ...)` or `RestartWith(part, WithResumedMetadata(...))`. Client must persist response/history.

`POST /threads/{tid}/runs/stream` with `command: {resume: 'approved' | {interrupt_id: value}}` is first-class. `StateSnapshot.interrupts` is the observable pause state. State edits via `POST /threads/{tid}/state` compose cleanly with resume.

`ctx.wait_for_event(HumanResponseEvent, waiter_id=..., waiter_event=InputRequiredEvent(...), requirements={...})` pauses inside a tool. Client sees `InputRequiredEvent` on the stream and replies via `handler.ctx.send_event(HumanResponseEvent(...))`. Cleanly typed.

`POST /agents/:id/approve-tool-call` and `decline-tool-call` (plus `-generate` variants for non-streaming) take `{runId, toolCallId}` and return a new SSE stream that resumes execution. `/resume-stream` handles generic tool.suspend; `/observe-stream` lets observers attach mid-stream.

Tools with `approval_mode='always_require'` emit `function_approval_request`; client inspects `result.user_input_requests`, builds `function_approval_response(approved=True|False)`, re-invokes `agent.run(approval_response, session=session)`. DevUI exposes `response.function_approval.requested/responded` events.

Tools mark `function_tool(needs_approval=True | callable)`; `result.interruptions` yields `ToolApprovalItem`s; serialize `RunResult.to_state().to_json()`, on approval `state.approve(interruption)` and re-run. MCP tools have `require_approval='always'|'never'|dict|callable`.

Tools with `needsApproval: true` return `result.interruptions: RunToolApprovalItem[]`. Serialize `result.state`, present approvals, then `state.approve(interruption)` / `state.reject(interruption)` and re-run. End-to-end example shipped.

`@agent.tool(requires_approval=True)` or `raise ApprovalRequired` yields `DeferredToolRequests`. Client gathers approvals, runs again with `deferred_tool_results=DeferredToolResults(approvals={call_id: True}, calls={call_id: ...})`. `HandleDeferredToolCalls` capability allows inline resolution. Explicitly typed primitives.
`PauseControl` only gates polling; no tool-approval-verdict channel. For HITL you implement `on_tool_call -> Skip { reason }` to reject and ask user to re-submit. Cannot persist and resume.

`BeforeToolCallEvent` is `_Interruptible`; a hook raises `InterruptException(Interrupt(name=..., reason=...))` and the agent yields `EventLoopStopEvent` with `stop_reason='interrupt'`. Client re-invokes `agent('...')` with `list[InterruptResponseContent]`. State persisted via session manager.

`context.interrupt({name, reason})` from a tool stores `pendingToolExecution` state and emits `InterruptEvent`s; client resumes with `agent.invoke([{type: 'interruptResponseContent', toolUseId, name, response}])`. New `interventions` subsystem ships structured `Confirm` actions wrapping the interrupt machinery.

Server emits `tool-approval-request` chunk for tools that returned `'user-approval'`. Client `chat.addToolApprovalResponse({id, approved, reason})` then re-POSTs the messages (auto-trigger via `sendAutomaticallyWhen`). No dedicated `/approve` endpoint — same `POST /api/chat` carries everything. Correlated by `approvalId`.

Runner is stateless w.r.t. sessions; each Run looks up session via sessionService, with isolation enforced at storage layer (GORM Transaction + stale-session optimistic concurrency). Single-writer per session semantics prevent state bleed. Live (bidi) sessions are pod-local, requiring sticky sessions.

Each run/arun call creates its own RunContext; Agent is shared but mostly immutable. Concurrent invocations on the same Agent are safe under async; sessions are keyed by session_id and isolated via DB. AgentOS hosts many agents/sessions with no in-process bleeding.

Runtime does not model sessions as first-class. Each BaseAgent has its own memory; if you share an agent across sessions, memory bleeds. No tenant-scoped isolation primitives - you must build per-session topics yourself.

Isolation enforced at OS subprocess boundary: each session is its own claude CLI process with its own cwd, env, JSONL transcript path. State cannot bleed between subprocesses but shared Python tool handlers share closures/globals. No in-process multi-tenant primitive.

State bleeds across tenants if you reuse a single subprocess. The SDK does not enforce isolation - you must spawn one subprocess per (tenant, session). Known concurrency hazard with SDK MCP servers (#122). Subprocess-per-session is the only safe model.

Multiple Crew instances each have their own id/memory/tools, BUT the event bus is a process-wide singleton and hooks are registered globally. A hook for tenant A fires for tenant B too. No (tenant, hook) scoping primitive.

Isolation enforced by context: each Runner.Run seeds a fresh runContext with its own runSession; mutexes guard internal maps. Parallel sub-agents fork/join the context. Risk: shared state outside runSession.Values is not isolated by the framework.

Each request gets a fresh context.Context (Go HTTP convention). Genkit registry is shared but concurrency-safe-for-reads after Init. No shared mutable session state on the Genkit object; sessions stored in your session.Store[S] implementation.

PregelLoop is one Python instance per run; state lives in checkpointer keyed on thread_id. Inside langgraph_api, @auth.on.* filters enforce resource-scoping at the data layer. BaseStore namespaces can be tenant-scoped by convention but not enforced.
Each workflow.run() creates a new Context (unless explicitly resumed). Sessions are isolated by construction. Context.store is a per-context KV with no global sharing.

RequestContext, MessageList, and SaveQueueManager are all per-call/per-thread. Reserved requestContext keys (MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY, MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY) are server-controlled and cannot be spoofed at HTTP layer. Tool authors must avoid module-level mutable state.

AgentSession holds session_id and per-session mutable state shared with providers. Agents are typically singletons, only sessions are per-conversation. .NET AgentSessionStateBag uses concurrent dictionary entries. State bleed only on anti-pattern usage.

Isolation per Session instance (session_id bound at store layer) and per RunContextWrapper (fresh dataclass per Runner.run). Approvals are per-RunContextWrapper. Cross-session bleeding not possible inside SDK unless app shares mutable state via TContext.

Each run() invocation constructs a fresh RunState. RunContext<TContext> carries app context; no shared runtime to bleed across runs. Approvals/usage shared between parent/forked nested contexts, but app context shared by reference.

Fresh RunContext per run, plus a ContextVar _CURRENT_RUN_CONTEXT scoped via set_current_run_context so concurrent runs in same process don't bleed. Toolset.for_run lets a toolset spawn fresh instance per run for state isolation.

Agent state is largely immutable (model, preamble, static_context, hooks). Mutable surface is ToolServerHandle (Arc<RwLock>) shared across uses. Conversation memory is per-session per backend. Per-call PromptRequest clones agent data so concurrent prompts isolated.

Each Agent holds its own messages/state/tool_registry/hooks/locks/metrics. Agent.stream_async uses threading.Lock that throws ConcurrencyException on concurrent invocations of same instance. UNSAFE_REENTRANT mode opt-in. One Agent per session is required.

Agent.invoke acquires a lock and throws ConcurrentInvocationError if called concurrently on same instance. All state (messages, appState, modelState, registries, hooks) is per-instance. Multi-tenant fan-out requires per-request new Agent(...).

No in-process session bag in `ai`; each request has its own JS scope, messages, runtimeContext. No shared mutable state that one tenant could leak to another, provided messages and runtimeContext come from request scope.

Session state externalized to database (or Vertex Agent Engine), so N pods share session pool. Stale-session check prevents lost updates from racing pods. No leader election. Live (bidi) sessions are pod-local requiring sticky sessions.

Stateless workers share session pool via same database (PostgresDb or AsyncPostgresDb). Session keyed by session_id (UUID). No general leader election, but scheduler uses DB-backed leader election via agno_schedules rows and SchedulePoller claiming locks.
Runtime is SingleThreadedRuntime, no leader election, no distributed lock, no shared store. 'N pods serve same session pool' pattern is BYO entirely. No primitives provided.

No leader election, no shared coordinator. SessionStore adapter is the only shared-state primitive, and it is append-only - concurrent writes to same session from two pods would interleave unsafely. SDK assumes one process owns one session at a time. SessionKey.project_key is documented sharding lever.

SessionStore interface plus Postgres adapter (examples/session-stores/postgres/) lets any pod resume any session ID. forkSession is store-aware. No leader election; pods can serve different sessions but not the same session pool without external store.

OSS: no shared state, no leader election, no message-queue support. Two pods running same crew code do not share state (LanceDB/SQLite are local). Externalize memory backend or implement custom checkpoint BaseProvider yourself. AMP solves this by hosting the runtime.

Stateless Go binary scales trivially. For shared state across pods, your CheckPointStore implementation is the seam - point all pods at same Postgres CheckPointStore. Leader election, locking, partition assignment not provided - layer optimistic concurrency on top of your store.

Stateless workers replicate behind Cloud Run/GKE. FirestoreSessionStore lets multiple instances read/write same session via Firestore concurrency. For Postgres-backed Store, you handle locking. No leader election, no cross-instance coordination.

All N workers point to same Postgres PostgresSaver; thread_id is partition key. Pregel loop on any worker replays from persisted checkpoint. Inside langgraph_api: run queue serializes work per thread via multitask strategy. OSS: BYO queue but checkpointer is first-class.

BYO in OSS framework: serialize Context (ctx.to_dict()) and stash in your store (Postgres/Redis), rehydrate on next request from any worker. llama_deploy provides hosted control-plane + queue but is separate repo.

Stateless workers share storage backend; no leader election. Resumable streams let any worker pick up in-progress run because workflow snapshot lives in storage. Suspended HITL state durable via workflow snapshots.

AgentSessionStore abstraction allows N pods to share Cosmos/Redis. CosmosCheckpointStorage and CosmosChatHistoryProvider designed for this. DurableTask provides leader-elected, queue-backed orchestration. Both stateless+shared-store and durable orchestrator paths supported.

Stateless workers + shared store. 10 session backends (SQLAlchemy, Redis, MongoDB, Dapr, OpenAIConversations) live in shared external store. Sticky routing not required if store is consistent. No leader election or centralized run scheduler. Some OpenAI conversation-lock retry logic only.

Stateless: as long as session state lives in external store (custom Session impl backed by Postgres/Redis), any number of pods serve same session pool. No leader election. RunState.toString/fromString serializes paused run to any KV store. nextjs example uses generic db().set.

Stateless: N Python workers all serve same logical Agent instance; user owns message_history storage (DB/Redis/file) and re-passes per request. Durable execution via Temporal/DBOS/Prefect provides per-workflow horizontal recovery.
Not provided by Rig itself. Multi-pod scaling is responsibility of caller's deployment (e.g., axum behind LB); shared state goes through whatever ConversationMemory backend you ship.

Stateless workers: keep Agent instances ephemeral and rehydrate from shared SessionRepository. SDK ships FileSessionManager, S3SessionManager, RepositorySessionManager. No leader election or cluster-aware coordination - SDK is unopinionated.

No leader election, no built-in shared state. Horizontal scaling means N stateless Node processes behind LB, each loading session state from S3Storage (or other SnapshotStorage) on demand. No worker registration/heartbeat/queue.

Standard stateless-worker model: N Node processes (Next.js/Fargate/Cloud Run/Vercel Functions), each pulls session state from shared store (Postgres/Redis/S3/Blob). No leader election, no shared in-memory map. Canonical durable-stream pattern via resumable-stream + Redis.

First-party Pub/Sub and Eventarc trigger controllers in REST server, with semaphore concurrency limiter and exponential-backoff retries (RetriableRunner). Long-running tools supported via IsLongRunning() pause/resume. No in-box cron; wire Cloud Scheduler -> Pub/Sub -> ADK trigger.

First-party: ScheduleManager + SchedulePoller + ScheduleExecutor (croniter-driven) with DB-stored cron schedules. Background agent runs via arun(background=True) produce resumable SSE streams with /resume endpoint. FastAPI BackgroundTasks for hooks. Memory tasks spawned in threads/asyncio.
Not provided. No cron, no schedulers, no webhook receivers. Long-running background work via your own tokio::spawn through Topic<Task>. No first-party primitive.
Not provided as host-level scheduler. AgentDefinition.background:bool is only a sub-agent hint for the CLI. No cron, no webhook trigger, no agent-as-background-worker primitive.

Background sub-agents via AgentDefinition.background and AgentInput.run_in_background (parent turn completes immediately, task_notification fires on completion). Background Bash with run_in_background. AssistantWorkerOptions.scheduling.dir polls scheduled_tasks.json every 10s - local-only filesystem cron, not distributed.

OSS: BYO entirely - kickoff() is blocking, nothing schedules anything. AMP (commercial): first-party Automations + Triggers (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Outlook, HubSpot, Salesforce, Slack, Zapier, Webhook, Cron). Vendor-managed; no equivalent in OSS repo.
Not provided. No cron, no webhook trigger system, no scheduled-job framework. Use Go stdlib time.AfterFunc/Ticker or a job library (Asynq, Temporal, Cloud Tasks) in your host.

BackgroundModel abstraction and GenerateOperation for long-running model ops (video/Imagen) - poll with CheckModelOperation; for model calls only, not general tasks. Durable streaming via StreamManager (experimental) keeps flows running across HTTP client disconnect. Cron/webhooks BYO.

Pure OSS: not provided - BYO Celery/arq/Temporal/cron. LangGraph Platform (closed-source): ships crons (crons.create/search/delete) and webhooks (run create accepts webhook URL). Platform queue persists scheduled runs in Postgres.
Not provided - BYO (Celery, Temporal, RQ, your own asyncio task).

Three first-party mechanisms: schedulers (Mastra({scheduler}) with cron-like jobs, /api/scheduled-jobs routes), background tasks (disableBackgroundTasks flag, backgroundTaskCheckStep, dedicated chunk family), webhooks/channels (channels/slack, channels/discord packages wire agents into chat events).

Cron/trigger BYO via Azure Functions hosting (Timer/HTTP/MCPTool triggers). Long-running background via Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask treats each agent run as durable orchestration with replay-on-crash. Python equivalent in agent-framework-durabletask (beta).

Not provided - BYO. No scheduler, no cron, no webhook trigger, no long-running background-agent runtime. Optional temporal extra integrates Temporal workflows for durable orchestration but is separate runtime you stand up. Report flags this as biggest architectural gap.
Not provided. No cron, no webhook trigger primitives, no queues. Run a worker process (BullMQ, AWS SQS, etc.) and call run() from inside it.
Not provided directly - BYO via Temporal scheduling, Prefect deployments, DBOS workflows, or any external scheduler. The framework only provides the agent runtime.
Not provided. No cron, no webhook trigger, no background agent. Tokio runtime can spawn your own tasks but Rig offers no scheduling abstraction.
Not provided - BYO. Library is invocation-driven; nothing schedules cron or webhook triggers. (strands-agents-tools ships cron.py as a tool the agent uses, but tool-side not runtime-side.)
Not provided - BYO. No cron primitive, no webhook trigger surface. Use BullMQ/Cloudflare Queues/etc. and call agent.invoke() inside the worker handler.
Not provided. No cron, no scheduler, no webhook trigger primitive. Use your host (Vercel Cron, Cloud Scheduler, Trigger.dev) and invoke agent.generate() from there.

Triggers ship a semaphore-based concurrency limiter (MaxConcurrentRuns) - a thin worker pool. Beyond this, runtime assumes short-lived HTTP request scope. Long runs require IsLongRunning() tools or fire-and-forget Pub/Sub trigger pattern.

No first-party in-process queue (no Celery integration). Scheduler is DB-polling. Long-running runs supported via background=True for fire-and-forget with /resume, or schedules for cron-driven runs. BYO Celery/RQ/Arq for richer queue.
Not provided. Tasks delivered to actors via actor_ref.cast(). No durable queue, no retry semantics at queue layer (only LLM-level retries in optim::RetryLayer).
Not provided - BYO. Runtime model is one CLI subprocess per active session. For queue-shaped workloads, layer your own (Celery, RQ, Temporal, AWS SQS).

Not provided - BYO. Query interface includes streamInput() and stopTask() which give primitives for long-running streaming session, but no shipped queue, no enqueue() API, no leasing semantics. Build on top with BullMQ/Cloud Tasks.
OSS: none. AMP: implicit - each Automation is a separate managed deployment that receives trigger events and runs the crew. No explicit queue API in OSS.

Not provided. Framework assumes short-lived calls into Runner.Run from your HTTP handler. Long-running background work is your responsibility (typical pattern: enqueue, then worker pool calls Runner.Run).

Not provided - BYO. No built-in job queue. Expected model is HTTP request -> run flow synchronously -> respond. For async work, put request on Pub/Sub/SQS/etc. yourself and have separate worker call genkit.Generate on dequeue.

Inside langgraph_api (Platform, closed-source): Postgres-backed work queue with one logical lane per thread_id. Long-running runs are default expectation, with re-attaching client picking up via stream_resumable. OSS: no queue - short-lived HTTP scope unless wrapped.
Not provided - BYO. llama_deploy provides this in a separate project.

Not first-party. Mastra assumes you put it behind normal Node/Edge HTTP infra. pubsub/ directory contains internal pub/sub abstraction but for production queues you bring your own (BullMQ, SQS, etc.).

DurableTask is the explicit queue/orchestrator model (DurableAIAgent, AgentEntity with EntityAgentWrapper). Azure Functions triggers fan out to worker pool. Vanilla in-process agent does not expose queue API but the dedicated path is first-class.

Not provided. SDK assumes you embed loop in your own HTTP request scope (or any async task). No internal task queue, no worker pool. For long-running agents: expose streaming endpoint over run_streamed() or persist RunState.to_json() and resume via Celery/RQ/SQS.
Not provided. SDK assumes short-lived HTTP request scope by default. Long-running agents need serialized RunState checkpoint pattern (HITL example).
No built-in queue. ThreadExecutor lets you supply your own concurrent.futures.Executor for sync tool functions in long-running servers. Otherwise short-lived HTTP request scope assumed.
Not provided. Harness assumes short-lived agent.prompt().await usage. No queue, no worker pool. Long-running runs can stream via agent.stream_prompt() to keep client connected.
Not provided - BYO. ConcurrentToolExecutor parallelizes tool calls within one cycle, but no inter-session queue.
Not provided - BYO. SDK assumes you wrap agent.stream() in your host's request-scoped wrapper. Lone exception is optional A2AExpressServer which assumes one-task-at-a-time per TaskStore.

Not provided - BYO. No queue. SDK assumes request scope. The new @ai-sdk/workflow package adds WorkflowAgent stepped-workflow abstraction wrapping streamText with serializable step IO, but is not a horizontal multi-tenant runtime.

First-class `session.Session` interface with composite `(AppName, UserID, ID)` key, event-sourced storage, and scoped `app:`/`user:`/`temp:` state prefixes auto-routed into separate tables. Provides a richly-typed session/event model purpose-built for multi-tenant chat. Strongest data model in the comparison together with LangGraph and Mastra.

`AgentSession` dataclass carries `session_id`, `user_id`, `team_id`, `workflow_id`, `runs`, `summary`, `session_data`, plus sibling `TeamSession` and `WorkflowSession` types. Storage is per-run (each `RunOutput` upserted into the list), not per-message. Has identity fields and summary but no tenant_id or parent_session_id.

No `Session` type, no persistence store, no `id/tenant_id/user_id/created_at` fields anywhere. Only a `Task` (per-run input) and a `MemoryProvider` trait whose default `SlidingWindowMemory` holds a bounded `VecDeque<ChatMessage>`. Report explicitly calls this 'the weakest section of the framework.'

No single dataclass but a clear model: `SessionKey {project_key, session_id, subpath}` plus `SDKSessionInfo` metadata (summary, lastModified, customTitle, gitBranch, cwd, tag). Per-message rows are opaque `SessionStoreEntry`. `project_key` is the explicit multi-tenant scoping field. Strong identity model, slightly less rich than LangGraph or ADK.

Mirrors the Python SDK: `SessionKey {projectKey, sessionId, subpath}` plus `SDKSessionInfo` with summary, customTitle, gitBranch, cwd, tag, createdAt. Per-message messages carry `session_id`, `uuid`, `parent_tool_use_id`, `subagent_type`. `projectKey` is explicitly documented for multi-tenant scoping.

No session abstraction; closest equivalent is a Crew/Flow/Agent `id: UUID4` plus per-execution `_inputs` / `_kickoff_event_id`. No `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `created_at` or `parent_session_id` fields. Checkpoint data when enabled holds the entire Pydantic model dump.

No `Session` type; only an internal `runSession {Values, Events, LaneEvents}` per `Runner.Run` and a `serialization` checkpoint payload. Lacks `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `model`, `summary` — anything chat-like is BYO and reconstructed on each request.

`Session[S any]` is a user-defined typed state blob keyed by `id`; no `messages`, no `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `created_at`, `metadata`, `model`, `summary`. Embedding chat history is BYO inside your `State S` struct. Genuinely typed but session-as-chat is unmodeled.

`thread_id` is the session primitive; the data model is the `Checkpoint` with `channel_values`, `channel_versions`, per-step history, and rich `CheckpointMetadata` (source, step, parents, writes). Stores every super-step's snapshot, not just the latest — foundation for forks and replay.

No formal `Session`; persistence centers on `Memory` (with `session_id`, `token_limit`, `memory_blocks`, `sql_store`) and the workflow `Context`. Single `session_id` per conversation. Reasonable model, but split across two abstractions and missing rich identity fields.

'Thread' is the session primitive: `{threadId, resourceId, ...}` paired together, with `MastraDBMessage` carrying `threadId`, `resourceId`, `role`, `content`, `createdAt`, `metadata`. `resourceId` provides built-in tenant/user scoping. Stores messages, tool calls, suspended-tool metadata, working memory.

`AgentSession {session_id, service_session_id, state}` in Python and `AgentSession.StateBag` in .NET. State is namespaced by `ContextProvider.source_id`. No first-class `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `created_at` — BYO via state keys. Distinct workflow-layer `CheckpointStorage` for graph-style branching.

`Session` Protocol with only `session_id` and `session_settings` plus 4 item methods. Concrete `SQLiteSession` adds `created_at/updated_at` columns. Minimal by design — tenant scoping is done by namespacing `session_id`. Items are `TResponseInputItem`s, no `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `metadata`, `summary` fields.

`Session` interface is 7 methods over `{sessionId, items: AgentInputItem[]}`. No first-class `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `metadata`, `summary` fields. Minimal by design — tenant scoping is done outside the type. Mirrors the Python SDK.

Explicitly no `Session` object. Closest equivalents are `conversation_id` (UUID7) and `run_id` on `RunContext`, plus caller-owned `metadata` and `deps`. `message_history` is passed in and out of every `run()` — fully caller-managed.
No `Session` type; only a `(conversation_id, Vec<Message>)` pair managed by the `ConversationMemory` trait. No `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `metadata`, `parent_session_id` — just the id and the messages.

Three dataclasses: `Session {session_id, session_type, created_at, updated_at}`, `SessionAgent {agent_id, state, conversation_manager_state, _internal_state, ...}`, `SessionMessage {message, message_id, redact_message, ...}`. Clean typed model but missing `tenant_id`/`user_id` fields (BYO in `agent.state`).

Session is a `Snapshot {scope, schemaVersion, createdAt, data, appData}` blob plus `SnapshotLocation {sessionId, scope, scopeId}`. Snapshot fields include `messages, state, systemPrompt, modelState, interrupts`. Schema-versioned and well-structured but no first-class tenant fields.
Explicitly 'no SDK-provided Session / Thread type.' You persist `UIMessage[]` keyed by your own `id`. Client-side `Chat` state machine is in-memory only. Strictly BYO data model.

Three first-party stores: `InMemoryService`, `database.NewSessionService` (GORM → Postgres/SQLite/MySQL/Spanner) and `vertexai.NewSessionService`. No JSONL/Redis/S3 adapters, but Postgres/Cloud SQL coverage is production-ready. Strong but slightly narrower than Agno or OpenAI Agents Python.

13+ adapters: Postgres (sync + async), MySQL, SQLite, Redis, Mongo, DynamoDB, Firestore, Singlestore, SurrealDB, GCS JSON, JSON file, in-memory. Auto-provisions table set (`agno_sessions`, `agno_memories`, …). Broadest store coverage among Python frameworks.
No JSONL, no SQLite, no Postgres, no Redis, no S3 — nothing ships. `MemoryProvider` trait has `preload/export` hooks but you build any backend yourself.

Default JSONL on disk (CLI-owned) plus `InMemorySessionStore`. Postgres/Redis/S3 adapters ship as reference examples under `examples/session_stores/` (with a 13-contract conformance harness) but are not in the wheel — copy-in.

Default JSONL on disk plus `InMemorySessionStore`. Postgres, Redis, S3 reference adapters in `examples/session-stores/` with a conformance suite, plus an alpha `attachBridgeSession` for claude.ai sync. Adapters are example code, not in the package.

Two checkpoint providers ship: `JsonProvider` (file-per-checkpoint) and `SqliteProvider` (WAL-mode DB), plus `SQLiteFlowPersistence` for Flow state. No Postgres/Redis/S3/cloud-blob providers. For memory there's LanceDB and Qdrant edge.

`CheckPointStore` interface is the only contract; eino-ext ships no implementations (verified by grep). Even Postgres / Redis / SQLite / in-memory are entirely BYO. Internal `bridgeStore` exists but is framework-private.
Two: `InMemoryStore[S]` (experimental, process-local) and `FirestoreSessionStore[S]` (production). No Postgres/SQLite/JSONL/Redis/S3/GCS adapter — anything beyond Firestore is BYO.

Four shipped: `InMemorySaver`, `PostgresSaver`+`AsyncPostgresSaver`, `SqliteSaver`+`AsyncSqliteSaver`. Postgres saver also doubles as `BaseStore` (namespaced KV + vector). No bundled Redis/Mongo/S3 store — narrower than Agno but each is production-grade.

`Memory` defaults to `SQLAlchemyChatStore` covering any SQLAlchemy DB (SQLite/Postgres/MySQL). Additional community chat stores under `core/storage/chat_store/` include Postgres, Redis. Workflow `Context` itself is BYO storage. Broad coverage via SQLAlchemy.

15+ adapters under `stores/`: libsql (default), pg, mysql, mssql, dsql, cloudflare, cloudflare-d1, dynamodb, mongodb, opensearch, couchbase, plus vector stores (pinecone, qdrant, chroma, astra, lance, elasticsearch). Most opinionated, most batteries-included.

First-party: in-memory, experimental `FileHistoryProvider`, Redis (separate `agent-framework-redis` pkg), Cosmos NoSql (Python + .NET), Foundry Persistent Agents (server-side threads). Cosmos `CheckpointStorage` covers workflow checkpoints. Strong cross-language coverage but Postgres/SQLite are BYO.

Ten first-party backends: SQLiteSession (default), OpenAIConversationsSession, OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession, AdvancedSQLiteSession, AsyncSQLiteSession, SQLAlchemySession (Postgres/MySQL/…), RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, EncryptedSession (wrapper). Lazy-imported optional extras. Most session backends of any Python stack.

Only `MemorySession`, `OpenAIConversationsSession`, and `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession`. No SQLite/Postgres/Redis/S3/JSONL built-in — BYO. Reference examples (`file.ts`, `prisma.ts`) but not shipped as packages. Far thinner than the Python sibling.
Explicitly 'none ship out-of-box.' BYO Postgres/SQLite/Redis/S3 against `result.all_messages_json()`. The only first-party path to durability is wrapping the agent in Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate.

Only `InMemoryConversationMemory` ships in-tree. Companion `rig-memory` crate ships history-shaping policies, not new backends. Postgres/SQLite/Mongo/Redis/S3 are all BYO (note `rig-postgres` etc. are vector-store, not memory-store, crates).
