`FileSessionManager`, `S3SessionManager`, plus `RepositorySessionManager` abstract base requiring a `SessionRepository`. Postgres/Redis are BYO via `SessionRepository` implementation. Solid trio but no SQLite/Postgres/Redis out-of-the-box.
Two `SnapshotStorage` impls ship: `FileStorage` and `S3Storage`. Postgres/Redis/DynamoDB/SQLite are BYO. Thinner than the Python sibling.
Explicitly none. No JSONL, no SQLite, no Postgres adapter, no Redis adapter, no Blob adapter. SDK has 'zero opinion on storage.'

`session.Service` interface with `Create/Get/List/Delete/AppendEvent`. Returns `Session` as an interface so the concrete struct is yours. Clean, small, production-suitable — BYO Redis/S3/Cassandra by implementing five methods.

`BaseDb`/`AsyncBaseDb` cover ~50 abstract methods spanning session, memory, eval, trace, knowledge, component, schedule, approval CRUD. Well-typed but a heavy contract — implementing a new backend is ambitious. Migration manager and versioning are first-class.

`MemoryProvider` async trait: `remember/recall/clear/clone_box/preload/export/needs_summary/...`. The plug point exists and is async-friendly, but it's a memory-window contract, not a real session/checkpoint store.

`SessionStore` Protocol with 2 required + 4 optional methods, plus a shipped 13-contract conformance test harness (`run_session_store_conformance`) authors can run on their adapters. Small surface, well-documented mirror semantics.

`SessionStore` interface with 2 required + 4 optional methods (alpha-marked). Shared 13-test conformance suite vendored in `examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts`. `foldSessionSummary` helper for adapter authors. Mirror semantics fully documented.

Three distinct plug points: `BaseProvider` ABC for state/checkpoint (discriminated-union registration on `CheckpointConfig.provider`), `StorageBackend` Protocol for memory, `FlowPersistence` ABC for Flow's `@persist`. Comprehensive but multiple parallel interfaces.

`CheckPointStore` interface with two methods on opaque `[]byte` (`Get`/`Set`). Trivial to implement but the framework hands you gob-encoded bytes — no schema, no migration helpers, no versioning hook. Plug exists but it's the bare minimum.

`Store[S any]` is a 2-method generic interface (`Get`/`Save`). Trivial to BYO and Firestore impl is the canonical reference. Clean and type-safe but no per-message or per-tool granularity — it's a state-blob store.

`BaseCheckpointSaver` with `get_tuple/list/put/put_writes` (plus async siblings) is the canonical interface. Shipped conformance harness at `libs/checkpoint-conformance/`. The widely-cited gold standard for plug-in checkpointers.

`BaseMemory` is the memory interface; `BaseChatStore` is the message persistence interface. Community implementations include `RedisChatStore`, `PostgresChatStore`, `AzureChatStore`. Two parallel interfaces but well-supported.

`MastraStorage` with sub-interfaces for each storage domain (memory, workflows, observability, scores, …). BYO by implementing the domain interfaces and passing to `new Mastra({ storage })`. Very rich surface — powerful but a large API to implement.

Python: `HistoryProvider` ABC with `get_messages`/`save_messages`. .NET: `AgentSessionStore` abstract class with `Save/Get`, plus `ChatHistoryProvider` for message-history backends. Plus a separate `CheckpointStorage` interface for workflows. Multiple but well-documented surfaces.

Both `Session` Protocol (structural) and `SessionABC` (nominal) with just 4 methods: `get_items`, `add_items`, `pop_item`, `clear_session`. Minimal, easy to BYO. Extension protocols `OpenAIResponsesCompactionAwareSession` available for richer integrations.

`Session` interface with 7 methods plus optional `SessionHistoryRewriteAwareSession` and `OpenAIResponsesCompactionAwareSession` extensions. ~119-line reference adapter shows the pattern. Mirrors the Python design — minimal, well-typed.
No `SessionStore` / `Checkpointer` abstraction shipped. UI adapter docs show the pattern (caller persists `message_history` keyed by thread/session id) but you implement everything from scratch.

`ConversationMemory` trait with `load/append/clear` over `&str` conversation IDs and `Vec<Message>` payloads. Sits behind `Arc<dyn ConversationMemory>` on `Agent`. Easy to BYO but it's a chat-log contract, not a checkpoint store.

`SessionRepository` ABC defines `create/read/update_session|agent|message`, `list_messages(limit, offset)`, plus optional multi-agent methods. `RepositorySessionManager` ties an arbitrary repository to standard hook-based persistence. Clean message-granular contract.

`SnapshotStorage` interface with six methods (`saveSnapshot/loadSnapshot/listSnapshotIds/deleteSession/loadManifest/saveManifest`). File-system and S3 implementations are reference impls. Snapshot-blob granularity, not message granularity.
Explicitly 'no interface to plug.' Persistence is a callback inside `onStepFinish`/`onFinish`. There is no `SessionStore` or `Checkpointer` abstraction whatsoever.

Per-event durability: every non-partial event is written inside a GORM transaction. Crashing mid-tool-call leaves the tool-call event but no response; the runner does NOT auto-replay the in-flight tool. Strong per-message durability, weaker than LangGraph's per-task `put_writes`.

No per-tool-call checkpoint on normal runs. Durable interrupt is only `RunStatus.paused` for HITL approvals — `handle_agent_run_paused` writes that state. A mid-tool-call crash on a non-paused run loses the entire run.
Explicitly 'Not provided — BYO. A crash mid-tool-call loses all in-memory state.' No checkpointer concept at all.

Local JSONL is written by the CLI per entry, so a crash leaves the transcript intact up to the last flushed line. External `SessionStore` is batched (~100ms) and post-local, with `session_store_flush='eager'` to tighten the window. No transactional commit-per-tool-write like LangGraph; mid-tool-call call itself is lost on restart.

Subprocess writes JSONL line-by-line as the durability boundary. External store is batched + post-local + eventually consistent (~100ms drop window) with `importSessionToStore` to reconcile. No per-task commit primitive — mid-tool-call call itself lost on resume.

With `on_events=['*']` (or selecting `tool_usage_started/finished`), a checkpoint fires per tool call. `Crew.from_checkpoint` + `_restore_runtime` walks the event record to find tasks in flight and marks `_resuming=True`. Report calls this 'gold-standard mid-tool-call resumability' — comparable to LangGraph but defaults to `task_completed` only.

Persistence fires only when `Interrupt`/`StatefulInterrupt` is called inside a tool. A crash without a deliberate interrupt loses everything since the last interrupt. Report: 'no equivalent of LangGraph's per-task `put_writes`.' Resume via `Runner.Resume` works only for explicit interrupt points.

Explicitly 'Not provided.' Streaming output chunks can be replayed to a disconnected client, but if the server crashes mid-tool-call the in-flight state is lost — next request starts fresh. True resume is BYO via `WrapTool` middleware.

Per-task `put_writes` makes durability sub-super-step. Under `durability='async'`, each tool task commits on completion; on resume the completed tool results are in `checkpoint_pending_writes` and do NOT re-execute. Even with 4 parallel tools, completed ones survive a crash. Gold standard in the comparison; only mid-tool-call (inside a single HTTP call) is not covered.

Not automatic. Workflows pause at `ctx.wait_for_event(...)` and you serialize via `ctx.to_dict(...)`, but a crash mid-tool-call loses the in-flight result. Explicitly weaker than LangGraph in the report.

Mid-run checkpointing via workflow snapshots: when a tool with `requireApproval: true` suspends, `flushMessagesBeforeSuspension` and `suspend({__streamState: streamState.serialize()})` write a snapshot, and `agent.approveToolCall` restores it. Survives restarts for HITL — but a crash on a non-approval tool call loses progress.

Three layers: agent-level `PerServiceCallChatHistoryPersistingChatClient` persists chat history between every LLM round-trip (opt-in); workflow-level `CheckpointStorage` between executor transitions; `DurableAIAgent` (DurableTask) makes every agent step a durable orchestration step, replayable from any failure. Opt-in, but very strong when enabled.

`RunState.to_json()` is the durable checkpoint primitive (~3,300 lines), capturing original input, current agent, generated items, session items, model responses, guardrails, current step, tool-use tracker, approvals, schema version. `Runner.run(agent, state)` resumes — but automatic checkpoint is per-turn, not per-tool-call; per-tool granularity is a manual `to_state().to_json()`.

No automatic mid-tool-call durability; closest is HITL state serialization: when `needsApproval` halts, you serialize `RunResult.state` via `state.toString()` / `RunState.fromString(agent, str)` and re-run. Not a substitute for LangGraph per-tool checkpoints, but cleanly works for human-approval pause/resume.

`Agent` itself has no checkpointer. Mid-run durability is only via the durable execution layers (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate): the agent loop runs as a workflow and tool calls become activities. Strong when wired up, but requires bolting on an external durable runtime.

Explicitly 'Not provided.' `ConversationMemory::append` fires only at end-of-turn after a successful response. A mid-tool-call crash means `append` never runs and the partial trajectory is lost. Test `memory_unchanged_on_provider_error` verifies this.

`experimental/checkpoint/checkpoint.py` ships a checkpoint with `position ∈ {after_model, after_tools}` and resume via a `checkpointResume` content block. Comment explicitly says 'Per-tool granularity within a cycle requires a custom ToolExecutor (e.g. TemporalToolExecutor).' Experimental tag.

'Not durable mid-tool-call.' Snapshots fire on `AfterInvocationEvent`/`MessageAddedEvent`/`AfterModelCallEvent` — there is no per-task `commit()` inside `executeTool`. HITL pauses persist `pendingToolExecution` via the interrupt subsystem, but a crashed run mid-tool-call cannot resume.

Explicitly 'Not provided — BYO.' The closest pattern is the resumable-stream recipe (Redis-backed stream replay so a client can reconnect), but if the server crashes mid-tool-call the tool call dies and the next request has to start a new run. 'Resumable stream, not durable runtime.'

Single linear list of events per session. `Branch` field on `Event` is NOT a fork — it's a dotted-path filter (`agent_1.agent_2`) used by parallel sub-agents to scope which history they see. Report calls it 'horizontal slice filter, not vertical fork.'
Single conversation per session (linear list of `RunOutput`s). No first-class fork/branch — you fork manually by reading a session, copying the runs you want, and writing under a new session_id.
'One in-memory window per agent instance. No thread/branch model, no forking.' If you want to fork you'd `clone_box()` the memory provider and start a fresh agent.

`fork_session=True` + `resume=<id>` creates a new session branching from a prior one; helper `fork_session()` re-exported at module level. Plus `resume`/`continue_conversation` for resume semantics. First-class branching primitive.

`forkSession(sessionId, {upToMessageId?, title?, sessionStore?})` branches at a specific message UUID with full UUID remapping and `parentUuid` chain preservation. No cyclical graph but fork is genuinely first-class — strongest dedicated fork API in the comparison.

`Crew.fork(config, branch=...)` restores from a checkpoint and forks the underlying `RuntimeState` to a new branch label. Same on `Flow.fork` and `Agent.fork`. Conceptually similar to LangGraph forks, riding on the checkpoint engine.
'No fork/branch model — you cannot `session.fork()` LangGraph-style.' Thread of execution is linear; only parallel sub-agents get lanes inside one run. A new `checkPointID` = a new session.
'One session = one state blob keyed by id. No native fork/branch model. No parent-child session relationship.' If you need branching, you encode it in your state struct.

Pregel checkpointer supports forking: `graph.get_state_history(config)` returns every step; `graph.update_state(config_at_step_N, values)` creates a new branch from step N. Multiple branches per thread are first-class. Built on per-step checkpoint snapshots — uniquely powerful.
'One `session_id` per conversation; no fork/branch primitive in the OSS framework.' Workflow `Context` resume after pause is the closest mechanic, but it's not really a fork.
'Fork/branch is not first-class; you'd `cloneThread` and write to the new id.' Single conversation per `threadId` — no built-in branching graph.

One session = one conversation, no fork on `AgentSession` itself. Branching exists at the **workflow** layer via `CheckpointStorage` — you can resume a workflow from any checkpoint. Decent fork, but split from the session abstraction.

'Single conversation per `session_id`. No native thread/branch model, no `fork()` semantics.' If you need parallel branches you create separate `session_id`s and copy prefix items yourself. `RunState` is interruption-resume, not fork.
'Single linear conversation per session. No fork/branch model. No parent_session_id. If you need branching you implement a graph layer on top.' Mirror of the Python sibling.

'Single conversation per `conversation_id`. Branching = pass an explicit `conversation_id='new'` to fork while keeping prior `message_history`.' Documented pattern, but it's a manual convention rather than a fork primitive.
'Linear conversation per `conversation_id`. No fork/branch model.'
'Single linear conversation per `(session_id, agent_id)` pair. No branching/forking primitive.' Multi-agent sessions are supported but each agent has its own message log.

'Forking ≈ take a snapshot, hand it to another Agent instance, load it — the Snapshot is a JSON blob you can branch by copying.' Multi-agent orchestrators get separate `MultiAgentState` snapshots. Manual pattern, not a fork primitive.
'Single linear conversation per id. No branch/fork model. No checkpoint graph. If you want branching, you implement it as N sessions in your DB.'

Export: `session.Service.Get` returns the full event list (also exposed via REST). Replay: `internal/configurable/conformance/replayplugin/` mocks LLM + tool calls via a recordings YAML, but it's `internal/` and not exported — you can fork/copy it.
Export: `AgentSession.to_dict()` + `db.get_session(session_id)` returns fully-serializable dict. Replay: 'not a first-party concept' — you walk `runs` manually; no `replay_session` helper.
`MemoryProvider::export()` returns `Vec<ChatMessage>` and `preload()` re-hydrates. Replay (deterministic re-execution) is not provided — events are emitted but not stored.

Helpers: `list_sessions`, `get_session_messages`, `list_subagents`, `get_subagent_messages` (plus `_from_store` variants), `tag_session`, `rename_session`, `delete_session`, `fork_session`. JSONL is append-only and replayed by `resume=<id>`. Strong export, replay-by-resume.

`getSessionMessages`, `getSessionInfo`, `listSessions`, `listSubagents`. Deterministic replay via `query({options: {resume: sessionId}})`, optionally `resumeSessionAt: messageUuid` to replay up to a point. JSONL is transparent and append-only.

`crewai replay -t <task_id>` CLI re-runs from a saved task output. `RuntimeState.event_record` is fully-serializable JSON and restored on `from_checkpoint`. `crewai_event_bus._replaying` contextvar suppresses side effects. 'Replay is deterministic enough to reconstruct UI state but not to make HTTP calls again.'

Export: `r.store.Get(ctx, checkPointID)` returns the gob blob. Resume: `Runner.Resume` re-enters from the saved point. No deterministic record/replay framework — you'd build it by mocking `model.BaseChatModel` against recorded outputs.

'No first-party export/replay tooling for sessions.' Generation events emit OTel spans. Replaying = reconstruct messages from your DB and pass to `Generate(..., WithMessages(...))`. Dev UI replays individual actions, not full sessions.

Export: `get_state(config)` returns `StateSnapshot`; `get_state_history(config)` returns every step, both JSON-serializable via the `langgraph-checkpoint` codec. Replay: pass `config[\configurable\"][\"checkpoint_id\"]` to `graph.stream(None

`Context.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer())` / `Context.from_dict(...)` is the canonical export pattern. Deterministic replay = re-feed `chat_history` to a new run with mocked LLM responses; no built-in record/replay harness.

Export via `storage.getMessages({threadId})` and resumable-stream / observe-stream endpoints. `_llm-recorder` package for test fixture replay. No deterministic full-session replay engine — closer to fixture recording than first-class replay.

Session export: `AgentSession.to_dict()` JSON envelope. Workflow checkpoint export via `CheckpointStorage`. Deterministic replay: **DurableTask** provides replay-from-checkpoint (`Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask`). Strong when DurableTask is in use, but split across abstractions.

`RunResult.to_input_list(mode=…)` exports as input items; `RunState.to_json()`/`from_json()` enables full state replay across processes; `result.raw_responses` is the unmodified per-call log. No first-party replay viewer — uses tracing dashboard or exporters.

`RunResult.history` and `RunResult.state` serializable via JSON (`state.toJSON()`). `RunState.fromString(agent, json)` rebuilds for replay. Traces dashboard at `platform.openai.com/traces` is a hosted replay viewer.
`AgentRunResult.all_messages_json()` exports full conversation as JSON bytes. Replay = construct a new `Agent.run(..., message_history=...)`. No deterministic record/replay engine.

'Not provided as a first-class feature.' `PromptResponse.messages` gives new messages from a turn; replay = `PromptRequest::with_history(...)`. Deterministic replay against recorded provider responses is BYO (tests use `MockCompletionModel`).

`Agent.take_snapshot(preset='session', include=…, exclude=…, app_data={...})` returns a `Snapshot` dataclass capturing messages/state/conv_mgr_state/interrupt_state/system_prompt. `Agent.load_snapshot(snapshot)` restores. `experimental/checkpoint` wraps this for durable pause/resume. No deterministic re-execution engine.

`agent.takeSnapshot({preset: 'session'})` returns a `Snapshot` you `JSON.stringify`; `agent.loadSnapshot(snapshot)` restores. 'Replay-from-event-stream is not a first-class primitive' — you re-issue `agent.invoke(initialPrompt)` against a restored snapshot but there's no deterministic event-by-event replay engine.
'You already have the messages — exporting is `JSON.stringify(messages)`. Replay = pass the same messages and pin model + seed. Determinism is not a first-party feature.'

ADK Go ships ReAct as the default loop via `llmagent.New` wiring `llminternal.Flow`; users configure agent+tools+callbacks and the framework runs ReAct under the hood with parallel tool dispatch and HITL pauses.

Agno ships a built-in tool-calling loop inside each Model adapter and additionally exposes an explicit ReAct-style reasoning mode via `agent.reasoning=True` with `reasoning_max_steps`. The harness owns the LLM->tool->LLM cycle through `call_model_with_fallback`.

AutoAgents ships built-in ReAct via `ReActAgent<T>` plus `BasicAgent` (single-turn) and `CodeActAgent` (sandboxed TS). The shared `TurnEngine::run_turn` drives the LLM-tool-LLM loop up to `max_turns` (default 10).

ReAct loop ships and runs inside the Claude Code CLI subprocess (Node). Python only sees streamed wire frames. You cannot intercept tool_call->tool_result inside Python, but the framework fully owns the loop end-to-end.

Built-in ReAct loop runs entirely inside the Claude Code CLI subprocess. The TS host iterates messages and can insert hooks/tools, but the framework owns the LLM->tool->LLM cycle plus PreToolUse/PostToolUse gating per call.

CrewAI's `AgentExecutor` runs a built-in loop with two flavors: native tool-calling for capable LLMs and string-parsed ReAct (`_invoke_loop_react`) for LLMs without native tools. The framework owns the LLM->tool->LLM cycle through `_invoke_loop`.

Eino's `adk.ChatModelAgent` ships a built-in ReAct loop compiled into a `compose.Graph[*reactInput, Message]` with Init->ChatModel->ToolNode->loop. Users configure via `ChatModelAgentConfig` — no graph building required.

Genkit's `ai.GenerateWithRequest` owns the LLM->tool->LLM loop bounded by `MaxTurns` (default 5). There is no `Thought:`/`Action:` text-parsing scaffold; the framework relies on the model's native tool-calling and feeds back tool results automatically.

LangGraph fully owns the loop via the Pregel super-step engine. `create_react_agent` ships a prebuilt three-node ReAct (now @deprecated in favor of `langchain.agents.create_agent`), but you can roll your own ReAct as a plain `StateGraph` with no special casing.

LlamaIndex ships both `FunctionAgent` (native function-calling) and `ReActAgent` (Thought/Action/Observation parsing) on top of the Workflow event graph. The framework fully owns the LLM->tool->LLM cycle through `run_agent_step`->`parse_agent_output`->`call_tool`->`aggregate_tool_results`.

Mastra owns the loop through the `agentic-execution` workflow (LLM call -> map tool-calls -> foreach tool -> mapping -> background task check -> completion check). The framework runs ReAct end-to-end with supervisor-style early-stop scorers and approval flows.

MAF owns the function-invocation loop automatically when tools are present in both Python (`_try_execute_function_calls`) and .NET (`FunctionInvokingChatClient`). The harness iterates until `finish_reason != 'tool_calls'`, with built-in HITL approval gating.

`Runner.run` ships the canonical ReAct loop, documented inline: invoke, check final output, handoff, or tool calls. `Agent.tool_use_behavior` lets you pick standard ReAct, stop-on-first-tool, stop-at-tool-names, or a custom function.

`run(agent, input, options)` is the built-in ReAct loop, documented inline as invoke -> final-output | handoff | tool-call -> repeat. `maxTurns` defaults to `DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS = 10` and can be `null` since 0.10.0 to disable.

Pydantic AI's pydantic_graph state machine ships ReAct via the `CallToolsNode -> ModelRequestNode` cycle, terminated by `end_strategy` (early/graceful/exhaustive) and bounded by `UsageLimits`. The framework owns dispatch, retry, and validation.

Rig owns a multi-turn tool-call loop in `PromptRequest::send` that is effectively ReAct (think->act->observe). It exposes a `ThinkTool` built-in for explicit reasoning, plus `max_turns` capping and concurrent tool dispatch.

Strands ships ReAct via `event_loop_cycle` plus `recurse_event_loop` that recurses after every tool batch. The framework drives the LLM->tool->LLM cycle, model-as-tool sub-agents, and conversation-manager compaction all on this single loop.

Strands TS ships a canonical ReAct loop as a `while(true)` in `_stream()` with `_invokeModel` -> tool execution -> next model call. Concurrent or sequential tool execution is selectable via `toolExecutor` config.

The `do { ... } while(...)` in `generateText`/`streamText` IS the ReAct loop. `ToolLoopAgent` wraps it with `isStepCount(20)` default. `stopWhen` (and `hasToolCall`, custom predicates) terminates; `prepareStep` lets you mutate per-iteration.

ADK Go dispatches tool calls in parallel goroutines under a WaitGroup, fires Before/After/OnError tool callbacks per call, matches results back by `FunctionCall.ID`, and merges parallel responses into a single `*session.Event` with multiple `Part.FunctionResponse` entries.

Tool dispatch lives inside each Model adapter (`Model.run_function_calls`) which drives the tool-call cycle and invokes `FunctionCall.execute()` with tool_hooks chain. Single-tool entrypoint, hooks pre/post, ToolExecution record. Less explicit framework-level orchestration than peers.

`ToolProcessor::process_single_tool_call_with_hooks` runs `on_tool_call` (Abort/Continue) -> `on_tool_start` -> execute -> `on_tool_result`/`on_tool_error`. Each call emits `ToolCallRequested`/`Completed`/`Failed` events. Tools are looked up by linear scan.

Three dispatch paths in the CLI: built-in tools, external MCP, and in-process SDK MCP via `mcp_message` control request back to Python. Tool results return as `ToolResultBlock` matched by `tool_use_id`; permission/PreToolUse hooks gate per call.

Same three dispatch paths as Python plus richer hooks: PreToolUse per call (can updatedInput/permissionDecision/additionalContext), optional `canUseTool` callback round-trip, PostToolUse per call, PostToolBatch once per batch. SDK MCP runs in-process via control_request.

Major caveat: both old and new executors `execute only the first tool call per turn` even if the LLM emits multiple parallel tool_calls. `execute_tool_and_check_finality` runs before_tool_call hooks -> tool.run -> after_tool_call. Parallelism only between independent plan todos.

`compose.ToolsNode` dispatches calls in parallel by default (`ExecuteSequentially: false`), matches results via `ToolMessage.ToolCallID == ToolCall.ID`, supports invokable/streamable middlewares plus `UnknownToolsHandler` for hallucinated names.

`handleToolRequests` fans out one goroutine per `ToolRequest`, runs each through `WrapTool` middleware via `runTool`, collects results, and folds them into a single `tool`-role message. Concurrent execution flagged in docs as unsafe-for-shared-state.

`ToolNode.invoke` takes the last AIMessage's tool_calls, splits them (parallel via `Send` in v2 create_react_agent), runs each via `_run_one`, and appends one `ToolMessage(tool_call_id=...)` per call. Linkage is always explicit via tool_call_id.

`parse_agent_output` emits one `ToolCall` event per LLM-generated call, the workflow runtime fans them out to parallel `call_tool` invocations, and `aggregate_tool_results` fans them in via `ctx.collect_events(...)`. Context-aware tools get the workflow ctx injected.

`toolCallStep` validates the tool is in the active set, runs `tool.execute(input, ctx)` with full `ToolExecutionContext`, supports approval gating via `requireApproval`/`needsApprovalFn` (emits `tool-call-approval` and `suspend`), and threads results through `llmMappingStep`.

Python `_try_execute_function_calls` iterates `FunctionCallContent` items, resolves `FunctionTool` from `tool_map`, invokes via `_execute_function_calls`. Approval gating inline via `function_approval_request`. .NET delegates to `FunctionInvokingChatClient`.

Dedicated dispatch paths for function tools, computer actions, shell calls, apply-patch, MCP approval requests. Each invocation receives `ToolContext` with tool_name/tool_call_id/tool_arguments. Results wrap as `FunctionToolResult` and thread back into LLM input via run_items_to_input_items.

`toolExecution.ts` runs concurrent dispatches up to `maxFunctionToolConcurrency`, runs per-tool input/output guardrails around `tool.invoke()`, builds `RunToolCallOutputItem` and feeds back. Approval flow via `tool_approval_requested`.

`ToolManager.handle_call` resolves the tool, validates args via `SchemaValidator`, and fires five hook points: `before_tool_validate -> wrap_tool_validate -> before_tool_execute -> wrap_tool_execute -> after_tool_execute`. ModelRetry returns become `RetryPromptPart` round-trips.

Rig dispatches tool calls via `futures::stream::iter(...).buffer_unordered(self.concurrency)` with per-call `on_tool_call` and `on_tool_result` hooks (Skip/Terminate). Results bind to `UserContent::ToolResult` with call IDs and push back into history.

`ToolExecutor._stream` looks up the tool, fires `BeforeToolCallEvent` (can swap selected_tool / mutate / cancel), streams `selected_tool.stream(...)`, fires `AfterToolCallEvent` with retry support, collects into one user-role tool-result message.

`executeTool` builds toolUse, fires `BeforeToolCallEvent` (mutable input/name/cancel/swap), resolves effectiveTool, runs `effectiveTool.stream(toolContext)`, builds ToolResultBlock, fires `AfterToolCallEvent` (mutable result/retry). Concurrent or sequential via `toolExecutor` config.

`executeTools(...)` runs approved tool calls in parallel via `Promise.all`, fires `onToolExecutionStart`/`onToolExecutionEnd`, runs approval gating (`resolveToolApproval`), and lets `tool.toModelOutput?` reshape raw output before it becomes model-visible.

Streaming tokens flow as `*session.Event` with `Partial=true`; the same `iter.Seq2[*Event, error]` carries deltas and final messages. Partial events stream through SSE/WS but are not persisted, separating transient deltas from canonical history.

Agno emits `RunContent` events with content deltas during streaming, plus `RunIntermediateContent` for partial pieces. Streaming mode toggled by `stream=True`; SSE wire format with named event types; `time_to_first_token` is tracked.

Streaming yields `Event::StreamChunk { chunk: StreamChunk::Text(...) }` per token plus `ToolUseInputDelta`, `ReasoningContent`, `Usage`, `Done` variants. `TurnEngine::stream_with_tools` accumulates chunks while emitting per-chunk events.

Token-level streaming via `StreamEvent` carrying the raw Anthropic SSE event, opt-in through `include_partial_messages=True`. Default iteration delivers chunked assistant/user messages without per-token deltas.

Token-level streaming via `SDKPartialAssistantMessage` (`type: 'stream_event'`) carrying the raw `BetaRawMessageStreamEvent`. Opt-in via `includePartialMessages: true`; otherwise iteration delivers aggregated assistant messages only.

Streaming requires `Crew(stream=True)`, which wires the singleton event bus into a queue and yields `StreamChunk` from `utilities/streaming.py`. Token deltas come through but require explicit opt-in and the bus indirection adds latency.

Streaming is via `*schema.StreamReader[*schema.Message]` chunks reduced into a final message. `Runner.enableStreaming` toggles streaming; `Runnable.Stream/Transform` are first-class on the compose layer.

Native streaming via `ModelStreamCallback` plus the `GenerateStream` `iter.Seq2[*ModelStreamValue, error]` (Go 1.23 range-over-func). The harness wraps the user callback to assign role-based indices and attach a format handler.

Token-level streaming via `StreamMessagesHandler.on_llm_new_token` callback installed at run start; emits `MessagesStreamPart` per token in `stream_mode='messages'`. AIMessageChunk/ToolMessageChunk variants are first-class.

Token streaming via `AgentStream` events with a `delta` field, written by `_get_llm_response` as tokens arrive. The consumer iterates `handler.stream_events()` to receive deltas in line with other workflow events.

Mastra streams a full ChunkType taxonomy with `text-start`/`text-delta`/`text-end`, `reasoning-start/-delta/-end`, `tool-call-delta`, etc., through a web-standard ReadableStream. ~40 chunk types cover every streaming pattern.

Python `AsyncIterable[AgentResponseUpdate]` and .NET `IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate>` carry partial Message updates with token-level deltas. `ResponseStream` aggregates into a final `AgentResponse[T]`.

Token streaming via `RawResponsesStreamEvent` wrapping raw OpenAI Responses API events (`ResponseTextDeltaEvent`, reasoning deltas, function-call-arg deltas). `RunResultStreaming.stream_events()` yields the rich `StreamEvent` union.

Token streaming via `RunRawModelStreamEvent` (raw provider chunks like `output_text_delta`). `StreamedRunResult` exposes the async iterable of `RunStreamEvent` including raw deltas plus item-level events.

Token streaming via `PartStartEvent`/`PartDeltaEvent`/`PartEndEvent` carrying `TextPartDelta`, `ThinkingPartDelta`, `ToolCallPartDelta`. `Agent.run_stream_events()` yields the unified `AgentStreamEvent | AgentRunResultEvent` async iterator.
Streaming is a separate surface: `Stream<MultiTurnStreamItem<R>>` yielding `StreamedAssistantContent::Text` deltas plus tool-call deltas and reasoning deltas. Non-streaming path has no event stream.

Token streaming via `TextStreamEvent`, `ToolUseStreamEvent`, `ReasoningTextStreamEvent`, `CitationStreamEvent`, plus raw `ModelStreamChunkEvent` from streaming/_events.py. `stream_async` is the primary surface yielding raw event dicts.

Token-level streaming via `ModelStreamUpdateEvent` (deltas) and `ContentBlockEvent` (assembled blocks) wrapping the lower-layer model streaming events. Generator-based `Agent.stream()` yields the unified `AgentStreamEvent`.

Streaming is first-class via `streamText(...).fullStream` yielding `TextStreamPart` with `text-delta`, `reasoning-delta`, `tool-input-delta`, etc. ~24 stream-part variants cover every streaming surface; UIMessageChunk maps to wire SSE.

Turn boundary is `event.IsFinalResponse()` returning true (no function calls + no function responses + not partial + no trailing code-execution result). Invocations are modeled by `invocationID` plumbed through every event with an ASCII diagram of nested calls/steps.

Agno uses `run()` = one turn = one LLM invocation cycle that may include N tool calls; turn boundary is `RunOutput.run_id` (UUID). Sessions hold `AgentSession.runs: list[RunOutput]`. No mid-run turn type; one run is the unit.

Explicit `Event::TurnStarted{turn_number, max_turns}` and `Event::TurnCompleted{turn_number, final_turn}` boundaries emitted by `TurnEngine`. A turn is one trip through `run_turn` = one LLM call + optional one batch of tool dispatches.

Turn is defined by `ResultMessage` (one per user prompt) carrying `num_turns`, `stop_reason`, `total_cost_usd`. `max_turns` caps the CLI's internal turn loop and triggers an `error_max_turns` result on overrun.

Turn = one assistant message + the synthetic user message containing tool_results. `SDKResultMessage` emits once per request loop terminator with `num_turns`, `terminal_reason`, `stop_reason`. `maxTurns`/`maxBudgetUsd`/hook-stop all terminate.

A turn = one LLM call + one tool execution + appended tool result. `self.iterations` increments per LLM call but there's no first-class Turn type. `max_iter` default 25 caps the loop; new AgentExecutor enforces budget per-todo.
Eino has no first-class Turn type. A turn boundary is implicit, defined by the loop branch from ChatModel to either ToolNode or END. The closest thing to a turn-event is the generic `AgentEvent`.
A turn = one trip through `runGenerate` (one `model.Generate` + optional tool dispatch). `MaxTurns` counts these as an `int` carried through recursion. No `Turn` type, no Turn event.
No explicit turn object. The closest first-class boundary is the super-step. A ReAct turn is roughly: super-step `agent` runs (LLM->AIMessage) -> super-step `tools` runs (one or more ToolMessage).

A turn = 'one LLM call -> N parallel tool calls -> fan-in -> next LLM call'. The framework caps via `max_iterations` (default 20) and exposes `early_stopping_method = 'force' | 'generate'`. No explicit Turn type.
A turn is one full pass through the 6-step workflow chain. The `step-finish` and `finish` stream chunks demarcate turn boundaries; `StepResult[]` accumulates step data in `GenerateTextResult`.

A turn ends implicitly when the LLM returns a non-tool-call response (`finish_reason in {stop,length,content_filter}`) or `MiddlewareTermination` is raised. No explicit Turn type; the run accumulates updates until terminal.

Explicit docstring: 'A turn is defined as one AI invocation (including any tool calls that might occur).' `max_turns` (default 10) is first-class; `state._currentTurn` tracks per-run. Resumed runs do not increment the turn counter.

A turn is bounded by `prepareTurn -> model call -> resolveTurnAfterModelResponse -> applyTurnResult`. `state._currentTurn` increments per turn. Loop terminates only on `next_step_final_output` or `next_step_interruption`.

A turn is 'one trip around the graph until either another ModelRequestNode is queued or End fires'. `RunContext.run_step` increments per iteration. Three graph nodes (UserPromptNode, ModelRequestNode, CallToolsNode) make turns observable.

A turn is 'one LLM call + zero-to-many tool dispatches that follow'. The loop increments `current_max_turns` once per iteration; terminates when LLM returns no tool calls or `max_turns + 1` is exceeded.

A cycle ≈ one model call + zero-or-more tool calls. Loop continues until `stop_reason in {end_turn,max_tokens,cancelled,interrupt,stop_sequence}` then `EventLoopStopEvent` yields. Each tool batch recurses into a fresh cycle.

A cycle is the unit (`Meter.startCycle/endCycle`): one model call + any triggered tools. `stopReason` enum (`endTurn|toolUse|maxTokens|stopSequence|guardrailIntervened|cancelled|interrupt`) signals turn outcomes.

A step = one LLM call + zero-or-more parallel tool executions. `stopWhen` predicates (default `isStepCount(20)` for ToolLoopAgent, `isStepCount(1)` for raw generateText) define termination. `step-start`/`step-finish` chunks first-class.

Go 1.23 `iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error]` everywhere — no EventEmitter, no channel, no callback hell. Every layer (agent, runner, flow, sub-agents) returns the same type, composable via `for ev, err := range agent.Run(ctx)`. Bidi RunLive wraps a channel back into iter.Seq2.

Plain Python `yield` from `_run_stream`/`_arun_stream` yields `RunOutputEvent` instances. 39 distinct event types across run/hook/tool/reasoning/memory/session/parser/model/compression/followups/custom categories.

Events emitted via `mpsc::Sender<Event>` on `Context.tx` through an `EventHelper` wrapper. Two consumption modes: DirectAgent has `rx: BoxEventStream<Event>` with `subscribe_events()` fanout; ActorAgent uses runtime broadcast or single consumer.

anyio memory-object stream (asyncio Queue equivalent) with `max_buffer_size=100`. Transport read loop pushes; `receive_messages()` pops. Single unified iterator carries all event categories. Backpressure via bounded buffer.

AsyncGenerator on `Query` extending it with control methods. Each yielded value is a discriminated union member of `SDKMessage`. Node process parses stdout JSONL from CLI, peels off control frames, yields the rest as typed messages.

Singleton `CrewAIEventsBus` with separate sync and async handler queues. Sync handlers dispatched to a `ThreadPoolExecutor`; async via a daemon thread running an asyncio loop. 151 BaseEvent subclasses. `Crew(stream=True)` wires bus into queue for StreamChunk yields.

`*AsyncIterator[*AgentEvent]` backed by an unbounded Go channel (`internal.UnboundedChan`). `AsyncIteratorPair[T]` constructs the iterator/generator pair. Consumer loops via `iter.Next()`; producer via `gen.Send`/`gen.Close`.

Streaming uses `ModelStreamCallback = func(context.Context, *ModelResponseChunk) error` plus `GenerateStream` `iter.Seq2`. No async EventEmitter or topic bus; just a callback or an iterator. Limited event taxonomy compared to peers.

Per-call `SyncQueue`/`asyncio.Queue` carries frames between super-step ticks. 7 stream modes: values/updates/messages/custom/checkpoints/tasks/debug. `StreamMessagesHandler` callback installed at run start emits per-token frames. `GraphCallbackHandler` parallel callback channel.

Two complementary mechanisms: step-routing events emitted via `return` or `ctx.send_event(ev)` (fan-out) with `ctx.collect_events` fan-in; plus `ctx.write_event_to_stream(event)` consumer stream. `handler.stream_events()` is the async iterator surface.

Web-standard `ReadableStream<ChunkType>` (not EventEmitter or async generator). `MastraModelOutput` wraps it and exposes `fullStream` plus per-property promises (text, usage, toolCalls, toolResults, finishReason, messageList).

Async generator-style: Python returns `AsyncIterable[AgentResponseUpdate]`; .NET returns `IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate>`. Middleware wraps via `with_transform_hook`/`with_result_hook`. Separate `WorkflowEvent` taxonomy for the workflow layer.

Internal `asyncio.Queue[StreamEvent | QueueCompleteSentinel]`. Background run-loop task writes; `RunResultStreaming.stream_events()` reads. Separate `_input_guardrail_queue` for streaming guardrail trips. Rich `StreamEvent` union (Raw/RunItem/AgentUpdated).
Two mechanisms: runner/agent lifecycle EventEmitter (agent_start/end/handoff/tool_start/end) plus `StreamedRunResult` async iterable of `RunStreamEvent` (raw model / run-item / agent-updated).

`Agent.run_stream_events()` returns an `AgentEventStream` async context manager yielding `AgentStreamEvent | AgentRunResultEvent`. Each graph node implements `async def stream(ctx) -> AsyncIterator[AgentStreamEvent]`. `event` capability hook + `run_event_stream` interception.

Non-streaming path returns `PromptResponse` after the entire loop — no event stream. Streaming uses `futures::Stream<MultiTurnStreamItem<R>>`. Hook callbacks are orthogonal regardless of mode. Tracing spans cover GenAI semconv fields.

Pure async generator: `Agent._run_loop` yields `TypedEvent` instances; `stream_async` routes each event through `event.prepare()` and `callback_handler(**event.as_dict())`. Rich taxonomy across lifecycle/model/tool/multi-agent/hook event groups.

Native `AsyncGenerator<AgentStreamEvent, AgentResult, undefined>` from `Agent.stream()`. Every yielded value is a class instance from the `AgentStreamEvent` discriminated union. Hooks invoked synchronously inline via `_invokeCallbacks` before each yield, allowing event mutation.

Two parallel mechanisms both driven by `notify({event, callbacks})`: push callbacks (`onStepStart/onLanguageModelCallStart/End/onToolExecutionStart/End/onStepFinish/onFinish`) and pull async iterator `streamText(...).fullStream: AsyncIterableStream<TextStreamPart<TOOLS>>`.
No built-in fallback. retryandreflect plugin retries tool errors not model errors. You write an OnModelErrorCallback to retry on different model. Native providers limited to Gemini + Apigee Vertex.

First-class FallbackConfig in libs/agno/agno/models/fallback.py:20-40 with separate fallback lists for on_error, on_rate_limit, on_context_overflow plus optional callback for instrumentation. Shortcut Agent(fallback_models=[...]). 49 native providers.

First-class FallbackLayer in crates/autoagents-llm/src/optim/fallback.rs:64. Composes with RetryLayer via PipelineBuilder. default_is_fallbackable classifies HttpError, ProviderError, NoToolSupport as fallback-eligible; Auth and InvalidRequest propagate.

fallback_model: str on ClaudeAgentOptions (types.py:1679-1680) is single-step only, not a multi-rung chain. On overage/outage the underlying CLI falls back. ResultMessage.model_usage shows the split. Anthropic-only providers.

Options.fallbackModel (sdk.d.ts:1301) is single-step fallback triggered by API errors and rate-limit responses, not a chain of N models. Issue #313 requests exposing retry policy controls. Anthropic providers via gateway abstraction (firstParty/bedrock/vertex/foundry/etc).

No built-in cross-provider fallback. max_retry_limit=2 on Agent (agent/core.py:242) retries the same task on error but does not switch models. Workaround is LiteLLM's intra-provider retries. Native SDKs for OpenAI/Anthropic/Azure/Bedrock/Gemini plus LiteLLM.

ModelRetryConfig (adk/chatmodel.go:307) retries on the same model with backoff; not a fallback chain. To fall back to a different model you write a WrapModel that catches errors and dispatches to a backup. 11 first-party adapters.

Fallback middleware (plugins/middleware/fallback.go:59-70) accepts an ordered ModelRef list; triggers on UNAVAILABLE, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, INTERNAL etc. with configurable Statuses. Composes with Retry middleware (exponential backoff + jitter) in Retry{Fallback{model}} pattern.

langchain-core Runnable.with_fallbacks([fallback_model, ...]) is usable on the model passed to create_react_agent. Fires on Exception; you encode policy yourself. No built-in retry-on-rate-limit-with-different-provider semantic.

Not first-class in core. There is a Cloudflare AI Gateway integration that provides fallback, and you can wrap an LLM with retry/fallback yourself. 104 LLM integrations but no built-in fallback primitive.

loop() takes a models array (packages/core/src/loop/loop.ts:13); if the first model fails Mastra retries on the next. MODEL_GENERATION spans are re-stamped if a fallback served the request. No per-error-category classification like agno.

MAF does not ship a fallback decorator. Microsoft.Extensions.AI ecosystem has DistributedCachingChatClient and LoggingChatClient decorators and community-provided fallback decorators exist, but nothing first-class in MAF itself.

RetryPolicy (src/agents/retry.py) wraps individual model calls with structured retry advice including ModelRetryAdvice and ModelRetryBackoffSettings. Cross-provider fallback is BYO: wrap Runner.run in try/except and re-run with different RunConfig.model. No with_fallbacks builder.

getResponseWithRetry / getStreamedResponseWithRetry in packages/agents-core/src/runner/modelRetry.ts retries within a single provider. No automatic provider-fallback chain; you implement it as a custom ModelProvider wrapping multiple Model instances.

FallbackModel (models/fallback.py:69) wraps an ordered list of Model instances; on ResponseRejected or configured exception types falls through to the next. Pydantic AI Gateway adds load-balanced routing groups. Native providers across 14 vendors.
No retry-on-fallback-model mechanism. You write your own wrapper. 26 in-tree providers but no fallback or routing primitive.

ModelRetryStrategy (event_loop/_retry.py) is registered as a default hook with max_attempts=6, initial_delay=4s, max_delay=240s but retries the same model. For cross-provider fallback BYO via a custom Model wrapper or a hook that swaps agent.model on AfterModelCallEvent.exception.

DefaultModelRetryStrategy (strands-ts/src/retry/default-model-retry-strategy.ts) retries the same model on throttling/transient errors with exponential backoff. To swap providers on failure you write a custom ModelRetryStrategy or react to AfterModelCallEvent.error from a hook by mutating event.agent.model.

customProvider({ fallbackProvider }) (packages/ai/src/registry/custom-provider.ts) falls back to another provider only if the model id is missing, not on error. LanguageModelMiddleware.wrapGenerate/wrapStream lets you implement retry/fallback yourself. AI Gateway hosted product has it but not configurable from the SDK.

Each llmagent has its own Model model.LLM (llmagent.Config.Model). Different agents (supervisor vs workers) can use different models; within one agent the model is fixed. Cheap-for-triage pattern is architected as a triage agent delegating to a hard-work agent via agenttool or transfer_to_agent.

Model is assigned per agent (not per run), but additional task-specialist overrides exist: parser_model (agent.py:293), output_model (agent.py:297), reasoning_model (agent.py:192). agent.run(model=...) is not supported, so per-call routing requires multiple agents in a Team.

AgentBuilder::llm(Arc<dyn LLMProvider>) lets each agent take its own LLM, so different agents have different models. There is no built-in router that picks a model per task; the FallbackLayer and RetryLayer give composable primitives but no per-task selection primitive.

Sub-agent override via AgentDefinition.model (types.py:92). No per-call model option at run() level; the model is fixed on the session unless you transfer to a different sub-agent. Less flexible than the TypeScript SDK which exposes set_model at turn boundary.

Three layers: per-session Options.model (sdk.d.ts:1502), per-sub-agent AgentDefinition.model (sdk.d.ts:56), mid-session Query.setModel (sdk.d.ts:2076) at turn boundary. Aliases sonnet/opus/haiku supported. Cheap supervisor + expensive worker is straightforward.

Per-Agent llm setting and separately configurable manager_llm, function_calling_llm, planning_llm, chat_llm on Crew (crew.py:241-335). Native SDKs include OpenAI/Anthropic/Azure/Bedrock/Gemini plus LiteLLM. No first-party gateway that auto-routes by task class.

note: 3 — sub-agents plus WrapModel and skill middleware
details: Not first-class as a router, but achievable via different sub-agents (each ChatModelAgentConfig.Model independent) and WrapModel to swap models per turn. skill middleware can specify model: <name> per skill, fetched from ModelHub (adk/middlewares/skill/skill.go:79-88), giving per-skill model selection.

Per-call via ai.WithModelName(name) or ai.WithModel(modelRef) (go/ai/option.go:233-244). No registry/gateway; you write the dispatch logic in your code (e.g. switch on task type). Sub-agent overrides trivial since sub-agents are tools that call Generate.

Dynamic model selection (chat_agent_executor.py:325-356, 598-618). The model argument to create_react_agent can be a callable (state, runtime) -> BaseChatModel evaluated on every turn, enabling tier-based or task-based routing in code. Native via any langchain-* provider.

Each agent has its own llm field (base_agent.py:111-113). Different LLMs for each sub-agent in an AgentWorkflow (e.g. orchestrator Sonnet, workers Haiku). No first-party Router cheap-for-triage/expensive-for-hard abstraction; you build it as a routing tool or custom step.

note: 5 — dynamic model and streamOptions and prepareStep
details: model: DynamicArgument<MastraModelConfig> on Agent supports dynamic selection by requestContext (e.g. tier-based). Per-call streamOptions.model overrides. processInputStep can return { model: new model } mid-loop. Most flexible routing surface alongside vercel-ai and pydantic-ai.

No first-party gateway or router. You instantiate a different ChatClient per agent and select at construction time. For dynamic routing you write a custom IChatClient decorator. Sub-agent overrides are trivial via agent_as_tool composition.

Per-agent model override (Agent.model at src/agents/agent.py:311) plus per-run model override (RunConfig.model at src/agents/run_config.py:206) that forces every agent in the run to use a specific model. MultiProvider routes by string prefix (litellm/anthropic/...).

Per-agent (new Agent({ model })), per-run override (new Runner({ model }) or RunConfig.model), per-asTool override (Agent.asTool({ runConfig: { model } }) — see examples/agent-patterns/agents-as-tools.ts:33-39). No first-party registry but custom ModelProvider can route.

note: 5 — model kwarg on every run plus callable settings
details: model= kwarg on every run*() overrides the agent-level default. model_settings / AgentModelSettings (agent/__init__.py:177) accept a callable that receives RunContext and returns settings, enabling cheap-for-triage / expensive-for-hard-tasks routing inside one agent.

Not provided as a routing primitive. You build a different Agent per model (cheap = client.agent(GPT_4O_MINI), expensive = client.agent(GPT_5_2)) and choose which to call. OpenRouter provider gives per-call model selection at the API layer but framework has no first-party routing.

Per-agent. Each Agent instance has one model: Model. To route by task you build multiple Agent instances and switch with a manual dispatcher, or use the agent-as-tool pattern where each sub-agent uses a different model. No first-party gateway/router.

You pass model: Model | string per Agent (agent.ts:140). For per-task routing, instantiate multiple Agents (each with their own model) and dispatch to the right one, or use Graph/Swarm with different model on each node. No first-party gateway/router.

Three patterns: per-call model switch (pass different model to generate/streamText), prepareStep returning { model } to swap mid-loop, customProvider({ languageModels }) for aliases like 'chat-cheap' → gpt-4o-mini and 'chat-strong' → gpt-5. 50+ provider packages.

Each llmagent.New gets its own Model. A supervisor on Gemini Pro plus workers on Gemini Flash is the natural pattern. Different agents (supervisor vs workers, parent vs sub-agent) can use different models.
Each Team.members[i] is itself an Agent with its own model. Supervisor Claude / worker Haiku is straightforward. Composition via Team is the canonical pattern.

Every AgentBuilder takes its own llm naturally. You can wire Sonnet to a supervisor agent and Haiku to worker agents on the same runtime. No explicit override API; you just construct each sub-agent with the model you want.

AgentDefinition.model (types.py:92) is the first-class override (e.g. model='haiku'). Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers is the canonical pattern. Reuses the same CLI session with sub-agent-scoped model.
AgentDefinition.model (sdk.d.ts:56) is exactly this; set to 'haiku' for cheap workers, leave the parent on 'opus'. Required-but-trivial for tenant cost control.
Each sub-agent has its own llm. Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers crew is trivial via Process.hierarchical with manager_agent=supervisor. Native multi-model patterns documented.

Each ChatModelAgentConfig.Model is independent. NewChatModelAgent with claudeOpus for supervisor and claudeHaiku for workers, wired via SetSubAgents. Or via the prebuilt supervisor (adk/prebuilt/supervisor/supervisor.go).

Sub-agents are tools that internally call Generate; each can specify a different ai.WithModelName(...). Supervisor on gemini-2.5-pro, persona workers on gemini-2.5-flash is fully supported. No dedicated sub-agent abstraction but the pattern is trivial.
Each subgraph (sub-agent) is built with its own model argument. Sonnet-supervisor + Haiku-worker is the standard pattern. Dynamic model callable allows mixing too.

Each sub-agent in AgentWorkflow has its own llm (multi_agent_workflow.py:140 builds self.agents = {cfg.name: cfg for cfg in agents}; each cfg.llm is independent). Orchestrator on Sonnet, workers on Haiku is straightforward.
Every sub-agent declares its own model. Supervisor Opus + workers on Sonnet/Haiku is the canonical pattern. Dynamic model selection by requestContext makes per-tenant model routing easy.

Each sub-agent can be constructed with its own ChatClient so Sonnet supervisor + Haiku workers is straightforward via agent_as_tool composition. Implicit override since each agent is built independently.
Each Agent has its own model field, so a supervisor on gpt-5.1 can dispatch to a worker on gpt-5-mini via as_tool() or handoff. Per-run RunConfig.model can also force a uniform model across a run.

Agent.asTool({ runConfig: { model: 'gpt-5.4-mini' } }) — see examples/agent-patterns/agents-as-tools.ts:33-39. Handoff-target agents can each pin their own model. Per-agent and per-run also supported.

Each Agent instance carries its own model; agent delegation can mix any models. The doc warns USD computation may be limited if you mix providers (docs/multi-agent-applications.md:22-23) but the override itself is unrestricted.

Implicitly yes: each sub-agent is a separate Agent<M> and can be on a different model than the parent (parent wraps the sub-agent via agent/tool.rs:16-50). There's no explicit override API; you construct the sub-agent with the model you want.

Each sub-agent (whether as_tool(), Graph node, or Swarm node) carries its own model, so e.g. a Sonnet supervisor with Haiku workers is straightforward. Standard pattern across all multi-agent primitives.
Each sub-agent has its own model config: const supervisor = new Agent({ model: sonnet, tools: [haikuWorker] }) with haikuWorker on a different model. Standard pattern.
Trivial since sub-agents are BYO; you just instantiate each ToolLoopAgent with whatever model you want. No dedicated sub-agent abstraction but pattern is straightforward. customProvider aliases help.
No built-in summarizer or rolling-window. IncludeContents has only `default` or `none`. You implement a BeforeModelCallback that summarizes when message count exceeds a threshold.

CompressionManager compresses tool results when compress_tool_results=True. No automatic message-history compaction; hard caps via num_history_messages / num_history_runs. enable_session_summaries can produce a summary you can inject manually.
SlidingWindowMemory with TrimStrategy::Summarize marks memory as needs_summary on overflow but never actually summarizes. You call MemoryProvider::replace_with_summary externally.

CLI implements automatic context-window compaction near the limit. PreCompact hook fires with trigger=manual/auto and custom_instructions. ContextUsageResponse exposes thresholds and live get_context_usage().
Built-in CLI auto-compaction with PreCompact and PostCompact hooks. SDKCompactBoundaryMessage marks where compaction happened with preserved_segment for resume. /compact slash command available.
respect_context_window=True invokes handle_context_length on context-length-exceeded exceptions; summarizes/truncates reactively. Not proactive and no PreCompact hook.
adk/middlewares/summarization ships first-class summarization with configurable token threshold (default 190k)
No built-in summarization/truncation. You write a WrapGenerate middleware that watches len(messages) or token count and rewrites earlier messages into a summary.

Not built into OSS runtime. pre_model_hook is the documented place to wire summarization/trimming. langchain-core ships trim_messages; community/deepagents ship a compress tool. No first-party primitive.

Memory has token-budget-driven FIFO flush at chat_history_token_ratio threshold. Memory.memory_blocks lets you plug FactExtractionMemoryBlock for summarization. ChatSummaryMemoryBuffer is deprecated path.
TokenLimiterProcessor and BatchPartsProcessor ship built-in; trigger when token budget exceeded with drop-oldest strategy. LLM-summarized compaction is BYO via custom processor.

CompactionProvider with ContextWindowCompactionStrategy / SummarizationCompactionStrategy / ToolResultCompactionStrategy / ChatReducerCompactionStrategy / PipelineCompactionStrategy. HarnessAgent wires this by default in .NET.

OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession (521 LOC) with run_compaction supporting auto / previous_response_id / input modes; coordinates with server-side compaction on OpenAI. No support for non-OpenAI providers.

OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession wrapper calls responses.compact on OpenAI side after each turn with configurable force/compactionMode. Not built into MemorySession or generic stores; OpenAI-Responses-only.
Provider-native compaction via OpenAICompaction and AnthropicCompaction capabilities. No provider-agnostic compaction in core; ProcessHistory capability lets you plug a custom summarizer.
Not in core. rig-memory ships sliding-window and token-budget policies that filter history during memory load. InMemoryConversationMemory::with_filter takes a closure that shapes history each load.

SlidingWindowConversationManager (default 40 msgs) and SummarizingConversationManager (LLM summary with configurable prompt) ship as first-class conversation managers. Triggers each cycle and on ContextWindowOverflowException.

ConversationManager base with reduce() runs reactively on ContextWindowOverflowError and proactively before BeforeModelCallEvent. SlidingWindow (default 40) and Summarizing managers shipped. Proactive trigger at projectedInputTokens/contextWindowLimit > 0.7.
Not provided. You use prepareStep to truncate messages before each call or LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams to compact at provider level. No first-party summarize-and-truncate.

Two callback layers — plugin.Config (across all agents) and llmagent.Config (per agent) — plus agent.Config BeforeAgent/AfterAgent. 12 named callbacks including OnUserMessage / BeforeRun / AfterRun / OnEvent / BeforeModel / AfterModel / OnModelError / BeforeTool / AfterTool / OnToolError. No SessionStart specifically; no PreCompact.

pre_hooks and post_hooks on Agent/Team plus tool_hooks (nested middleware chain) and per-Function pre_hook/post_hook. Guardrails subclass pre/post. No SessionStart or per-LLM-call hook beyond pre/post-of-run.

AgentHooks trait has 9 methods including on_run_start / on_turn_start / on_tool_call / on_tool_result. All observe-only or abort-only; no pre/post-LLM-call hooks. Single registered hooks impl per agent struct (no fan-out).

Documented HookEvent type with PreToolUse / PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure / UserPromptSubmit / SessionStart / Stop / SubagentStop / SubagentStart / PreCompact / Notification / PermissionRequest. Reported as the most comprehensive hook system among Python SDKs.

HOOK_EVENTS exposes 29 distinct lifecycle events including Pre/Post tool/batch/compact and many session/permission/elicitation/worktree variants. Described as the most comprehensive hook surface across the studied stacks.

note: 3 — four typed hook types + crew callbacks
details: before_llm_call / after_llm_call / before_tool_call / after_tool_call plus Crew.before_kickoff / after_kickoff / step_callback / task_callback. Narrow but well-typed. No SessionStart / PreCompact / UserPromptSubmit equivalents.

callbacks.Handler with OnStart/OnEnd/OnError/StreamInput/StreamOutput plus deprecated AgentMiddleware and new ChatModelAgentMiddleware (BeforeAgent / BeforeModelRewriteState / AfterModelRewriteState / WrapInvokableToolCall / WrapStreamableToolCall / WrapModel). Strong coverage of LLM-call and tool-call lifecycle.

Middleware contract returns Hooks with WrapGenerate (each tool-loop iteration) / WrapModel (each API call) / WrapTool (each tool exec). Plus passive Tools[]. No traditional lifecycle hooks like SessionStart / BeforeMessage / OnTurnComplete.

pre_model_hook (before LLM) and post_model_hook (after LLM) as graph nodes; wrap_tool_call / awrap_tool_call as ToolNode wrappers. Plus GraphCallbackHandler (interrupt/resume) and full LangChain BaseCallbackHandler surface. No PreCompact or SessionStart-specific hooks.

No first-class hook system. Closest is subclassing BaseWorkflowAgent @step methods (init_run / setup_agent / run_agent_step / parse_agent_output / call_tool / aggregate_tool_results) plus FunctionTool(callback=...) for post-tool. Dispatcher events are observe-only.

Processor interface with 8 slots: processInput / processInputStep / processLLMRequest / processLLMResponse / processOutputStream / processOutputStep / processOutputResult / processAPIError. Plus onChunk/onStepFinish/onFinish/onError/onAbort/onIterationComplete and delegation callbacks. Covers every pre/post point cleanly.

note: 4 — three middleware types + context provider lifecycle
details: AgentMiddleware / ChatMiddleware / FunctionMiddleware plus ContextProvider with before_run / after_run / before_chat_call / after_chat_call. ResponseStream hooks for streaming. Builder hooks in .NET. No SessionStart/PreCompact specifically but functional equivalents available.

RunHooks/AgentHooks with on_llm_start/end / on_agent_start/end / on_handoff / on_tool_start/end (read-only). Plus four guardrail decorators (tool input/output can mutate) and RunConfig.call_model_input_filter / session_input_callback / tool_error_formatter. Lifecycle hooks are read-only.

RunHooks/AgentHooks emit agent_start/end/handoff/tool_start/end (read-only). Input/output guardrails plus ToolInputGuardrail and ToolOutputGuardrail which can mutate or block. RunConfig.callModelInputFilter and sessionInputCallback. No first-class PostToolUse mutation; no SessionStart specifically.

Hooks capability exposes before_/after_/wrap_/on_*_error variants for run/node/model_request/tool_validate/tool_execute/output_validate/output_process. Plus prepare_tools / deferred_tool_calls / run_event_stream / event. Tool filters and timeouts supported. Broadest hook taxonomy in the comparison.

PromptHook trait has on_completion_call / on_completion_response / on_tool_call / on_tool_result / on_text_delta / on_tool_call_delta / on_stream_completion_response_finish. All read-only with only HookAction::Terminate / ToolCallHookAction::Skip available. No mutate-args / mutate-result.

Hookable events: AgentInitialized / BeforeInvocation / AfterInvocation / MessageAdded / BeforeModelCall / AfterModelCall / BeforeToolCall / AfterToolCall. Plus multi-agent variants and experimental Bidi. Hooks dispatched in reverse for After* events.

InitializedEvent / BeforeInvocation / AfterInvocation / MessageAdded / BeforeModelCall / AfterModelCall / BeforeTools / AfterTools / BeforeToolCall / AfterToolCall plus ContentBlock / ModelStream / ModelMessage / ToolStream / ToolResult / AgentResult / Interrupt. HookOrder enum (SDK_FIRST/INTERVENTION_OUTPUT/DEFAULT/INTERVENTION_INPUT/SDK_LAST).

prepareCall (once) / prepareStep (per step) / experimental_onStart / experimental_onStepStart / experimental_onLanguageModelCallStart/End / onToolExecutionStart/End / onStepFinish / onFinish plus per-tool onInputStart/Delta/Available / toModelOutput and LanguageModelMiddleware (transformParams / wrapGenerate / wrapStream). No SessionStart or PreCompact.

BeforeModelCallback mutates *model.LLMRequest; AfterModelCallback mutates/replaces *model.LLMResponse; BeforeToolCallback mutates args map[string]any in place; AfterToolCallback mutates result map. Plugin BeforeRun returns content to short-circuit. Cannot inject additional tool calls.

pre_hooks mutate run_input; post_hooks mutate run_output (or raise InputCheckError/OutputCheckError). tool_hooks form nested chain mutating args and results. Cannot mutate per-LLM-call messages directly. No additional_messages from post tool.

Hooks are observe-and-abort: on_run_start / on_tool_call return HookOutcome::Continue or Abort. on_tool_call args are &ToolCall (not mut). on_tool_result is observe-only. Mutation patterns require executor-layer overrides.

Hook output schema includes continue_ / decision: block / systemMessage / reason / hookSpecificOutput with updatedInput on PreToolUse and updatedToolOutput on PostToolUse plus additionalContext on SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit. Can block

Hook outputs support updatedInput (PreToolUse) / updatedToolOutput / updatedMCPToolOutput (PostToolUse) / additionalContext / permissionDecision / suppressOriginalPrompt / initialUserMessage / watchPaths. Multiple matchers merge with last-wins on updatedInput. Async hooks supported.

before_llm_call mutates messages in place; after_llm_call returns str to replace response; before_tool_call mutates tool_input dict; after_tool_call returns str to replace result. before_kickoff returns modified inputs. No additional_messages equivalent.

BeforeModelRewriteState mutates the message list to be sent to model; WrapInvokableToolCall wraps endpoint to mutate args and results; WrapModel can replace the model entirely. callbacks.Handler observers only. Cannot synthesize tool messages mid-step.

Only stack with first-class additional-tool-calls-from-hook.

Override @step methods (init_run / setup_agent / call_tool / aggregate_tool_results) for read/mutate/block/branch. FunctionTool callback returns ToolOutput or str to override. partial_params only fills defaults; LLM values still win. ctx.send_event(ToolCall) can route additional calls but not as a first-class hook.

Per-tool toModelOutput rewrites results.

Error hooks can recover.

Hooks expose &Message / &str args; mutation is absent everywhere. on_tool_call can return ToolCallHookAction::Skip{reason} which returns reason as tool result (the only way to short-circuit). on_tool_result is purely observational.

model.LLMRequest.Config can carry CachedContent (Gemini)

Reports cache_read_tokens / cache_write_tokens in Metrics and surfaces them in ModelRequestCompletedEvent. Does not automatically place Anthropic/OpenAI cache breakpoints. Stable prefixes arranged manually via instructions and add_history_to_context.

CacheLayer in LLM pipeline is a result cache (same input → same response) not stable-prefix breakpoints. No automatic cache_control insertion; you manage it in provider wrapper or ChatMessage construction.

CLI auto-handles Anthropic prompt-caching; cache tokens surfaced on AssistantMessage.usage. SystemPromptPreset.exclude_dynamic_sections strips per-user dynamic sections out of system prompt and re-injects into first user message (cross-user cache hits). Manual breakpoint placement is CLI-owned.

Three mechanisms: SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY constant splits static (cacheable cross-session) from dynamic suffix; excludeDynamicSections strips per-user dynamic sections for cross-user cache hits; CLI auto-places breakpoints for stable-prefix content. Cache stats on SDKResultMessage.usage.

Manual breakpoints with mark_cache_breakpoint helper; tagged on system prompt and per-task user prompt in _setup_messages. Provider adapter translates cache_breakpoint=True into Anthropic cache_control: ephemeral. OpenAI/Gemini cache implicitly so marker stripped. Engineering is solid but not a hook-surface.

Provider-cache-aware indirectly via message-list stability — Anthropic/OpenAI cache lands naturally if you append rather than prepend. No first-class cache_control breakpoint helper; you set provider-specific fields via *schema.Message.Extra. PromptTokenDetails.CachedTokens observable.

googlegenai plugin has explicit cache support (plugins/googlegenai/cache.go) — attach cachedContents reference. No generic prompt-cache-breakpoint mechanism across providers. Each plugin handles its own provider's cache features.

Provider-aware via pre_model_hook: engineers wire Anthropic cache_control flags into specific SystemMessage/HumanMessage content blocks; the hook ensures stable prefix. No automatic breakpoint placement.
Not first-class. ChatMessage supports a CachePoint content block which Anthropic/OpenAI providers honor — but framework does not auto-place breakpoints; the developer inserts them.

Built-in ResponseCacheProcessor caches full LLM responses (processLLMRequest returns cached chunks). Anthropic-style cache breakpoints are not auto-managed; you place them in system prompt yourself or via a processor.

No first-party prompt-cache breakpoint controller. Providers (Anthropic) handle cache via their own ChatClient (agent-framework-anthropic sets breakpoints). MAF does not expose a generic stable-prefix knob.

prompt_cache_key.py defines PromptCacheKeyResolver; runner generates a per-run cache key (RunResult._generated_prompt_cache_key) threaded via model_settings_with_prompt_cache_key. Opts into OpenAI's prompt-caching tier. Anthropic-style breakpoints not natively wired.

Passes previousResponseId to OpenAI Responses API for server-side caching. Does not manage Anthropic-style cache_control breakpoints. ai-sdk extension caching depends on underlying Vercel AI provider.

Cache breakpoints first-class: CachePoint message part; cache_write_tokens / cache_read_tokens on RequestUsage; provider-specific model-settings flags (e.g. bedrock_supports_prompt_caching). InstructionPart split into static vs dynamic so stable prefix is cache-friendly.

Usage struct exposes cached_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens — observe cache hit rate per turn. No automatic cache-breakpoint placement; configure provider-side caching via provider's additional_params.

system_prompt accepts a list[SystemContentBlock] including cachePoint blocks; Message content blocks also accept cachePoint. BedrockModel and AnthropicModel wire them to API. Manual placement; AgentSkills plugin demonstrates preserving cache points while injecting skills XML.

Per-provider Model.CacheConfig with strategy auto (inject after tools + last user msg) or anthropic. CachePointBlock carries markers. Bedrock + Anthropic providers wire this in; OpenAI doesn't need explicit markers.

LanguageModelUsage exposes inputTokenDetails: noCacheTokens / cacheReadTokens / cacheWriteTokens — better visibility than most stacks. SDK does not auto-place Anthropic-style breakpoints; you set provider-specific cache markers via providerOptions or LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams.

compress_tool_results + CompressionManager for in-place compression. store_tool_messages flag to drop tool messages from RunOutput. Skills are a progressive-disclosure pattern: only skill metadata in system prompt; full body fetched on demand via get_skill_instructions/reference/script tools.
Tool results go directly into MemoryAdapter::store_tool_interaction. Only knob is sliding-window size which pushes older messages out. No primitive for stashing or summarizing large outputs.
PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput lets you replace large tool outputs with a summary before the model sees them. No first-party stash-to-filesystem-and-replace-with-budget-summary pattern.

PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput replaces tool result in-place. Built-in Write/Edit/Read tools encode progressive-disclosure naturally (large outputs to disk; model receives path). getContextUsage() exposes per-category breakdown. MCP tool descriptions deferred by default (alwaysLoad:false) until tool-search invoked.

Manual after_tool_call hook to summarize/truncate when over threshold. No filesystem-stash / on-demand-re-read pattern. Skills with RESOURCES disclosure level catalog file lists in prompt; agent fetches contents via separate tool you provide.

adk/middlewares/reduction truncates oversized tool outputs in message list leaving summary. adk/middlewares/filesystem/large_tool_result.go stashes oversized results into a filesystem.Backend and replaces tool message with a short reference + first-10-lines preview suggesting read_file with offset/limit. Closest match to Claude Code progressive disclosure in any Go framework.
Filesystem middleware has file-state dedup (returns fileUnchangedStub when tool re-reads unchanged file). No generic stash-large-tool-outputs-to-disk pattern.
wrap_tool_call can rewrite ToolMessage to summary + pointer; BaseStore is a natural stash backend. No first-party tool-result-clearing primitive.
Not provided. You return a summary string from a FunctionTool async_callback and stash the full payload elsewhere yourself.

Each tool declares toModelOutput to return a truncated/summarized version to LLM while persisting full result in storage (used by sub-agent wrapper). processOutputStream can drop/rewrite tool-result chunks. Workspace+Skills system encourages filesystem stash: tool writes full output to workspace file and returns short summary + path; LLM uses skill_read for slices.

ToolResultCompactionStrategy explicitly clears or summarizes tool results when exceeding a threshold. Skills follow progressive-disclosure pattern (metadata-only in prompt; body loaded on demand via load_skill).

defer_loading on FunctionTool pairs with ToolSearchTool / ToolSearchCallItem / ToolSearchOutputItem — LLM searches a tool catalogue and explicitly loads the ones it wants. For large outputs Codex/Shell tools have tool_output_trimmer; ad-hoc tools use @tool_output_guardrail to summarize.

Not first-class outside of Sandbox Agents. Sandbox Agents have a filesystem workspace where tools can write large outputs to disk and reference them by path. Non-sandbox tools just return their result string to the LLM.

after_tool_execute hook returns a summary instead of raw result. Tool Search capability defers tool loading — tools marked defer_loading=True only included in model's tool list after search_tools meta-tool call. Available native (Anthropic / OpenAI Responses) or local. defer_loading() on any toolset.
Not provided. No filesystem-stash strategy or auto-summarization of large tool outputs. Use rig-memory policy or implement on-the-fly truncation inside the tool's call body.

SlidingWindowConversationManager(should_truncate_results=True) truncates large tool results to first+last 200 chars and replaces images with text placeholders. Vended context_offloader plugin stashes large content out-of-context with fetch-on-demand retrieval.

ContextOffloaderPlugin registers AfterToolCallEvent hook that stores full tool output in configurable Storage keyed by mem_<id> reference and replaces in-context content with preview + reference + sibling retrieve_offloaded_content tool (with grep / line-range). Sliding/summarizing managers also drop or summarize older turns.
Not provided harness-side. tool.toModelOutput lets you summarize at tool-author time but there's no harness-level after-step-N drop-tool-result-from-history. BYO.

`memory.Service` interface with InMemory (keyword) and Vertex AI RAG backends, namespaced per AppName+UserID. LLM accesses via `loadmemorytool`. The framework does not auto-add sessions; you call `AddSessionToMemory` explicitly. Usable, but only Vertex is a real semantic backend out of the box.

First-class `MemoryManager` with `enable_agentic_memory` / `update_memory_on_run` flags. Stores `UserMemory` rows keyed by `user_id` with topics, feedback, timestamps. Auto-extracts facts and auto-injects via `add_memories_to_context`. Strongest fit for cross-session user memory in this benchmark.

No first-party long-term memory abstraction. Provides `VectorStore` trait (in-memory + Qdrant), embeddings, and a `MemoryProvider` slot, but no pre-built cross-session memory. You assemble it yourself.

Partial via on-disk `CLAUDE.md` files loaded by `setting_sources`; `AgentDefinition.memory: 'user'|'project'|'local'` scopes which file a sub-agent sees. No vector store, embeddings, or semantic recall — purely filesystem-shaped.

First-party `agent-memory/<agentType>/` directory recall with selector + LLM-synthesized modes via `SDKMemoryRecallMessage`. User/project/local scopes from `AgentDefinition.memory`. Still file-based, no vector index — semantic retrieval is BYO MCP.

Sophisticated `unified_memory.Memory` with LanceDB/Qdrant backends, automatic fact extraction, hierarchical scope, consolidation, recency/semantic/importance weighting, and adaptive LLM-driven recall flow. Directly fits the benchmark use case for cross-session memory.

No `Memory` type, no `MemoryStore`, no auto-recall. Cross-session memory must be assembled from `components/retriever` plus a custom middleware that injects retrieved snippets — meaningful effort around the framework.
Genkit does not ship a memory abstraction. The closest substitutes are sessions (state, not vector) and retrievers (RAG at query time). You encode any cross-session memory as documents yourself.

`BaseStore` (namespaced KV + optional vector search) is the long-term memory primitive. Postgres+pgvector and in-memory backends ship; tools call `runtime.store.put/search`. Strong, with the minor gap that there is no auto-extract/auto-recall flow built on top.

First-class `Memory.memory_blocks` with `StaticMemoryBlock`, `VectorMemoryBlock`, and `FactExtractionMemoryBlock`. Blocks are processed in priority order and ejected short-term messages are pushed into vector blocks automatically. Directly fits the benchmark.

`@mastra/memory` ships conversation history, working memory (LLM-summarized), semantic recall (vector-backed), and observational memory across threads. Vector store adapters for Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Astra, Lance, Elasticsearch. First-class fit.

Mem0 adapter (`agent-framework-mem0`, `Mem0Provider.cs`) is the main first-party path, with an experimental in-tree `MemoryFileStore`/`MemoryStore` in `_harness/_memory.py`. Plus Azure AI Search and .NET `TextSearchProvider`. Usable but distributed across adapters; main path is Mem0.

Not built-in. The 10 Session backends store turn-level history only. No vector-search long-term memory primitive ships. For RAG/memory you must wire `FileSearchTool` (OpenAI Vector Stores) or a custom `@function_tool`.

No built-in cross-session semantic memory. The only memory surfaces are `Session` (in-conversation) and the sandbox-only filesystem `memory()` capability (scratchpad inside one sandbox run). Cross-session is BYO.

Built-in `MemoryTool` exists but is Anthropic-native with no in-tree local fallback. For provider-agnostic memory you reach for third-party `pydantic-ai-memory`/`pydantic-ai-backend` packages — partial primitive.
