ConversationMemory is in-conversation only. Cross-conversation recall is the combination of `dynamic_context(num_samples, vector_store_index)` plus a `VectorStoreIndexDyn` adapter (12+ companion crates). Partial primitive — you wire the memory layer yourself.

Not in SDK core. `strands-agents-tools` ships `mem0_memory`, `agent_core_memory`, `elasticsearch_memory`, `mongodb_memory` as tools the LLM calls explicitly. Production use is mostly host-built around these tools.

No vector store integration, no embeddings primitive, no memories/facts object. Cross-session continuity is only via re-hydrating from a `SessionManager` snapshot. Long-term semantic memory is fully BYO.
No `Memory` class, no semantic-recall primitive, no concept of cross-session memory in the SDK. Reference report explicitly contrasts this with Mastra/LangGraph. BYO via a vector DB.

Vertex AI RAG via `memory/vertexai/` and the `loadmemorytool` are the only built-in retrieval primitives. No first-party Pinecone/Weaviate/Qdrant/pgvector adapter, no chunkers, no rerankers. You build the rest.

First-class `Knowledge` class with Chroma, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Mongo Atlas, Lance, PgVector, Singlestore, Cassandra, ClickHouse; many embedders and readers; agentic filters; automatic `search_knowledge` tool. Directly fits the benchmark.

Library-level: `document.rs`, `readers/` (PDF etc.), `embeddings/`, `vector_store/` plus Qdrant integration. Examples like `rag_qdrant_agent` show the pattern. You assemble retrieval; the framework provides building blocks.
No first-party RAG. You layer it as an MCP server or SDK tool. No chunkers, vector stores, embedders, or citation primitives ship.
No built-in vector store, no chunker, no retriever, no citation primitive. BYO via MCP server.

`crewai.knowledge.Knowledge` ships 8+ source types (string/text/CSV/JSON/PDF/Excel/Docx/Docling/custom), automatic chunking + embedding, ChromaDB default + Qdrant, multi-embedder support. Wired at agent/crew level. First-class RAG fit.

First-class `Retriever`, `Indexer`, `Embedder`, `Loader`/`Parser`/`Transformer` interfaces and `eino-ext` adapters for Qdrant, Milvus v1/v2, Redis, OpenSearch v2/v3, Elasticsearch v7-v9, Volc VikingDB, Dify. Strong; minor gap is no out-of-the-box citation primitive.

Strong first-party. `ai.Retriever` action type with built-in plugins (localvec, pinecone, weaviate, postgres+pgvector, alloydb, firebase), chunkers, embedders per provider, and a `Reranker` abstraction. `WithDocs(...)` inlines retrieved docs. Minor gap: no citation rendering primitive.
No native retriever; relies on separately-packaged `langchain-*` vector stores. `BaseStore.search()` covers basic semantic recall but no chunkers, no citation, no reranking ship in this repo.

RAG is LlamaIndex's historical core. 60+ vector store integrations, multiple index types (Vector, Summary, Tree, KnowledgeGraph, PropertyGraph), retrievers (Base/Router/Fusion), built-in citation via CitableBlock/CitationBlock. Best fit in the benchmark.
`@mastra/rag` ships retrievers, chunkers (e.g. recursiveChunker), citation support, integrated with the memory vector adapters. First-class.

`.NET TextSearchProvider` plus `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Vector` `IVectorStore` are the generic primitives; Azure AI Search adapter is first-party. Usable, but most stores beyond Azure require BYO or community adapters and no built-in citation.
Hosted only: `FileSearchTool` over OpenAI Vector Stores. For non-OpenAI RAG you write `@function_tool` wrappers. Partial primitive — production use is mostly host-built.
`fileSearchTool` (OpenAI hosted file search over vector stores) is the closest built-in. Otherwise BYO retriever as a function tool. No chunkers/citations in-tree.
Embeddings package with OpenAI/Cohere/Google/Bedrock/sentence-transformers/voyage providers, plus a `docs/examples/rag.md`. Vector stores are BYO. Partial primitive.

First-class: `VectorStoreIndex`/`VectorStoreIndexDyn` traits with 12+ companion crates (mongodb, lancedb, qdrant, sqlite, surrealdb, milvus, scylladb, postgres, s3vectors, neo4j, etc.), `EmbeddingsBuilder`, and `agent.dynamic_context(n, store)` to auto-inline retrieved docs. Strong; gap: no in-tree chunkers/citations.
Via `strands-agents-tools/retrieve.py` (Bedrock Knowledge Base) and memory tools. No first-party chunker / embedder primitives in the SDK core. Partial primitive.

Not provided as a first-class subsystem. The `ContextOffloaderPlugin` (offloads tool results to disk/blob with a `retrieve_offloaded_content` tool) is the closest built-in retrieval pattern. Build a vector-search tool yourself.
Ships `embed`, `embedMany`, `cosineSimilarity`, and `rerank`, but no vector store, chunker, retriever, or citation rendering. Use `@ai-sdk/langchain` / `@ai-sdk/llamaindex` for higher-level RAG.

`SearchRequest.AppName` + `SearchRequest.UserID` give per-user scoping naturally. Tenant scoping is by using `AppName` as the tenant key — pays the cost of fully-isolated memory across apps. Usable, with the gap that there is no separate tenant axis.
`UserMemory.user_id` is the scoping key. Per-tenant means prefixing user IDs (`acme:alice`) or filtering at query time on `metadata`. Usable, but no separate tenant dimension.
Not provided — BYO. You namespace your vector-store collections per tenant. The framework offers no tenancy primitive.
Filesystem-shaped — per-tenant `CLAUDE.md` lives under `tenants/<tid>/` and the SDK loads it via `cwd`. Works but is purely directory-based with no enforcement of tenant boundaries.

Not natural: memory dirs are global-per-machine (`~/.claude/agent-memory/`) or project-scoped under `cwd`. To scope per-tenant you set `cwd: /tenants/${tenantId}`. For true cross-tenant served memory, BYO MCP.

`Memory(root_scope='/tenant/acme')` is the natural fit and prefixes all `remember`/`recall` paths. But the framework does not automatically scope by tenant — you instantiate one `Memory` per tenant manually. Usable, with the gap that there is no runtime `with_tenant` filter.

Retriever `Retrieve(ctx, query, opts...)` receives ctx so you pass tenant scope through; the adapter's `Options.SubIndexes` or query filter respects it. Framework does not enforce — your adapter does. Small primitive only.
Not automatic. Retrievers accept a free-form `Options` (e.g. Pinecone namespace, Postgres WHERE) you encode tenant filters into. No Mastra-style automatic namespacing.

Convention via `BaseStore` namespace tuples like `(tenant_id, 'memories')`. Tightened by `@auth.on.store` at the HTTP layer which injects the tenant prefix server-side so external callers cannot escape it. Strong, with the minor gap that enforcement on raw OSS runtime is still BYO.

`Memory.session_id` is the only first-class scoping key. Per-tenant separation requires encoding `tenant:user:session` into `session_id` or using a per-tenant `SQLAlchemyChatStore` (separate DB/schema). Partial primitive.

Memory scoped per `resourceId` in the `memory: { thread, resource }` tuple. `MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY` is server-controlled so a client cannot read another tenant's memory. Cross-tenant vector separation via index prefixes. First-class fit.

Memory adapters expose `Scope` options (e.g. `Mem0ProviderScope` — `User`, `Session`, `Global`). Tenancy = scope-by-user with tenant ID encoded into the user. Partial primitive — no deeper tenant dimension.
BYO — namespace your vector indexes by tenant_id. No first-party tenancy primitive in the SDK.
Not provided. You namespace yourself by per-tenant `vectorStoreIds` passed to `fileSearchTool`, or by partitioning a custom `Session` implementation. Small primitive only.
Per-tenant scoping is your responsibility — namespace by `tenant_id` in your vector index. No framework primitive.
Not first-class. You scope vector-store collections per tenant yourself (namespace by `tenant_id` in Postgres/Qdrant schema). No framework support.
BYO. The memory tools accept user/agent IDs but tenancy must be encoded in those IDs. Small primitive only.
BYO. Namespace your vector store / DB / S3 prefix by `tenantId` from `invocationState`. No framework support.
BYO — namespace yourself in your vector DB. No first-party tenancy primitive.

First-class SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools) per agentskills.io v1.2 spec. Validators enforce name/description length, directory-name match. Layout includes references/, assets/, scripts/ subfolders.

Native Skills module with SKILL.md + YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, metadata, compatibility, allowed-tools). validate_skill_directory enforces frontmatter parseable + non-empty description. Optional scripts/ and references/ subfolders.
No SKILL.md, no Skill trait, no loader, no directory convention. The term "skill" does not appear in the codebase. Workflow is Rust agent types instead.

SKILL.md format is owned by the bundled Claude Code CLI, not the Python SDK source. The SDK exposes a single skills filter option; format documentation lives in the Node CLI. First-class for the end user but not parsed by Python SDK code.
SKILL.md format is owned by Claude Code CLI, not the TS SDK. SDK doesn't parse frontmatter itself — it reads what the CLI surfaces. First-class for end users authoring skills.

Complete skills/ subsystem (parser, loader, validator, models). SkillFrontmatter Pydantic model with name regex, 1-1024 char description, license, compatibility, allowed-tools (space-delimited), metadata dict. Body up to ~50,000 chars. Directory layout with scripts/, references/, assets/.
SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter including name, description, context (fork/fork_with_context/inline), agent, model. Free-form markdown body. Unique among Go frameworks for the explicit context mode.
SKILL.md with optional minimal YAML frontmatter (just name + description). No validated schema; body is free-form markdown injected verbatim. Loose format vs. competitors' validated schemas.
Grep for SKILL.md / loadSkills / class Skill returns zero matches. Not provided — BYO. Closest analog is BaseStore namespaced memory or langgraph-deepagents template (separate repo).
No SKILL.md analog. LlamaPacks are pip-installable code templates, not markdown skills. Not provided — BYO.

SKILL.md with full frontmatter (name 1-64, path, description 1-1024, license, compatibility, user-invocable, metadata). validateSkillMetadata schema. Layout with references/, scripts/, assets/. Cites the Anthropic skills repo at types.ts:7.

SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, compatibility, allowed_tools, metadata) per agentskills.io spec. Validators for name/description/compatibility. Layout with references/, assets/, scripts/. Still marked @experimental.

Real Skill model with canonical SKILL.md frontmatter (name, description, compatibility) plus scripts/references/assets dicts. Scope is narrower: skills materialize into a sandbox filesystem, not into the LLM prompt directly. Built for Codex / Shell / Apply-Patch sandboxes.
parseSkillFrontmatter parses SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter. SkillDescriptor includes scripts/references/assets entries. Only exposed inside SandboxAgent capability flavor.

No in-tree SKILL.md format. Docs point at third-party pydantic-ai-skills SkillsCapability for agentskills.io support. In-tree analog is AgentSpec YAML (model + capabilities) — config not workflow markdown.
No SKILL.md concept. Word "skill" does not appear as runtime primitive. Closest analog is ToolDefinition.description or Agent.preamble. Not provided — BYO.

AgentSkills vended plugin per agentskills.io spec. SKILL.md with frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, metadata, license, compatibility). _validate_skill_name enforces format + directory-name match (strict mode).

AgentSkills vended plugin compatible with Claude Code SKILL.md format. YAML frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, license, compatibility, metadata). Validates name pattern and directory match.

No SKILL.md concept in the SDK. The upload-skill package is a thin client around Anthropic's /v1/skills HTTP endpoint (upload bundle, get providerReference). SDK never reads SKILL.md locally. Repo-root skills/ is contributor docs.

Toolset injects three tools to the LLM: list_skills, load_skill, load_skill_resource. Plus a system instruction injection appending XML list of name+description for every request. The model invokes via tool_use.

Hybrid: skill metadata (name, description, scripts/references lists) injected into system prompt as <skills_system> XML block. Three auto-generated tools: get_skill_instructions, get_skill_reference, get_skill_script (can execute scripts via subprocess).
N/A — no skills concept.

CLI exposes built-in Skill tool. Model calls Skill(name="X") which loads SKILL.md body into context. SDK auto-configures setting_sources + allowed_tools when options.skills is set. Observable from Python as ToolUseBlock.
Same CLI-backed Skill tool as Python SDK. Skill list emitted in SDKSystemMessage.skills. Lazy fetch by tool_use with name 'Skill'. Options.skills filters which skills are visible.

System-prompt injection via format_skill_context wraps each skill in <skill name="..."> tags rendered at construction time. No read_skill tool by default — resources cataloged in prompt but not auto-fetched. Bodies live entirely in the system prompt.

LLM sees a skill tool. Inline mode returns markdown body as tool result. Fork mode spawns a sub-agent with skill content as system message. Fork-with-context replays parent history. Per-skill model override via WrapModel.
System prompt injects <skills> block listing names+descriptions. Model calls use_skill(skillName) tool which reads SKILL.md and returns body as tool result.
Not provided — BYO. Common pattern uses pre_model_hook to search BaseStore and append SystemMessage; no built-in tool or registry.
N/A — no skills concept. tool_retriever is for tools not skills. BYO loader producing a FunctionTool wrapper is the closest pattern.

SkillsProcessor injects metadata-only <available_skills> XML block. Three tools: skill(name) loads instructions, skill_search(query, topK) BM25/vector/hybrid search, skill_read(skillName, path, lineRange) reads bundled files with binary detection.
Three tools per agentskills.io spec: load_skill, read_skill_resource, run_skill_script (registered only if any skill has scripts). System prompt holds names+descriptions; bodies fetched on demand.

System prompt holds skill index (name + description + path). For lazy skills a synthetic load_skill function tool fetches body into sandbox. For eager skills the LLM is instructed to open SKILL.md directly via shell tool. Not a tool-call per skill — relies on filesystem access.

Capability.instructions injects available-skills section into agent instructions. Lazy mode adds load_skill tool to materialize skill files on demand. Eager mode materializes into .agents/<skill>/ and shows full metadata.
In-tree: capabilities are added via Agent constructor or AgentSpec YAML. Third-party SkillsCapability reportedly uses progressive disclosure with skill_read-style tool — not in this repo.
Not provided. Would have to stuff skill markdown into preamble or dynamic_context manually.
<available_skills> XML block in system prompt with name+description+location. LLM calls skills(skill_name) tool which returns full instructions plus list of bundled scripts/references/assets.

BeforeInvocationEvent injects <available_skills> XML block into systemPrompt. Registered skills tool returns Skill.instructions body when LLM calls with skill_name. Activation tracked in agent.appState.
No SDK-side invocation. uploadSkill posts to Anthropic /v1/skills and returns providerReference; the model sees skills only because Anthropic's server attaches them. No local invocation primitive.

Lazy. Only frontmatters (name + description) are in the system prompt; bodies are fetched only when the agent calls load_skill. Resources are fetched via separate load_skill_resource tool. WithFrontmatterPreloadSource caches metadata only.

Progressive disclosure: only metadata in prompt; agent must call get_skill_instructions to load body. get_skill_reference fetches reference files. get_skill_script reads or executes scripts. Matches Anthropic Agent Skills pattern.
N/A — no skills concept.

Metadata (name + description from frontmatter) goes in the system prompt; full body loads on Skill(name=...) invocation. Confirmed by ContextUsageResponse.skills showing 'frontmatter breakdown'. Native Claude Code design.
Lazy by default — metadata in system prompt; body fetched on use. Options.skills controls which skills are listed (omitted/all/string[]). Body never eagerly loaded.

Three disclosure levels (METADATA, INSTRUCTIONS, RESOURCES) but loaded skills are rendered into the system prompt at construction. No lazy body fetch via tool — full instructions sit in prompt. Resources are only listed in prompt, not auto-fetched.
Lazy. Tool description enumerates names + 1-line descriptions only (renderToolDescription). Full markdown body loads only when the LLM invokes the skill tool. Scales to hundreds of skills.
System prompt lists name + description; use_skill tool returns full SKILL.md body when invoked. No resource-level disclosure (no separate references/scripts tools).
Not provided. BYO via pre_model_hook to lazily inject SystemMessage from BaseStore.
N/A — no skills concept.

Cleanest tradeoff in benchmark. Only metadata in system prompt; body fetched via skill tool, resources via skill_read with line ranges and binary detection, plus skill_search for content discovery. Stateless: skill body returned as tool result.

Lazy. Skill names + descriptions in system prompt (~100 tokens per skill). Bodies via load_skill, resources via read_skill_resource, scripts via run_skill_script. Per agentskills.io progressive disclosure design.

Both eager and lazy supported. Lazy mode shows index in prompt; load_skill tool fetches body into sandbox. Resources/scripts staged into sandbox filesystem and accessed via shell tool — not separate disclosure tools.

Both lazy (lazyFrom: localDirLazySkillSource) and eager (skills: [...]) supported. Lazy mode shows only index; load_skill materializes on demand. Eager mode materializes everything to .agents/<skill>/.
In-tree AgentSpec is eager (config loaded at construction). Third-party SkillsCapability reportedly does progressive disclosure but not in this repo. Dynamic capabilities factory runs once per run.
Not provided. Could approximate with dynamic_context(sample, vector_store_index) which RAG-selects snippets, but not skill-aware.

Lazy by design. Only descriptions + names in system prompt; bodies loaded via skills tool. Activated skills tracked in agent.state["agent_skills"]["activated_skills"] across turns. Resource files listed (max 20) in activation response.

Lazy. Only metadata in system prompt; body via skills tool. Activation tracked in agent.appState[stateKey].activatedSkills. Resource files included in activation response capped at maxResourceFiles (default 20).
No SDK-side skill loading at all. Whatever progressive disclosure exists is Anthropic-side after upload.

Source interface accepts ctx on every List/Get so per-request tenant filtering is plausible. NewMergedSource composes global + tenant sources. But no first-party TenantAwareSource — you build your own ctx-reading Source wrapper.

Skills object built once at Agent construction. To vary per tenant: callable factory for agent.tools returning different Skills.get_tools() per request, or one Agent per tenant. No built-in Skills(filter=lambda run_context: ...) hook.
N/A — no skills concept.

No programmatic per-tenant scoping API. Either materialize per-tenant .claude/skills/ tree and set cwd, or use options.skills as a filter over global registry (acknowledged in code as a context filter not a sandbox). Non-trivial filesystem hygiene work.
No tenantId → skills mapping API. Either per-tenant .claude/skills/ trees with cwd swap, or shared registry with Options.skills whitelist per call. Same gap as Python SDK.
Skills loaded at Agent construction; no per-request filter or runtime context hook. Different tenants need different Agent instances.
Backend interface gets ctx on List/Get so you can filter by tenant from context. No first-class skill-scope field in FrontMatter; you add it via backend metadata. Possible but you build it.
SkillPaths is on the middleware config; varies per Generate call site but no built-in tenant resolver.
Not provided. BaseStore namespace tuples make scoping straightforward (e.g. ('skills', tenant_id, ...)) but you build the whole skill loader on top.
N/A — BYO via your own loader feeding tool_retriever or tools=[...].

SkillsResolver can be a function reading requestContext: (ctx) => tier === 'premium' ? [...] : [...]. First-class runtime scoping primitive that returns different path sets per request — unique in this benchmark.

Not first-class but composable: FilteringSkillsSource(AggregatingSkillsSource([base, tenant]), predicate=lambda s: tenant_id in s.frontmatter.metadata.get('tenants', '').split()). Build one SkillsProvider per tenant.
Skills configured on ShellTool/SandboxAgent at construction. Per-tenant agent instances or agent.clone(tools=[...]). No dynamic per-turn filtering like tools' is_enabled callable.
Attach different defaultManifest per SandboxAgent or override via options.sandbox.manifestPatch. No built-in tenant-aware skill catalog — caller composes based on runContext.context.tenantId.

Yes — via dynamic capabilities. def user_skill(ctx: RunContext[str]) -> Capability | None: return load_from_db(ctx.deps.user_id, ctx.deps.tenant_id). Factory runs once per run and returns the resolved capability.
Not provided.
AgentSkills loads fixed set at construction. Either per-tenant plugin instance or mutate plugin.set_available_skills([...]) between invocations (affects all sharing agents).
Plugin attached to one agent; all invocations on that agent see same catalog. Per-tenant requires per-tenant AgentSkills instance. No built-in invocationState.tenantId filter primitive.
No SDK-side concept. Scoping would be at the providerReference level by storing per-tenant skill IDs in your own DB.

SKILL.md body can mention other tools/skills by name (composition by reference) or instruct the agent to call load_skill_resource for files in references/assets/scripts/. No @include other-skill directive; no first-class sub-skill mechanism.

Limited. SKILL.md body can describe a workflow including "call this script" or "read this reference". No programmatic include of other skills; no imports: [other-skill] frontmatter. Scripts/references are first-class via dedicated tools.
N/A.

Cross-skill references implicit via skill bodies mentioning each other; plugins bundle multiple skills (SdkPluginConfig); AgentDefinition.skills scopes per sub-agent. Programmatic composition primitives BYO at SDK level.
Reference other skills via plugin-qualified names (<plugin>:skill-name). Can call sub-agents via Agent tool. Pull bundled assets via Read/Bash on relative paths inside skill directory.

Directory layout supports scripts/, references/, assets/ subfolders. Cataloged in system prompt at RESOURCES disclosure level but not auto-fetched (need Read tool). No cross-skill references in frontmatter.

A skill in fork mode spawns a sub-agent that can itself have tools, sub-agents, skills — full recursion. Skill body can reference files in BaseDirectory (passed via userContent template). Skills can call other skills if the spawned sub-agent has the skill middleware.
Each skill is a directory with SKILL.md. No documented references/scripts/assets subfolders. Composition is the LLM reading the body text and calling other tools.
Not provided — BYO.
N/A.

Skills can include references/, scripts/, assets/ subfolders. skill_read reads any file with line range + binary detection. skill_search indexes content for retrieval. CompositeVersionedSkillSource mixes versioned and live skills.

Skills ship references/ (markdown/json/yaml/csv/xml/txt), assets/, scripts/ (.py default). Scripts execute through pluggable SkillScriptRunner with optional HITL approval. A skill can reference another only by mentioning it in instructions — no extends: mechanism.

Skill model has scripts/references/assets dict fields per BaseEntry. Progressive-disclosure prompt instructs LLM to "open scripts/ instead of retyping large code blocks" and "reuse assets/ instead of recreating". Skills don't cross-reference directly; LLM-driven.

SkillDescriptor includes scripts, references, assets Records. Injected instructions tell model to load files from references/, run scripts/, reuse assets/. Skills cannot directly call other skills but lazy loader lets a skill request loading another at runtime.

Capabilities compose via CombinedCapability with ordering and overlap (capabilities/abstract.py:135). A capability can ship its own toolset, hooks, instructions, native tools, model settings. Skills-as-capabilities can stack.
Not provided.

Skills can reference bundled resources (scripts/, references/, assets/) listed in activation response (max 20). No direct cross-skill references; activated instructions can instruct the LLM to invoke other skills via the skills tool — text-driven chaining.

Bundle scripts/, references/, assets/ alongside SKILL.md. Resource files listed (capped at 20) in activation response. LLM reads them via separate file-reading tools. Skills cannot directly reference other skills or call sub-agents.
Composition is opaque to the SDK — Anthropic-side after upload. No SDK primitives.

Three first-class mechanisms: agents-as-tools (agenttool.New), workflow agents (parallel/sequential/loop), and LLM-driven transfer_to_agent handoff. SubAgents declared on agent.Config. Covers every common orchestration pattern.

Team is a first-class agent-like object with members and a leader that gets auto-generated delegation tools (delegate_task_to_member, broadcast/route/coordinate modes). Members can be Agents or nested Teams. Single mechanism but well-integrated.

No SubAgent or handoff primitive. Multi-agent is implicit: subscribe agents to a Topic on a SingleThreadedRuntime and publish Tasks; collect via Event::TaskComplete on the event stream. No agent-as-tool wrapper ships.

First-class via CLI's built-in Task tool that the parent LLM calls to delegate. AgentDefinition or .claude/agents/<name>.md frontmatter. Background tasks and stop_task supported. CLI handles parallel dispatch.

First-class via CLI's built-in Agent tool (renamed from Task). Inline Options.agents map or markdown files in .claude/agents/. Background execution, task notifications and forwardSubagentText for nested transcript rendering.

Two awkward mechanisms: Crew hierarchical process exposes DelegateWorkTool to a manager LLM, and Flow uses @start/@listen/@router decorators with manual asyncio.gather. A2A protocol for cross-org. No first-class agents-as-tools.

Three first-class mechanisms: SetSubAgents handoff via transfer_to_agent tool, NewAgentTool agents-as-tools, and workflow agents (Sequential/Parallel/Loop). Prebuilts include supervisor, deep, planexecute patterns.
No SubAgent or handoff primitive. The idiomatic pattern is define a tool whose execute calls genkit.Generate with a different prompt. No registry, no markdown configs, no first-class concept.

No SubAgent or handoff primitive. Two patterns: subgraph-as-node via add_node(name, compiled_subgraph) or subgraph-as-tool. Build-time static registration. langgraph-supervisor third-party packages this.
Two complementary mechanisms: first-class AgentWorkflow with can_handoff_to and auto-generated handoff tool, plus agents-as-tools by wrapping .run() in a FunctionTool. Python-only registration.

Sub-agents are first-class on Agent.agents (static or DynamicArgument). Listed at runtime as synthesized agent-<name> tools via listAgentTools(). Also lightweight SubAgent interface and explicit network() supervisor pattern.

Two complementary mechanisms: Python agent.as_tool() wraps any agent as a FunctionTool; .NET SubAgentsProvider exposes six tools (StartTask, WaitForFirstCompletion, GetTaskResults, etc.) for concurrent fan-out. Also WorkflowBuilder.
Two first-class mechanisms: Handoffs transfer control with optional HandoffInputFilter, and Agent.as_tool() wraps agents as FunctionTool. Both first-class — no special-tool hack.

Two first-class mechanisms: Agent.handoffs declares transfer_to_<agent> handoffs, and Agent.asTool() wraps an agent as a FunctionTool. Cleanly designed; nested RunResult exposed via FunctionToolResult.agentRunResult.
No first-class sub-agent primitive. Pattern is to write a @tool whose body calls await child_agent.run(...). Docs call this 'agent delegation' but no Task, Swarm, or handoff analog exists in core.

Agents-as-tools only. Agent<M> implements Tool so parent_agent.tool(child_agent) registers it. The LLM sees only sub-agent name, description, system prompt. No handoff, no workflow, no first-class multi-agent abstraction.

Two first-class patterns plus orchestrators: agent.as_tool() with streaming, Graph deterministic DAG, Swarm collaborative team with handoffs, and A2AServer to expose agents as HTTP endpoints. Wide coverage.
Three first-class patterns: agent.asTool() (auto-wrapped when passing Agent in tools=[]), Graph deterministic DAG with maxConcurrency, and Swarm with model-driven HandoffResult routing.
No subAgent, handoff, delegate, Crew, or Swarm primitive. Idiomatic pattern is wrapping ToolLoopAgent.generate(...) inside a tool({ ... execute }) yourself. No registry, no streaming integration.

Parallel by default: parallelagent uses errgroup with one goroutine per sub-agent, and agents-as-tools run concurrently because Flow.handleFunctionCalls runs each tool in its own goroutine. Sequential and loop workflow agents also available.
Sequential by default in sync delegate_task_to_members. Parallel only in async path adelegate_task_to_members which uses asyncio.gather. Requires async-capable model. Default sync path is sequential.

Parallel via independent actor handle()s — runtime publishes to subscribers sequentially but each subscriber processes in its own tokio task. Parent collects results by matching actor_name on event stream. Concurrency works but is implicit, not orchestrated.

Parallel is first-class. CLI's Task tool supports parallel sub-agent fan-out natively; tool-lifecycle hooks interleave on the control channel with agent_id attribution. background=true and stop_task(task_id) for fire-and-forget.

Parallel via multiple Agent tool_use blocks in one assistant turn. CLI dispatches concurrently, PostToolBatch fires once after all resolve. AgentDefinition.background and run_in_background for fire-and-forget; polling via TaskOutputInput.block.

Sequential by default. Crew hierarchical picks one delegate at a time. Task.async_execution=True runs marked tasks in parallel via Futures. Native executor only executes first tool per turn. Persona fan-out requires hand-rolled Flow + asyncio.gather.

Parallel via runParallel using sync.WaitGroup + goroutines. Agents-as-tools also get free parallelism because ToolsNode runs tool calls in parallel goroutines. Sequential, parallel, and loop workflow primitives all ship.

Parallel by default within one Generate call — tool dispatch fans out goroutines (one per tool_request). No parent-level rate limit or pool. Concurrency comes from LLM emitting parallel tool calls, not from an explicit fan-out primitive.
Parallel fan-out is first-class via the Send API (return [Send(node, payload) for ... in state]). create_react_agent v2 uses this for parallel tool calls. Serial by default for add_edge-only graphs.

AgentWorkflow itself is serial (one agent active at a time, hand-off swarm). Parallelism happens with agents-as-tools: parent LLM emits multiple tool calls, parse_agent_output fans them out via ctx.send_event, workflows runtime executes in parallel. allow_parallel_tool_calls default True.

Parallel by default: sub-agent invocations are tool calls and go through the same .foreach(toolCallStep, { concurrency }) machinery as tools. Default toolCallConcurrency=10. Drops to 1 only if any tool has requireApproval/suspendSchema.

SubAgentsProvider StartTask is non-blocking with WaitForFirstCompletion. Sub-tasks run via Task.Run in parallel. Python as_tool relies on LLM emitting parallel tool calls — _execute_function_calls iterates sequentially in code but providers do parallel tool calls.

Serial by default but parallel when LLM emits multiple parallel tool calls in one turn — runner dispatches them concurrently via execute_function_tool_calls, bounded by max_function_tool_concurrency. Programmatic fan-out via asyncio.gather is BYO. No swarm() helper.

Concurrent — Agent.asTool invocations in one turn dispatch in parallel up to toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency. Implemented via Promise.all in runner/toolExecution.ts. Handoffs are sequential by definition.
Whatever you write. No built-in Promise.all wrapper or fan-out helper. Parallelism = asyncio.gather(child_a.run(...), child_b.run(...)) inside the parent tool. Fully BYO orchestration.

Parent loop uses buffer_unordered(self.concurrency) for tool calls. If the LLM emits multiple tool calls in a single turn they run in parallel up to configured concurrency. Default concurrency=1 (sequential); must opt in via .with_tool_concurrency(n).

Parallel by default: ConcurrentToolExecutor creates an asyncio.Task per tool and awaits them concurrently. Graph runs DAG layers concurrently via asyncio.gather across nodes with satisfied dependencies. Swarm is sequential by handoff.
Parallel by default: parent uses toolExecutor: 'concurrent' (Promise.race scheduler). Graph schedules ready nodes up to maxConcurrency: Infinity with AND-semantics on edges. Swarm is sequential.

Serial if you await, parallel if you Promise.all. Multiple tool calls within one step do run in parallel (generate-text.ts:1284). But there's no sub-agent primitive so all fan-out lives in your tool's execute body.

Not supported. Sub-agent configs (system prompt, tools, model) cannot be generated by the LLM on the fly. You can build a factory but the resulting agent must be agent.New(...)-constructed in Go code.
Not supported. Members must be pre-registered or resolved by a host-controlled callable factory. The parent LLM cannot author a new sub-agent with a custom system prompt at runtime.
Configs are static, compile-time Rust types. Each agent is a #[agent(name=..., tools=...)] macro on a struct. The parent LLM cannot generate a sub-agent config on the fly.

Partial. AgentDefinition is a dataclass the host can construct per-tenant per-request and pass via ClaudeAgentOptions.agents. The parent LLM cannot itself generate a new AgentDefinition mid-run, but the Python harness can decide per-request which agents to register.

Configs must be statically registered at session start via Options.agents or on disk. The parent LLM cannot generate a new sub-agent config on the fly — it can only choose subagent_type from registered agents.

Parent LLM cannot synthesize a sub-agent on the fly. Sub-agents must be statically registered in code, YAML, or fetched from AMP (Agent(from_repository=name) calls PlusAPI.get_agent). DelegateWorkTool lets LLM pick among pre-registered coworkers.

Not supported. Static typing of Agent configuration is enforced by Go. Closest workaround is the taskTool pattern where LLM picks a subagent_type from a fixed registry and supplies a free-text description.
Parent LLM cannot generate a sub-agent config, but it can call a tool that accepts a free-form prompt and forwards it to a Generate call you wrote. No registry, no structured per-call config.

Not supported. parent.add_node(name, research_agent) is build-time. The parent LLM cannot dynamically construct a new sub-agent with this system prompt and these tools mid-run. Closest workaround: dynamic-model selection inside an existing sub-agent.
Not first-class. You can build a FunctionAgent dynamically inside a tool, but there's no markdown-loader analogue to Claude's Task tool. No structured per-call AgentDefinition.

Configs are statically registered, OR returned by a DynamicArgument resolver at the start of the run (per-tenant maps). The LLM picks an existing agent-<name> tool; it cannot define a new agent at call time. It CAN pass extra instructions/maxSteps/threadId at the tool call.

The parent LLM cannot create a brand-new sub-agent with a custom system prompt at runtime. Sub-agents must be registered ahead of time. Workaround: implement a custom tool that constructs an Agent from a dict and invokes it.

Sub-agent configs are static Python objects. The parent LLM cannot synthesize a system_prompt for a fresh sub-agent at runtime. You could give the parent a tool that constructs an Agent from arguments and runs it, but that's BYO.

Not provided. Sub-agents are statically declared TypeScript. Cannot have the parent LLM generate a fresh system prompt + tools and spawn a child at runtime. Closest: parameterize via Agent.asTool({ parameters, inputBuilder }) so parent passes structured input.

Not directly first-class. A capability factory can synthesize an agent at run time from ctx. Parent's tools can call Agent.from_spec(dict) if you wire it that way — there's an in-tree AgentSpec format that supports dict construction.
Not supported. Sub-agents are statically registered Rust structs. The parent LLM cannot dynamically generate a sub-agent's preamble or toolset.

Not natively. The parent LLM can call a tool that itself constructs a new Agent (strands-agents-tools provides use_agent.py for this), but there is no 'generate a sub-agent description on the fly' primitive baked into the loop.

Not supported. Sub-agent configs are statically constructed in code. A Swarm route is dynamic at runtime (the LLM picks which agentId to hand off to), but the set of agents is fixed at swarm construction.

No native support. You can write a meta-tool whose execute body instantiates a ToolLoopAgent from arguments the LLM provides, but the SDK has no opinion on this and no telemetry / streaming integration.

Each sub-agent invocation gets a new InvocationContext with its own Branch. ContentsRequestProcessor filters events for the LLM by branch — logical isolation, shared storage. Agent-tool is stronger: creates a brand new InMemoryService so sub-agent events are NOT mixed with parent's session.

Each member call passes a copy of run_context.session_state so member mutations don't bleed back unless leader explicitly merges. Member knowledge filters fall back to leader's. All members share the same session_id.

Strong by default. Each agent has its own BaseAgent with its own memory, tools, and Context. Parent's memory is not shared. You pass data via the Task::prompt you publish, but parent's chat history is not.

Each sub-agent has its own transcript at <projects_dir>/<project_key>/<session_id>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl. The parent does not see sub-agent's internal turns; only the final summary. Sub-agent starts fresh with its prompt + initialPrompt; parent context not inherited.

Sub-agent starts fresh. Does NOT see parent's context — only its own system prompt, initialPrompt, and tool catalog. Transcripts persist separately under <sessionId>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl or SessionKey.subpath.

Each Agent has its own executor.messages list — agents inside the same Crew do not share message history unless wired through context in Task.execute_sync(agent, context, tools). DelegateWorkTool coworker receives only task + context strings — clean isolation.

Workflow Parallel forks runContext via forkRunCtx — per-lane runSession shares Values+valuesMtx with parent but has its own LaneEvents. Agent-tool keeps session Values shared via withSharedParentSession but inner agent has its own runContext. Transfer destination agent inherits same runContext. ClearRunCtx for explicit isolation.

Each sub-agent starts fresh. Sub-agent's Generate(...) call has its own Messages (whatever the parent's tool function passes); parent's message history is NOT automatically inherited. The context.Context is inherited (ActionContext flows through).

Not enforced — depends on state schema design. Same state_schema → subgraph sees parent's full messages (shared scratchpad). Own state_schema → parent state invisible except via explicit channel mapping. Command(graph=Command.PARENT) can write back.
Each sub-agent invocation via .run(...) gets its own Context by default — fresh memory, fresh state. Or you can pass ctx=parent_ctx to share state. Explicit opt-in to share.

Sub-agent gets a sanitized copy of parent's message history. stripParentToolParts removes parent's tool-call and tool messages because sub-agent doesn't have those tools. Parent's MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY / MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY cleared so sub-agent writes to its own isolated thread.

as_tool(propagate_session=False) gives sub-agent a fresh session — context isolated. as_tool(propagate_session=True) forwards parent's session. SubAgentsProvider each sub-task runs in its own session by default. Clean explicit knob.

Sub-agent gets a fresh ToolContext derived from parent's RunContextWrapper. Sub-agent does NOT see parent's conversation history; only the input string the parent generated (or structured parameters Pydantic model). Approvals propagate. Handoffs are the opposite (full history flows, filter via HandoffInputFilter).

Nested Agent.asTool runs share parent's RunContext.context, approvals, and usage (_cloneSharedState). The toolInput on the fork is the structured input that triggered the nested run. So no isolation by default — useful for shared todo list, dangerous if strict separation wanted.
By default each agent.run(...) gets a fresh RunContext and an empty message_history — full isolation. To share, pass message_history=ctx.messages or shared deps/usage.

Sub-agent starts with its own Vec<Message> (just args.prompt) — parent's history is not passed through. Enforced at agent/tool.rs:43-45 via self.prompt(args.prompt) building a fresh PromptRequest from &Agent<M>.

Strong by default. as_tool(preserve_context=False) snapshots child's initial messages + state and _reset_agent_state() resets them before every invocation. preserve_context=True keeps conversation across calls. GraphNode/SwarmNode follow same pattern.

AgentAsTool.preserveContext: false (default) reloads sub-agent's initial snapshot before each call — fresh conversation. preserveContext=true retains messages across calls. Sub-agent does not see parent's agent.messages either way; only the tool's input string crosses the boundary.
Each child ToolLoopAgent.generate({ messages }) starts with whatever messages you give it. No automatic parent-context inheritance, no automatic redaction. Fully caller-controlled.

Depends on mechanism. Agents-as-tools: sub-agent's last text-bearing event text concatenated and returned as map with 'result' key; optionally parsed against OutputSchema. Workflow agents: events stream directly into parent's event stream. Transfer: new agent's events stream directly.

Each member run produces a RunOutput (or TeamRunOutput) re-injected as a tool result into the leader's loop. Member runs linked to parent via parent_run_id. Four output modes: coordinate (synthesize), route (return directly), broadcast (concatenate), tasks (decompose+loop).

Output reaches the parent only via Event::TaskComplete{sub_id, actor_name, result} broadcast through the runtime's event stream. The parent must track submission_ids, filter incoming events by sub_id and actor_name, and assemble results manually.

Parent LLM calls Task tool; sub-agent runs to completion; result returns as ToolResultBlock (text summary) on next user message. Parent sees a single result string per call — not a stream. Harness gets per-task progress/usage telemetry even though parent LLM gets just summary.

Parent sees sub-agent result as a regular tool_result block on user-role message, linked by tool_use_id. By default only tool_use/tool_result blocks emit; forwardSubagentText=true forwards assistant text and thinking as nested SDKAssistantMessages with parent_tool_use_id. AgentOutput shape includes toolStats, usage, duration.

Crew delegation: delegating LLM gets a single string back (coworker's task output) wrapped in standard tool-result message. Flow: each @listen method returns a Python value to downstream methods. No parent_tool_use_id linkage by default — only A2A* events carry parent IDs.

Single result string (last assistant message content) returned via agentTool.InvokableRun. Optionally all sub-agent events streamed up via ToolsConfig.EmitInternalEvents=true (useful for UI, not recorded in parent's session). Linked back to parent's tool_use.id via tool_call_id.

Parent receives a single ToolResponse.Output (text or structured output of sub-agent). Parent does NOT see sub-agent's intermediate tool calls or token stream by default — those are recorded as child spans in tracing but not surfaced in the parent's message stream.

Pattern A subgraph-as-node: sub-agent's final state is the node's writes; reducer on parent's channels merges. Shared messages channel with add_messages appends sub-agent's messages. Pattern B subgraph-as-tool: output is ToolMessage.content string. Command(graph=Command.PARENT) for handoff-style writes.

AgentWorkflow handoff: handoff tool returns a string, workflow switches current_agent_name and re-enters setup_agent. Final StopEvent.result is an AgentOutput. Agents-as-tools: sub-agent's .run(...) awaited; result string returned to parent LLM as normal tool result.

Synthesized agent-<name> tool returns { text, subAgentThreadId, subAgentResourceId, subAgentToolResults }. toModelOutput strips to text by default unless delegation.includeSubAgentToolResultsInModelContext=true. Mastra also streams sub-agent chunks to parent stream as nested agent-execution-event-* chunks.

as_tool: parent receives a string (final response text) as function_result content; intermediate updates observable via stream_callback. SubAgentsProvider: results pulled via SubAgents_GetTaskResults; state lives in SubAgentState (running/completed/failed).

Agents-as-tools: nested agent's final_output returned as tool result string. custom_output_extractor callback can rewrite. on_stream callback re-emits nested stream events to parent as AgentToolStreamEvent. Linked via call_id. Handoffs: new agent receives full conversation history (optionally filtered).

Handoff: new agent's final output, linked via RunAgentUpdatedStreamEvent. asTool: nested agent's final output becomes function tool result (string by default, customizable via customOutputExtractor). Full nested RunResult exposed on FunctionToolResult.agentRunResult. Linked via tool_use_id.
Child returns an AgentRunResult[OutputDataT]; parent tool returns its .output (or string summary). Linkage to a parent tool_use_id is implicit through the parent's ToolCallPart/ToolReturnPart pair.
Parent receives sub-agent's final String (Tool::Output) as a regular tool result, bound to parent's tool_call_id. No streaming events bubble up — parent only sees sub-agent's terminal text.

_AgentAsTool.stream yields AgentAsToolStreamEvent for every intermediate event from child's stream_async, then ToolInterruptEvent (HITL pause) or ToolResultEvent with text/json content. Linked via tool_use_id. Graph/Swarm aggregate results into MultiAgentResult with dedicated events.

agent.asTool() returns a ToolResultBlock containing either sub-agent's structured output (JsonBlock) or TextBlock of result.toString(). Linked via tool_use_id. Graph/Swarm aggregate node results into MultiAgentResult streamed via MultiAgentStreamEvent events (NodeResultEvent, MultiAgentHandoffEvent).

Whatever the tool returns. To stream sub-agent results to parent UI, use createUIMessageStream and writer.merge(subAgent.stream(...).toUIMessageStream(...)). No automatic tool_use_id correlation between parent and child agents — you build that yourself.

Sub-agent lifecycle events bubble up. Each sub-agent's BeforeAgentCallback/AfterAgentCallback fires; events forwarded to parent's iterator. No dedicated 'sub-agent started/completed' lifecycle event type — infer from Author and Branch changes on consecutive events.
TeamRunEvent emits MemberDelegationStarted, MemberDelegationCompleted, and propagates member RunStarted/ToolCallStarted/RunCompleted upward with parent_run_id set on each frame.

Parent gets TaskStarted, TurnStarted/Completed, ToolCallRequested/Completed, TaskComplete from the child agent's event stream because all actors share runtime's single broadcast channel. To filter, match on actor_id/actor_name and sub_id.

TaskStartedMessage / TaskProgressMessage / TaskNotificationMessage (0.1.46+) carry per-task task_id, description, usage, status. Combined with SubagentStart / SubagentStop hooks, parent observes sub-agent lifecycle in flight.

SubagentStart hook, SubagentStop hook, TaskCreated/TaskCompleted hooks. SDKTaskStartedMessage, SDKTaskProgressMessage (with summary if agentProgressSummaries:true), SDKTaskUpdatedMessage, SDKTaskNotificationMessage emitted on parent's stream so UI can render status.

AgentExecutionStartedEvent / Completed / Error fire per agent execution (events/types/agent_events.py). For A2A delegation, ~30 events including A2ADelegationStartedEvent, A2AStreamingChunkEvent. In-process delegation has lighter coverage than A2A.

callbacks.Handler.OnStart / OnEnd fire once per agent boundary (parent + each sub-agent). RunInfo.Component=ComponentOfAgent and Type=ChatModel/Sequential/Parallel/Loop/Supervisor distinguishes types. Sub-agent per-message/per-tool events NOT in parent iterator by default — opt in via ToolsConfig.EmitInternalEvents=true.

Sub-agent lifecycle observable via OTel tracing, NOT via parent's stream. Spans nest: parent generate-span → tool-span → sub-agent generate-span → sub-agent's tools. Parent's SSE stream just shows one toolResponse chunk for the sub-agent's final answer.

Yes via stream_mode='tasks'. Each subgraph dispatch emits a TasksStreamPart start frame and TasksResultStreamPart finish frame. With subgraphs=True on graph.stream(...), parent stream sees (ns, mode, data) triples where ns identifies the subgraph.
When AgentWorkflow hands off, AgentInput / AgentOutput / AgentStream events tagged with new current_agent_name are emitted on the stream. The parent stream sees each sub-agent's tokens.

delegation.onDelegationStart(ctx) runs before sub-agent fires; returns proceed/modifiedPrompt/modifiedInstructions/modifiedMaxSteps. delegation.onDelegationComplete(ctx) runs after with bail() to cancel sibling concurrent delegations. delegation.messageFilter lets supervisor pick which parent messages to forward. Sub-agent chunks stream to parent stream.
as_tool: yes if stream_callback is provided. Otherwise parent only sees the final string. SubAgentsProvider: status retrievable via SubAgents_GetAllTasks; not a streaming lifecycle (pull-based).

Yes via on_stream on as_tool(...). Callback receives AgentToolStreamEvent {event: StreamEvent, agent: Agent, tool_call}. Lets parent stream forward sub-agent progress events to its consumer. Not auto-merged into parent stream by default.
Yes. Agent.asTool({ onStream }) receives every RunStreamEvent from the nested run, plus a reference to the toolCall that triggered it. Caller decides how to surface.

Parent stream does not auto-include child events. To bubble them, parent's child-calling tool can iterate the child via child.run_stream_events() and yield events back (custom code; framework does not auto-merge streams).
Not provided. No sub_agent_started/completed event. Parent loop sees only the eventual tool result. Can attach tracing spans inside sub-agent's own prompt() call to follow it via OTel.

AgentAsToolStreamEvent forwards each child event to parent stream. For Graph/Swarm, dedicated multi-agent events: MultiAgentNodeStartEvent, MultiAgentNodeStopEvent, MultiAgentHandoffEvent, MultiAgentNodeStreamEvent, MultiAgentNodeCancelEvent, MultiAgentNodeInterruptEvent.

Parent stream sees ToolStreamUpdateEvents whose event.data carries sub-agent's AgentStreamEvents (passed through with re-wrapping). For Graph/Swarm: BeforeNodeCallEvent, AfterNodeCallEvent, NodeResultEvent, MultiAgentHandoffEvent.

None. Parent stream has no 'sub-agent started/progress/finished' event category. Child's events live in its streamText call and are not surfaced to parent's stream unless you explicitly writer.merge(...).

ADK Go ships a `Source` interface (`tool/skilltoolset/skill/source.go:41`) as a thin loader plus `MergedSource` for composition, but explicitly documents itself as a loader rather than a manager. There is no registry layer, no publishing workflow, no multi-tenant scoping at publish time, no versioning beyond what your Source decides, no governance/RBAC, and no environment promotion. The matrix flag of YAML-config + skill source covers versioning only if you check skills into git.

Agno ships a `Registry` dataclass (`libs/agno/agno/registry/registry.py:22`) as an in-process catalog of non-serializable Python objects (tools, models, agents, teams, dbs) with `get_*` lookup helpers but no runtime register API. A separate Components subsystem (`libs/agno/agno/os/routers/components/`) versions component configs in the DB with drafts/current/history. There is no unified skill/agent/tool registry — the Registry is read-only at construction, and Components only covers per-AgentOS configs, not per-tenant skills.

AutoAgents has no Registry, no SkillSource, no plugin marketplace, no versioning, no publish workflow. The only loader is the MCP TOML config (`crates/autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/config.rs:45`) which reads local MCP server definitions; this is not a general resource manager. Every other resource source (Git, OCI, S3, Postgres, vendor cloud, HTTP) is BYO.

The Claude Agent SDK Python has no registry, no source abstraction, no publishing workflow, and no versioning; its resource manager is the filesystem plus the `setting_sources` flag. Local plugins (`SdkPluginConfig{'type': 'local', 'path': ...}`) provide a minimal source primitive, and per-request `options.skills`, `options.agents`, `options.plugins`, `options.mcp_servers` allow registration scoped to one call. There is no `register_skill`/`promote_skill`/`pin_version` API.

The TypeScript SDK has no first-class Resource Manager but exposes a richer plugin/loading surface than its Python sibling: `plugins: SdkPluginConfig[]` (local only) discovers skills/agents/commands, and `Query.reloadPlugins()`, `Query.setMcpServers()`, `Query.supportedCommands()`, `Query.supportedAgents()`, `Query.getContextUsage()` provide programmatic introspection mid-session. The CLI side has settings cascade and a `marketplace` setting that can `autoUpdate` (sdk.d.ts:4556) but only as Settings config, not a programmatic API. Skills/sub-agents/slash commands remain filesystem-only.

note: 1 — Local skill loader + AMP-only agent repo
details: OSS CrewAI ships the skill loader (filesystem-only), `Agent(from_repository='<name>')` for fetching agent configs from the paid AMP (Agent Marketplace Platform), plus pluggable `BaseProvider` for checkpoints and `StorageBackend` for memory. There is no unified resource registry for skills + sub-agents + prompts + tools. AMP Agent Repositories is the closest, but it is vendor-locked, paid, and only stores agent configs (not skills or tools).

Eino ships three pluggable interfaces — `skill.Backend`, `skill.AgentHub`, `skill.ModelHub` (`adk/middlewares/skill/skill.go:66,79,86`) — but only the filesystem `Backend` implementation is provided. There is no registry, scoping, versioning, publishing workflow, or governance shipped at the platform level. Eino provides the seams; the manager is entirely yours to build on top.

Genkit Go's only `registry` is the in-process `*registry.Registry` (`go/internal/registry`) that holds tools, models, prompts, retrievers, evaluators for one running process; it is a runtime concept, not a publishing/scoping platform. A separate per-call `Resource` abstraction (`go/ai/resource.go`) is a URI-templated content-loading utility, not a marketplace. The Genkit philosophy is that prompts/skills are source code, not fetched artifacts.

LangGraph OSS ships no registry, no source abstraction, no publishing workflow under `libs/`. The closest is `BaseStore` (Postgres/Memory-backed) which can be misused as a row-as-resource store with namespace tuples like `('skills', tenant_id)`. LangGraph Platform's closed-source Assistants API ships versioned assistant configs (the only real registry), but it sits behind paid hosting and is not in OSS.

LlamaIndex has no Resource Manager — registry, sources, scoping, versioning, publishing, and governance are all BYO. Tools are loaded from Python imports or from a `tool_retriever` you wire in. The LlamaHub site is a community directory of LlamaPacks but offers no draft/review/promote workflow or programmatic registry API.

Mastra ships the strongest first-class resource manager in this benchmark: `VersionedSkillSource` + `CompositeVersionedSkillSource` (`packages/core/src/workspace/skills/composite-versioned-skill-source.ts:34`) layered over `BlobStore` for skills, plus stored agents/skills tracked in storage with `visibility: 'private' | 'public'` and `favoriteCount` (added in 1.35.0). Sub-agents have per-call versioning via `MASTRA_VERSIONS_KEY`. The gap is that no single `promote(tenantId, skillId, 'active')` API exists — promotion is via storage-domain calls + workspace skill resolution.

Microsoft Agent Framework ships a `SkillsSource` abstraction with concrete `FileSkillsSource`/`InMemorySkillsSource`/`AggregatingSkillsSource`/`FilteringSkillsSource`/`DeduplicatingSkillsSource`/`CachingSkillsSource` in both Python and .NET (`AgentFileSkillsSource` etc.). The loader primitives are real and composable, but there is no first-party Resource Manager above them: no draft/active/retired lifecycle, no publishing workflow, no RBAC. Custom Git/S3/HTTP/DB sources require subclassing `SkillsSource` / `AgentSkillsSource`.

OpenAI Agents Python has no concept of a registry; skills/sub-agents/prompts are Python objects constructed at boot. The two registry-shaped pieces are `MultiProviderMap` (a model-routing prefix map, not a skills registry) and `set_default_openai_agent_registration` (telemetry attribution). For skills, `LocalDirLazySkillSource(source=LocalDir(src='./skills'))` plus a `LazySkillSource` abstract base provide minimal lazy loading; everything else (multi-source, scoping, governance) is BYO.

OpenAI Agents JS has no registry/versioning/publishing workflow/marketplace/source abstraction outside the per-`SandboxAgent` `manifest.entries`. A `SandboxAgent` has one `defaultManifest`; merging is `cloneManifest` + capability `processManifest` (`packages/agents-core/src/sandbox/capabilities/skills.ts:147`). The `Manifest` class is the closest thing to a programmatic API but has no `registry.list()`, no `registry.search()`, no `registry.publish()`.

Pydantic AI's `AgentSpec.from_file(path)` / `Agent.from_spec({...})` is a single-source loader at the platform level — no built-in registry, source composition, or publish workflow. Capabilities compose at the Agent level (`CombinedCapability`) but resource sources do not. Pydantic AI Gateway is a managed-key product, not a skill registry.

Rig has no registry, no source abstraction, no publishing workflow. The only registry-like primitive is `ToolSet` (`crates/rig-core/src/tool/mod.rs:288`) — a `HashMap<String, ToolType>` in process memory, plus `ToolServerHandle.add_tool`/`append_toolset`/`remove_tool` for at-runtime tool mutation. All resource concerns (versioning, scoping, governance) are absent.

Strands Python has no registry abstraction managing many skills/sub-agents/tools across teams with versioning and publishing. The closest is the `AgentSkills(skills=[...])` plugin which accepts filesystem paths or HTTPS URLs (`vended_plugins/skills/agent_skills.py:303`) plus `Agent(load_tools_from_directory=True)` for tool hot-reload via watchdog. These are thin loaders, not a registry.

Strands TS has no `Registry`/`ResourceManager`, no versioning/publishing/scoping/RBAC layer for skills/tools/sub-agents. `AgentSkills` (`agent-skills.ts:34`) is the closest: a single in-memory `Map<string, Skill>` populated from instance / dir / parent-dir / URL loaders. The report explicitly calls Resource Manager the largest gap in Strands TS.

Vercel AI SDK has no registry/source abstraction/publishing workflow/lifecycle states. The only registry-shaped pieces — `customProvider({ languageModels: {...} })` and `createProviderRegistry({ openai, anthropic, ... })` — deal exclusively with models, not skills/sub-agents/prompts. No skill source loader, no Git/S3/OCI pull, no DB-row-as-resource, no Hub.

ADK Go ships only `NewFileSystemSource(os.DirFS('./skills'))` (`filesystem_source.go:44`); because it takes any `fs.FS`, compiled-in `embed.FS` works out of the box and `gocloud.dev/blob` adapters could in principle bridge to S3/GCS. Plus `MergedSource` for composition and `WithCompletePreloadSource`/`WithFrontmatterPreloadSource` preload wrappers. Git, OCI, cloud object storage (without an fs.FS adapter), Postgres, HTTP, and vendor managed registries are all BYO.

Agno ships `LocalSkills(path)` for skills (filesystem only) and Postgres-backed Knowledge content via `Knowledge(contents_db=...)`. Sessions, memories, traces, and components live in DB. Skills themselves do not live in DB — Git, OCI, cloud object storage, vendor managed registry, and HTTP fetch are all BYO. Custom `SkillLoader` subclasses can wrap any source.

AutoAgents loads only a local TOML config for MCP servers (`crates/autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/config.rs:45`). That is a local-filesystem TOML loader for MCP server definitions, not a general resource manager. Git, OCI, S3, Postgres, vendor cloud, and HTTP are all BYO.

Loads from local filesystem (`cwd` + `.claude/`, `~/.claude/`) and `setting_sources` flag, plus `SdkPluginConfig{'type': 'local', 'path': ...}` for plugin directories. Git, OCI, cloud object storage, Postgres, vendor cloud, and HTTP fetch are all BYO. The Postgres `SessionStore` adapter is for transcripts, not skills.

Loads from local filesystem (`~/.claude/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, agents/, commands/) plus `<plugin>/skills/`, `<plugin>/agents/` from local plugin directories. MCP servers can come from HTTP/SSE/WS (`McpHttpServerConfig`, `McpSSEServerConfig`) — the only non-filesystem dynamic source for tools. CHANGELOG mentions a marketplace setting that can `autoUpdate` but it's a CLI-side concept (not a programmatic SDK API).

OSS = local files only for skills (`skills=[Path('./skills/')]`), agents (`Agent(...)` inline or YAML `agents.yaml`), tools (inline), prompts (`prompt_file: str`). AMP adds managed Agent Repositories via `Agent(from_repository='<slug>')` (HTTPS to app.crewai.com, requires AMP API key) — but this covers agents only, not skills/tools/prompts. There is no abstraction for `this skill comes from S3/Git/vendor cloud`.

Eino ships only `filesystemBackend` (`adk/middlewares/skill/filesystem_backend.go`) via `NewBackendFromFilesystem(ctx, &Config{Backend, BaseDir})`. Git, OCI, cloud object storage, Postgres, vendor managed registries, and HTTP fetch are all BYO custom `Backend` implementations. Same for agents (only your in-process Go agents can be in an `AgentHub` you implement) and models.

Loads prompts from local filesystem (`WithPromptDir`) or embedded FS (`WithPromptFS(embed.FS, 'prompts')`, `go/genkit/genkit.go:155`); skills from `Skills{SkillPaths: []}` (filesystem paths only). Git, OCI, cloud object storage, vendor cloud, and HTTP fetch are all BYO. Embeddings can use Postgres via `alloydb`/`postgresql` plugins but skills cannot.

OSS LangGraph supports only local filesystem (via Python module imports) and Postgres via `BaseStore` as a row-as-resource proxy. Git, OCI, cloud object storage, vendor managed registry (closed-source LangGraph Platform Assistants API is paid), and HTTP fetch with caching are all unsupported in OSS.

LlamaIndex has no concept of loading a skill from S3/GCS/Git or any other source — tools are loaded from Python imports or from a custom `tool_retriever`. LlamaHub is a community directory, not a programmatic source. All sources are BYO.

note: 4 — Local + blob storage + Postgres + Mastra Cloud
details: Mastra ships the broadest source matrix: local filesystem (`skills: ['skills', '/path/to/external']`, `LocalFilesystem({ basePath })`), `VersionedSkillSource` backed by `BlobStore` for any cloud object storage adapter (S3/GCS/R2), `storage.getStore('agents'|'skills')` for Postgres-backed stored entities, and Mastra Cloud via the deployers/cloud package. Git is BYO (clone-into-filesystem) and HTTP fetch is BYO.

Ships `FileSkillsSource`/`AgentFileSkillsSource` for local filesystem, `InMemorySkillsSource`/`AgentInMemorySkillsSource` for programmatic, plus `AggregatingSkillsSource`, `FilteringSkillsSource`, `DeduplicatingSkillsSource`, and `CachingAgentSkillsSource` wrappers. No first-class Git, S3/GCS/Azure Blob, OCI, or vendor-managed registry source — custom subclasses required.

`LocalDirLazySkillSource(source=LocalDir(src='./skills'))` for skills, and Python imports for agents/tools. `agents.sandbox.entries.GitRepo` materializes a Git repo into the *sandbox* at run time, not into the SDK process. OCI, cloud object storage, Postgres, vendor cloud, and HTTP fetch are all BYO.

Per `manifest.entries`: `localDir({ src })` / `localFile({ src })` for local files (with `extraPathGrants`), `dir(...)` / `file(...)` for inline content, and crucially `gitRepo({ repo, ref, subpath? })` as a first-class Git source that clones into the sandbox session. This is the only stack with built-in Git source loading. OCI, S3/GCS/Azure/R2/Vercel Blob, Postgres, vendor cloud, and HTTP fetch are not provided.

Loads `AgentSpec.from_file(path)`, `Agent.from_spec({...})` for in-memory dicts, and MCP servers as toolsets (`MCPServerStdio`/`MCPServerSSE`/`MCPServerStreamableHTTP`). Git, OCI, S3/GCS/Blob, Postgres, vendor managed registry, and HTTP fetch with caching are all BYO.

Rig has `rig::loaders::file` for reading files (`crates/rig-core/src/loaders/file.rs`) but not as a resource registry. `rig-s3vectors` and `rig-postgres` are vector stores, not resource sources. Git, OCI, vendor managed registry, and HTTP-as-resource fetch are all unsupported.

`AgentSkills(skills=['./skills/', 'https://...'])` accepts filesystem paths and HTTPS URLs via `Skill.from_url` (`vended_plugins/skills/skill.py:341`). Also `Agent(load_tools_from_directory=True)` for tool hot-reload from `./tools/` via watchdog. Git, OCI, cloud object storage (only sessions via `S3SessionManager`), Postgres, and vendor managed registry are all BYO.

`AgentSkills` accepts skill instances, dir, parent-dir, or URL sources (`agent-skills.ts:34`); `Skill.fromUrl()` fetches raw `SKILL.md` content with a 30-second timeout (`skill.ts:17`). No first-class Git, OCI, S3/GCS, Postgres, or vendor managed registry source. HTTP fetch has no caching/ETag/resync.

Vercel AI ships no loading sources for skills — `customProvider`/`createProviderRegistry` deal exclusively with models. Local filesystem, Git, OCI, cloud object storage, Postgres, vendor managed registry, and HTTP fetch for resources are all BYO. Anthropic Skills is Anthropic-side, not Vercel-side.

`MergedSource` (`tool/skilltoolset/skill/merged_source.go:32`) composes multiple sources with documented semantics: `ListFrontmatters` collects from all sources and errors on duplicate names (`ErrDuplicateSkill`); `LoadFrontmatter`/`LoadInstructions`/`LoadResource` query in order with first-non-error wins. This rules out same-name override but gives clear, predictable priority — earlier sources win. Tenant-overrides-global requires hand-wired source filtering or wrappers.

`Skills(loaders=[a, b, c])` loads all three; on name collision the later loader wins with a logged warning (`agent_skills.py:42`). There is no declarative `local > tenant > global` cascade or per-tenant override pattern. Multi-source composition with priority/override is not modelled at the Skills layer.
AutoAgents provides no source composition or priority mechanism — there is no source abstraction at all.

Layered by `setting_sources` (`types.py:1800`): `user` → `~/.claude/`, `project` → `<cwd>/.claude/`, `local` → `<cwd>/.claude/settings.local.json`. When unset, all three load by default; pass `[]` to disable all (SDK isolation mode). Plugins add another layer via `options.plugins`. The conflict-resolution order is defined inside the CLI and not exposed for tuning from the SDK.

Settings cascade documented: `--settings` CLI flag > project local > project committed > user-global > managed settings. For resources themselves (skills/agents/commands), layering is plugin-bundled + project + user + managed, with project winning over user. Conflict resolution on name is later-loaded wins; precedence is not configurable from SDK options.

`Agent(skills=[Path('./skills/global'), Path('./skills/acme')])` iterates paths in order and de-duplicates by skill name (`agent/core.py:451`) — first occurrence wins. This is de-facto composition with reverse-order override (caller controls priority by path order). No declarative `tenant overrides global` semantic, no scoping at the source level.
Not provided. You implement your own composing `Backend` (e.g. a `layeredBackend` with tenants + global) and your priority logic inside it. The framework offers nothing built-in.

For skills, `middleware.Skills{SkillPaths: []string}` scans paths in order and later entries with the same skill name overwrite earlier ones (via `map[string]skillInfo` mutation in `scanSkills`). For prompts, no explicit priority — `WithPromptFS` and `WithPromptDir` are mutually exclusive (`go/genkit/genkit.go:80`). Tenant-overrides-global is reverse-order-list convention only.

OSS provides nothing for source composition or priority. `BaseStore.search()` accepts a namespace tuple; engineers can implement tenant > global override by trying `('skills', tenant_id)` first and falling back to `('skills', 'global')`. This is entirely BYO.
LlamaIndex has no source composition or priority mechanism — there is no source abstraction at all.

For skills the priority is documented as `local > managed > external` (`workspace-skills.ts:207`). Multiple sources stack via `CompositeVersionedSkillSource` which mounts versioned skill trees into a virtual filesystem with an optional fallback to a live filesystem source for actively-edited skills. This is the only stack with a documented multi-layer precedence semantic.

`AggregatingSkillsSource` composes multiple sources; `DeduplicatingSkillsSource` preserves first-occurrence when names clash; `FilteringSkillsSource(predicate=...)` applies after aggregation. No declarative priority like `local > tenant > global` — you choose precedence by ordering sources in the aggregator. The wrapper composition pattern is explicit and clean even without a declarative precedence model.

Not applicable — there is no source abstraction to compose. `LocalDirLazySkillSource` is a single source per Sandbox; multi-source priority requires writing your own `LazySkillSource` subclass that consults sources in order and de-duplicates by name.

Per-manifest composition only. A `SandboxAgent` has one `defaultManifest`; merging is `cloneManifest` + capability `processManifest` (`packages/agents-core/src/sandbox/capabilities/skills.ts:147`). No `local > tenant > global` cascading at the framework level.
Source composition is not provided — capabilities compose at the Agent level via `CombinedCapability`, but resource sources do not. Priority/override across sources is entirely BYO.

Not provided in any structured way. `add_tool` on `ToolServerHandle` (`tool/server.rs:117`) uses `HashMap` insertion (`tool/mod.rs:325`), so last write wins. There is no declared composition or priority semantic.
Not provided. `AgentSkills._resolve_skills` (`agent_skills.py:319`) is last-write-wins, logging a warning on duplicate names. Engineers control priority by ordering the sources list.

Within `AgentSkills`, sources are processed in order and a duplicate name overwrites the earlier one with a warning (`agent-skills.ts:191`). There is no priority/fallback/merge configuration — last-wins is the only model.
Vercel AI provides no source composition or priority mechanism for skills — there is no source abstraction at all.

Not provided. `Frontmatter` has no `version` field; `Compatibility` is free-text up to 500 chars (e.g. 'Claude 3.5+ models', 'ADK Go ≥0.5') with no enforcement. If you need versioning you bake a suffix into the directory name (`my-skill-v2/`) or rely on git commit SHA.

Components have versioned configs in the DB: `agno_components` (definition) + `agno_component_configs` (versioned configs), with drafts + current + version history. Schedules have run-history via `agno_schedule_runs`.
Not provided. Cargo handles crate versions, but per-skill/per-tool versioning is absent at the framework level.

No first-party skill or agent versioning. The CLI itself is pinned via `_cli_version.py` (currently `2.1.143`) but skills/agents/plugins are versioned by the file's mtime on disk. No content hash, no rollback API.

Skills/sub-agents in plugins are versioned by the plugin's own git tag (whatever the plugin directory came from); no semver enforcement by the SDK. The CLI itself is pinned via `claude_code_version: '2.1.143'`. No content-hash addressing, no immutable refs, no rollback — to roll back you replace the file on disk and call `Query.reloadPlugins()`.

No `version: '1.2.3'` field in SKILL.md frontmatter, no content-hash, no immutable refs, no rollback. AMP's Agent Repositories support versioning in the dashboard but no API field for 'pin to version' in `from_repository='...'`.
Not provided. Skills are mutable files (or rows in your store); no semver, no content-hash refs, no rollback. Versioning is up to your custom Backend implementation.
Not provided. Skills, prompts, tools are versioned by your source-control / deployment. No `@semver`, no content-hash, no immutable ref system.

Immutable content-hash refs, not semver, are the model.

functiontool.New[TArgs,TResults](cfg, handler) — 5-line minimal tool. JSON schema auto-inferred from Go struct tags via jsonschema-go reflection; cfg.InputSchema/OutputSchema overrides available. agenttool.New wraps a sub-agent as a tool.

@tool decorator inspects signature + type hints + docstring (docstring-parser) and builds a Function Pydantic model. Accepts name/description/strict/instructions/show_result/stop_after_tool_call/requires_confirmation/external_execution/pre_hook/post_hook/cache_results/cache_ttl. Best-in-class authoring surface.

#[tool(name, description, input)] proc-macro derives ToolT impl from a struct + ToolInput-derived args struct. JSON Schema generated from io_schema literal or schemars-derived JsonSchema. Standard Rust ergonomics; smallest tool is ~20 lines incl. struct/impl.

@tool decorator accepts dict {name: type}, TypedDict class, raw JSON Schema, or Annotated[type, 'desc'] per-param. Returns SdkMcpTool; create_sdk_mcp_server wraps them; in-process MCP bridge routes calls back to handler. Concise and flexible.

tool(name, description, zodSchema, handler) is the canonical surface. Zod (v3 or v4) types both schema-for-LLM and runtime validation. Tool name exposed to model as mcp__{server}__{tool}. Extremely terse for a typed surface.

Subclass BaseTool with Pydantic args_schema (auto-derived from _run signature if not provided), or use @tool decorator. Built-ins: max_usage_count enforcement, result_as_answer, cache_function. Class form is verbose vs decorator-style.

utils.InferTool(name, description, fn) — typed-struct input/output, JSON schema generated from jsonschema struct tags. InferOptionableTool for options-aware tools; utils.NewTool for manual schema; tool.InvokableTool interface for full control.

genkit.DefineTool(g, name, description, func(ctx, In) (Out, error)) — input schema inferred from Go type (string or struct) via core.InferSchemaMap. Override via ai.WithInputSchema. WithStrictSchema(true) for strict mode on supporting providers.

@tool decorator auto-generates JSON schema from function signature + docstring; supports Pydantic/dataclass arg classes and async tools. BaseTool subclass for richer control. Inherits LangChain's mature tool surface.

Pass a typed async/sync callable to FunctionAgent(tools=[...]) and the framework wraps it; or FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=..., name=..., description=..., callback=..., partial_params=...) for explicit overrides. JSON schema auto-generated via create_schema_from_function.

createTool({ id, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute }) — Zod (or any standard schema, JSON-Schema, Yup) for both input and output. requestContextSchema validates context. Cleanest typed-tool surface in TypeScript benchmark.

Python @tool decorator or input_model=PydanticClass form. .NET defines AIFunctions via AIFunctionFactory.Create(method); JSON schema inferred from C# parameter metadata. Dual-language symmetric surface.

@function_tool decorator inspects signature and Griffe-parsed docstring to generate JSON schema. Strict-mode by default. RunContextWrapper/ToolContext as first arg for context. needs_approval flag for HITL. Output types ToolOutputText/Image/FileContent.

tool({ name, description, parameters: ZodSchema, execute }) parses Zod/JSON schema, wires JSON parse/validate of LLM args, wraps timeouts and error handling, produces FunctionTool<Context, TParameters, Result>. Terse and typed.

@agent.tool (with RunContext) and @agent.tool_plain (no context). JSON-schema auto-derived from type hints + docstrings via _function_schema.FunctionSchema; schema_generator overridable. Tightest Python ergonomics among 19.

Tool trait requires implementing definition() (returning ToolDefinition with manual JSON schema) and call(args) → Result<Output, Error>. Smallest tool is ~25 lines. tool_macro proc-macro available behind derive feature to reduce boilerplate.

@tool extracts name/description/JSON schema from function signature, docstring, and type hints (Pydantic create_model). For framework context: tool_context: ToolContext parameter + @tool(context=True). Class-based tools via AgentTool.stream for streaming.

tool({ name, description, inputSchema: ZodSchema | JSONSchema, callback }) — Zod gives runtime validation, raw JSON schema gives schema-to-LLM only (unknown to callback). Subclass Tool for full streaming control.

tool({ description, inputSchema: Zod, execute }) — full surface includes contextSchema, onInputStart/Delta/Available, toModelOutput, needsApproval, outputSchema. Zod 3 and Zod 4 supported. Richest tool-authoring surface in TS benchmark.

Func[TArgs, TResults any] — reflects TArgs for JSON schema; runtime ConvertToWithJSONSchema converts LLM map[string]any into TArgs. Conversion failures return ErrInvalidArgument → OnToolErrorCallback chain. No built-in 'ask LLM to retry' (retryandreflect plugin is opt-in).

Pydantic-driven: type hints map to JSON Schema via Pydantic. On invalid args, model adapter raises AgentRunException, captured into ToolCallErrorEvent, result fed back to LLM as error message so the LLM can retry.
