Executor does serde_json::from_str into Value then tool.execute. Invalid arg JSON yields ToolCallResult{success:false, result:{error:'Failed to parse arguments…'}}. Tool body must serde_json::from_value into typed args (ToolCallError::SerdeError on failure). Optional output_schema.

JSON-schema-driven, validated by the MCP runtime. Invalid args cause an MCP error response sent back to the CLI, which the model sees as a tool error. Decorator converts Python type hints to JSON Schema (TypedDict support fixed in 0.1.51).

Zod (v3 or v4) for both schema generation (LLM-visible) and runtime validation. On invalid args, SDK MCP layer returns an error result and the loop sees is_error:true on tool_result, prompting model self-correction.

args_schema Pydantic model; _validate_kwargs catches ValidationError and raises 'Tool 'name' arguments validation failed' with build_schema_hint appended. Executor catches the ValueError and surfaces it to the LLM as a tool-error message so the LLM can retry with corrected args.

utils.InferTool runtime-validates by unmarshalling into the typed struct via sonic. Unmarshal errors propagate to the model as tool errors. No Pydantic-level field validation — user must layer go-playground/validator/v10 manually.

Go generic In any; schema inferred unless overridden with ai.WithInputSchema. Validation = json.Unmarshal into In — if it fails the error propagates back to the LLM. No explicit reject-on-bad-args mechanism beyond JSON decode error. WithStrictSchema(true) for OpenAI strict tool schemas.

Pydantic v2-driven validation on every tool call. Invalid args raise ToolException; ToolNode catches and converts to a ToolMessage with status='error' and the validation message in content, so the LLM can self-correct.

Runtime validation via Pydantic. create_schema_from_function builds a BaseModel subclass; on invalid LLM args the call raises Pydantic ValidationError, caught by _call_tool and wrapped in ToolOutput(is_error=True, content=str(e), …).

Input validation via Zod or any standard schema (JSON-Schema, Yup, etc.) via PublicSchema. On invalid args the framework returns a ValidationError to the model (not the host) so the LLM can self-correct. requestContextSchema validates context against the tool's expectations.

Python: Pydantic-based validation (_validate_arguments_against_schema). Invalid args raise ValidationError. Tools can declare input_model: type[BaseModel] for strict schema. .NET: AIFunctionFactory infers a JSON schema from C# parameter metadata; validation at deserialization.

Decorator builds Pydantic model from signature; schema.params_pydantic_model(**json_data) raises ModelBehaviorError('Invalid JSON input for tool…'). failure_error_function callback can transform that into a model-visible message (default: default_tool_error_function). Rich output types ToolOutputText/Image/FileContent.

Zod or JSON schema; with strict:true (default), LLM args are JSON.parse'd and Zod-validated. Invalid args throw InvalidToolInputError which is caught and routed through errorFunction (default: model-visible 'Invalid tool input' message; run continues for LLM retry).

Pydantic-validated: Tool.args_validator: SchemaValidator on every call. On invalid args, framework raises ModelRetry (a RetryPromptPart back to the model) — the model is automatically given the validation error and retries. Per-tool max_retries=. First-class retry semantic.

Args: Deserialize and Output: Serialize enforced statically. ToolDyn::call dispatcher deserializes the LLM-supplied JSON and returns ToolError::JsonError on failure; the loop renders to string and surfaces back to LLM as the tool result.
Pydantic validation in tools/decorator.py:62-65 and tools/_validator.py. Invalid args produce a ToolResult with status='error' and a descriptive message returned to the model so it can retry.

With Zod: ZodTool runtime validation via _inputSchema.parse(input). Invalid args throw at the boundary; agent catches and returns ToolResultBlock error. JSON-schema mode: declared schema goes to model but SDK does NOT validate the model's args against it; callback receives unknown.

Zod 3 or Zod 4 supported. Runtime validation via parseToolCall against inputSchema. On invalid LLM args, experimental_repairToolCall(toolCall, error) is called to potentially repair; if no repair, a tool-input-error chunk surfaces and the loop continues. Unique repair primitive.

Tool.Run returns (map[string]any, error) — single-shot. Long-running tools mark IsLongRunning: true (emits LongRunningToolIDs) and pause the agent loop, but they don't yield mid-execution progress events back to the model. LiveSession bidi streaming is for the LLM, not for tool-internal progress.

Generator-tool support exists. A tool can be a generator function returning chunks; FunctionCall.execute detects isgenerator(result) and stores the generator. Model adapter must consume it. No first-class 'tool yields progress events to LLM mid-execution' — chunks are aggregated for the LLM.

ToolRuntime::execute returns a single Value, not a stream. A tool cannot yield progress events back to the model mid-execution. tool.execute(args) has no Context access so even sending Event::SendMessage requires capturing the sender at tool construction time.

SDK MCP server path: tool handlers must return a single {content: [...]} dict. The CLI itself streams tool output (e.g. Monitor) but third-party SDK MCP tools are request/response only — no mid-execution yield.

Bash with run_in_background:true returns immediately; output polled via TaskOutputInput.block:true. SDKToolProgressMessage emits elapsed_time_seconds heartbeats during long tool calls so UI can show progress. Mid-execution partial results to the model: not supported.

Tool's _run returns a single value (string or Any cast to string). No mechanism for a tool to yield partial results to the model mid-execution. LLM only sees the final return value. For long tools, only option is logging to event bus / stdout and returning a single final string.

StreamableTool returns *schema.StreamReader[string] (components/tool/interface.go:53-57). Tool can yield chunks; framework concatenates / forwards them. EnhancedStreamableTool does the same for multimodal results. First-class streaming primitive.

Tool functions return (Out, error) after fully executing. No yield-style API for emitting partial results to the model mid-execution. MultipartToolResponse can return multiple parts at end but not during. For long ops, use BackgroundModel pattern or return Operation ID for polling.

A tool that takes runtime: ToolRuntime can call runtime.stream_writer({'progress': 0.5}) to emit CustomStreamPart frames mid-execution (tool_node.py:1663-1730). Visible to clients on stream_mode='custom'. First-class typed streaming.

Tools can write to the event stream via ctx.write_event_to_stream(ProgressEvent(pct=…)) inside the tool body (because they receive the live Context). Emits custom events to consumer mid-execution. Tools don't yield partial results back to the LLM mid-call though — the tool returns once.

Tools can yield mid-execution progress via ctx.writer: ToolStream — produces tool-output chunks in fullStream. Tools can also suspend(payload) via ctx.agent.suspend for HITL pauses with custom payloads. Both progress streaming and suspension are first-class.

Tools cannot yield partial results to the model mid-execution (LLM expects single function_result content). Within the agent loop, a tool can update session state which the next chat call will read. .NET FunctionInvocationDelegatingAgent does expose progress events to the surrounding agent stream so a UI can render in-flight progress.

Not native. Function-tool returns when its async function returns; no yield-partial-result-to-model primitive. Hosted ShellTool streams stdout deltas and ApplyPatchTool streams patch progress — but those are special-cased hosted-tool flows, not a generic API. Workaround: job_id + poll, or sub-agent.

Not first-class. execute returns Promise<Result>; no yield-based incremental output to the model. Have to buffer and return final string. For long-running tools, HITL approval pause is suggested as a poor substitute.

Limited. Tools return a single value (sync or async). For 'tool yields progress mid-execution', recommended pattern is to call back into the parent agent loop via additional ToolCallPart/ToolReturnParts, or use deferred external execution (CallDeferred).
Tool's call returns one Output; no incremental yield mechanism for a tool to emit progress while running.

Tools return an AsyncGenerator; yielded values are wrapped as ToolStreamEvents and surface to the agent stream. The final yield must be a ToolResult (executor extracts it). First-class streaming semantic with explicit terminator.

Tool callbacks can be async generators that yield ToolStreamEvent or arbitrary values (tools/tool.ts:93). Yielded objects become ToolStreamUpdateEvent; final return becomes ToolResultBlock. Symmetric with Python SDK.

Tool execute can return AsyncIterable<OUTPUT> (provider-utils/types/tool-execute-function.ts:38). Each yielded chunk becomes a tool-output-available chunk with preliminary:true, then a final non-preliminary chunk. Strong first-class streaming for progressive tools.

ADK ships tool/mcptoolset/ built on the official go-sdk v1.4.1 with lazy session connect, tool filter predicates, and HITL confirmation hooks per MCP tool. Usage is a one-liner that wraps any mcp.Transport and surfaces the tools to the agent.

agno.tools.mcp.MCPTools is a Toolkit that connects to external servers and exposes their tools to the agent with default streamable-http when a url is given. Header providers cover dynamic auth so external MCP servers are a drop-in toolkit.

McpToolsManager in autoagents-toolkit consumes one or many MCP servers behind the mcp feature flag, wrapping each tool as an McpToolAdapter. Client support is real and ergonomic but limited to stdio transport, which keeps it short of the strongest entries.

The bundled Claude Code CLI is itself the MCP client and the SDK surfaces mcp_servers, reconnect_mcp_server, get_mcp_status, toggle_mcp_server, and strict_mcp_config. That gives the deepest external MCP control surface of any Python stack here.

The CLI consumes MCP servers natively via Options.mcpServers with Stdio, SSE, HTTP, SDK and internal proxy/ws variants. Query.reconnectMcpServer, mcpServerStatus, toggleMcpServer, setMcpServers and background-connect with alwaysLoad make this the most complete client we observed.

crewai.mcp ships MCPServerStdio, MCPServerHTTP, MCPServerSSE config objects and an mcps argument on Agent that accepts slugs, URLs or full configs. Tool filtering, list caching and a 3-retry client round out solid first-class consumption.

eino-ext components/tool/mcp and components/tool/mcp/officialmcp give parallel adapters over mark3labs/mcp-go and the official Go SDK, returning standard []tool.BaseTool from mcp.GetTools. Auto-translation of MCP InputSchema makes external servers first-class tools.

go/plugins/mcp is a dedicated plugin with GenkitMCPClient plus an MCPHost that manages many servers and merges their tools into the Genkit registry. Built on mark3labs/mcp-go, it is one of the few stacks that explicitly orchestrates multi-server consumption.

MCP consumption goes through the separate langchain-mcp-adapters package, exposing servers as BaseTool instances usable in ToolNode or create_react_agent. The integration is documented and works, but the adapter living outside the core repo costs it the top mark.

llama-index-tools-mcp is first-party and wraps any mcp.ClientSession as FunctionTools via McpToolSpec, with BasicMCPClient transport auto-selection between stdio, SSE and streamable_http. OAuth token storage is part of the same client surface.

@mastra/mcp wires external MCP servers via mcpServers config, with HTTP routes under /api/mcp-clients/* for runtime management. Token forwarding through requestContext makes per-tenant auth tractable for production.

Python ships MCPStdioTool, MCPStreamableHTTPTool and MCPWebsocketTool as concrete MCPTool subclasses and the .NET side has Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows.Declarative.Mcp plus ModelContextProtocol SDK integration. Coverage on both runtimes is unusual and pushes this to first-class.

MCPServerStdio, MCPServerSse, MCPServerStreamableHttp implement the MCPServer ABC and attach to an Agent via mcp_servers with auto tool discovery. MCPServerManager pairs connect/cleanup explicitly so production wiring is well shaped.

Three built-in MCPServer types (stdio, streamable HTTP, SSE) plus a hostedMcpTool for the OpenAI Responses-API hosted variant, all auto-merged into the agent's tools per run. The MCPServers helper handles parallel connect and shutdown.

pydantic_ai.mcp.MCPToolset consumes external MCP servers as a standard toolset and the MCP capability bridges to provider-native MCP when supported. Concrete MCPServerStdio/SSE/StreamableHTTP plus FastMCP toolset cover every common shape.

With the rmcp feature, AgentBuilder.rmcp_tool/.rmcp_tools register McpTool adapters and McpClientHandler reacts to tools/list_changed by re-registering on the internal ToolServer. Capable but the auth and transport story is delegated entirely to the rmcp crate.

MCPClient wraps the official Python mcp SDK with allowed/rejected filter matchers, MCPAgentTool registration and clean context-manager usage. A background thread plus _NON_FATAL_ERROR_PATTERNS handles transient errors without tearing down the session.

An McpClient can be dropped directly into AgentConfig.tools and agent.initialize lists the server's tools into the ToolRegistry, with toolsChanged notifications driving hot reload. Built-in OAuth client credentials, custom auth providers, headers, failOpen and elicitation callbacks are unusually rich.

createMCPClient returns an MCPClient whose .tools() yields a ToolSet usable in any streamText or agent.tools, with stdio, SSE and streamable HTTP transports plus a mock transport for tests. OAuth and reconnection live in the same package.

ADK Go does not expose its tools as an MCP server out of the box; the report explicitly contrasts this with the experimental Python ADK MCP-server support. Anyone wanting to publish their ADK agent over MCP has to wrap it with the upstream Go SDK themselves.

AgentOS exposes an MCP server at /mcp through agno.os.mcp.get_mcp_server, attaching dozens of MCP tools (run_agent, run_team, run_workflow, knowledge search, memory CRUD) over streamable HTTP. The server lifecycle is bound to the AgentOS lifespan.
AutoAgents can consume MCP servers but has no helper to expose its own tools as one. The report explicitly calls this out as BYO.

createSdkMcpServer plus @tool publishes tools in-process via the control-protocol bridge, which is the headline pattern; no standalone stdio MCP server entrypoint ships. Useful for the SDK's CLI host but not for other MCP consumers without extra plumbing.

createSdkMcpServer exposes tools in-process via the CLI's JSON control protocol, ideal for production with no subprocess cost. External MCP clients still cannot connect because the server is not externally addressable.

CrewBase decoration provides _mcp_server_adapter and the dashboard 'Export as MCP' feature generates an MCP server from a deployed Automation, with docs/learn/custom-mcp-server.mdx walking through publishing a crew. This is a fully supported product-level workflow.
eino-ext provides no eino.NewMCPServer helper; publishing tools over MCP requires writing the server with mark3labs/mcp-go yourself. Server-side support is entirely absent from the framework.

mcp.NewMCPServer exposes all Genkit-registered tools, prompts and resources to MCP clients, so the same Go process can act as both server and client. This is the most balanced server story in the Go ecosystem reviewed.

Every deployed agent automatically gets an /mcp route on the langgraph_api server, with a disable_mcp escape hatch in the CLI schema. Exposing the deployment as an MCP server is the default, not an add-on.

workflow_as_mcp wraps any Workflow (including an AgentWorkflow) as a FastMCP server, exposing it as a tool and streaming workflow events as MCP log messages. Functions and workflows become MCP servers without leaving Python.

@mastra/mcp packages/mcp/src/server lets Mastra tools and skills be exposed as an MCP server for other agents/clients to consume. Server is a first-party package alongside the client and integrates with the in-process transport.

_mcp.py and dev.md describe exposing tools as an MCP server, and HostingAzureFunctions/McpToolTriggerOptions provides explicit Azure Functions triggers for MCP tools. The report flags the support but does not show a complete same-process server example, so it sits a notch below the strongest cases.

Only partial support: HostedMCPTool lets the agent consume an OpenAI-hosted MCP server, but there is no first-party wrapper to expose the agent's own tools as an MCP server. Self-hosting still means falling back to the upstream mcp SDK.
The SDK explicitly does not expose its own agent as an MCP server; the only path is to author a server with @modelcontextprotocol/sdk directly. Hosted MCP is consumer-side, not server-side.

FastMCP integration via toolsets/fastmcp.py and durable_exec _fastmcp_toolset.py exposes agent tools as an MCP server. The same machinery is shared by the in-process FastMCP toolset adapter so server-side support is unified.
tool/server.rs is Rig's internal tool dispatch, not an MCP exposure, and the report finds no rmcp_serve example. Publishing Rig tools to external MCP clients is not first-class.

The SDK itself does not run an MCP server, but the strands-agents/mcp-server companion repo exposes Strands agents over MCP. Support exists in the org but is out-of-tree, which limits how 'first-party' it can be considered for benchmark use.
The TS SDK ships no MCP server stack; the strands-agents/mcp-server repo provides it separately. Same pattern as the Python sibling: usable but not in the SDK package.
@ai-sdk/mcp is client-only; the SDK does not expose its own tools as an MCP server. Anyone wanting that builds it with the standard @modelcontextprotocol/sdk.
Whatever the official go-sdk supports is exposed: stdio, HTTP and SSE through user-constructed mcp.Transport. In-process is mechanically possible but not a dedicated API surface.

MCPTools(transport=) accepts stdio, sse and streamable-http, defaulting to streamable-http when a url is supplied and stdio otherwise. SSE is flagged deprecated in favor of streamable-http but in-process MCP is indirect.
Only stdio is wired up via rmcp::transport::TokioChildProcess even though rmcp itself supports SSE/HTTP. The other transports are explicitly noted as not supported.

McpStdioServerConfig, McpSSEServerConfig, McpHttpServerConfig and McpSdkServerConfig give the full transport matrix, with the in-process variant being the headline feature. Every documented MCP transport is covered.

The public McpServerConfig union covers stdio, SSE, streamable HTTP and SDK in-process, and the CLI internals add WebSocket and proxy variants for IDE servers. This is the widest transport surface in the benchmark.
mcp/transports/ ships stdio.py, http.py and sse.py for all three over-the-wire transports. The report explicitly notes no in-process / SDK-direct transport.

Through mark3labs/mcp-go you get stdio, SSE and HTTP; through the official go-sdk adapter you get stdio plus streamable HTTP, with in-process clients possible. Coverage is full but mediated by the underlying SDK choice.

StdioConfig, SSEConfig and StreamableHTTPConfig give the three standard transports for client and server. The report explicitly says no in-process transport, which knocks it down a step versus the in-process leaders.
Client supports stdio + HTTP via langchain-mcp-adapters and the server side is HTTP only on the /mcp route. SSE and in-process MCP are not surfaced.

BasicMCPClient auto-picks among stdio, sse and streamable_http based on URL or command, and workflow_as_mcp delivers an in-process FastMCP server. Full transport coverage on both client and server sides.
stdio, SSE/HTTP and in-process transports are all explicitly supported, with the in-process transport tailored for SDK-defined MCP servers. Coverage matches the strongest TypeScript stacks.

Python MCPTool subclasses cover stdio, streamable HTTP and WebSocket, and .NET adds HTTP/SSE via Microsoft.Extensions.AI. The Workflows.Declarative.Mcp pathway plus Python _mcp.py provide an in-process option without subprocess.
MCPServerStdio, MCPServerSse and MCPServerStreamableHttp cover all three protocol transports. In-process is technically possible through the mcp library but not shipped first-party.
MCPServerStdio, MCPServerStreamableHttp and MCPServerSSE plus hostedMcpTool give every common transport including the OpenAI hosted variant. The hosted option is unique to this SDK in the benchmark.
MCPServerStdio, MCPServerSSE and MCPServerStreamableHTTP cover the wire transports and the FastMCP toolset adds an in-process path. Full transport matrix on the same MCPToolset abstraction.

Transports inherit from the rmcp crate (stdio, SSE, HTTP depending on how ServerSink is constructed), with example code showing only the basic pattern. Coverage is real but underdocumented and not a first-class part of the Rig API.

Depends on mcp>=1.23.0 which supports stdio, SSE and streamable HTTP, with stdio_client+StdioServerParameters as the primary documented pattern. In-process is possible via mcp.client.session but not the advertised path.

StdioClientTransport for subprocesses and StreamableHTTPClientTransport when a url is given are first-class; any Transport conforming to the upstream interface also works. SSE is not called out and in-process is left to user code.
@ai-sdk/mcp ships stdio, SSE and streamable HTTP transports plus a mock transport for testing. No first-class in-process MCP tool wrapper since the SDK already accepts function tools directly.

Lazy connect on first ListTools (set.go:31) with connectionRefresher reconnecting on errors. Credentials pass through transport-specific mechanisms (HTTP headers, stdio env vars); no built-in OAuth flow.

HTTP transports accept static headers or a header_provider callable for dynamic per-request JWTs, and the Toolkit's connect/close is bound to the AgentOS lifespan via mcp_lifespan. Solid coverage although reconnection details are not explicit.
Auth is just env vars on the MCP server config and a 30s connection timeout. The report explicitly notes no automatic reconnection on failure.

ClaudeSDKClient exposes reconnect_mcp_server, get_mcp_status returning per-server McpServerStatus, and toggle_mcp_server enable/disable. strict_mcp_config provides multi-tenant isolation, and credentials pass via env or HTTP headers on the server configs.

stdio env, HTTP headers and full OAuth flow (clientId, callbackPort, authServerMetadataUrl, scopes) plus Query.reconnectMcpServer, mcpServerStatus with needs-auth state, toggleMcpServer, setMcpServers, background connect with alwaysLoad and onElicitation user input. The richest MCP lifecycle surface in the benchmark.
MCP_MAX_RETRIES=3 with 30s timeouts on connection/discovery/exec, a 5-minute tool schema cache and ToolFilter primitives. Auth is plain headers/env vars without dedicated OAuth helpers.

Config.CustomHeaders carries Bearer tokens or arbitrary headers on every call and Config.Meta passes metadata, but reconnection, health and version negotiation are explicitly delegated to the underlying SDK without framework wrappers.

Credentials go via Headers map for SSE/StreamableHTTP or env vars for stdio, and client.connect supports re-establishing while MCPHost tracks each GenkitMCPClient by name. No built-in health endpoint; failed transports surface as errors at call time.

Per-run MCP connections initialise in the langgraph_sdk MakeRuntimeContext ert.context callback, lifecycle-bound to the run. External MCP server auth follows standard langchain-mcp-adapters (env vars, OAuth).

OAuth is supported through OAuthClientProvider with a TokenStorage interface and DefaultInMemoryTokenStorage default, intended to be replaced for production persistence. Cleaner OAuth story than most peers but reconnection/health details are limited.

Credentials come from mcpClients config at boot or, at runtime, via requestContext.get(MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY), used by the editor to forward the same auth as the Mastra server itself. Reconnection and health are deferred to the client implementation.

MCPStreamableHTTPTool accepts a custom HTTP transport with auth headers and tools use lazy initialization documented as a DevUI gotcha. Health and version negotiation are handled by the underlying mcp SDK without framework-level controls.

Credentials pass via Sse/StreamableHttp headers or stdio env; connect()/cleanup() is explicit and MCPServerManager pairs grouped lifecycle. _InitializedNotificationTolerantStreamableHTTPTransport handles a known ordering bug and require_approval supports always/never/dict/callable approval policies.

Stdio env, HTTP/SSE headers and hosted MCP authorization/headers are all covered, with MCPServers/connectMcpServers opening connections in parallel and closing them at shutdown. Reconnection and version negotiation lean on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk basics.

MCPToolset carries an _MCPSessionState with reconnection logic, HTTP transports support headers/OAuth via _make_httpx_client_factory and MCP server-side sampling is wired to a Pydantic AI Model. Strong end-to-end coverage just shy of the Claude SDKs.

McpClientHandler reacts to tools/list_changed by re-registering on the ToolServer, but auth is opaque and inherited from the rmcp transport setup. The framework adds little beyond what the underlying crate provides.

MCPClient runs in a background thread with cleanup/finalizer and tool_registry.cleanup wires into agent destruction; _NON_FATAL_ERROR_PATTERNS keeps transient errors from tearing down the session. Auth is delegated entirely to the MCP server via transport headers.

McpClientConfig provides OAuth client_credentials, custom OAuthClientProvider, headers, failOpen, elicitationCallback, tasksConfig long-running tools, OTel propagation toggle and the agent cancel-signal is forwarded into MCP tool calls. Most complete TypeScript lifecycle surface outside the Claude SDK.

OAuth lives in packages/mcp/src/tool/oauth.ts and DefaultMCPClient has reconnection logic at mcp-client.ts:226. Standard HTTP auth headers work via HTTP/SSE transports but there is no per-server status or toggle API.

No PII redaction, prompt-injection detector, or hallucination scorer ships. Section 16.1 calls it "BYO" via BeforeModelCallback / AfterModelCallback. Engineer is responsible for sourcing and wiring all guardrails.

First-class BaseGuardrail interface with three shipped guardrails: PromptInjectionGuardrail, PIIDetectionGuardrail, and OpenAIModerationGuardrail wired via pre_hooks/post_hooks. Raises InputCheckError / OutputCheckError. Directly matches the benchmark's first-party filter expectation.

autoagents-guardrails crate ships prompt_injection, regex_pii_redaction, and toxicity guards with Block/Sanitize/Audit policies and an LLMLayer integration. GuardrailBlocked errors propagate through the executor. Among the strongest first-party guardrail offerings.
Section 16.1 marks it red: no PII redaction, no prompt-injection detection, no hallucination detection. Must be built via UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse hooks. No detector primitives shipped.

Not first-party; PII redaction / prompt-injection / hallucination detection are explicitly BYO via PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks. No built-in detectors. Sandbox primitives are strong but guardrails are not.

Agent.guardrail and Task.guardrail callables run on output with retry, and LLMGuardrail*Event events stream. Built-in HallucinationGuardrail and PII redaction are AMP-only (paid). OSS provides the framework but ships no detectors.
Not first-party. PII / prompt-injection / hallucination detection are BYO via ChatModelAgentMiddleware that runs regex/classifier/LLM-judge. No shipped detectors.
Not provided as a first-party primitive in go/. Must scrub via WrapGenerate or reject in WrapTool. No shipped detectors.

Not provided — BYO. PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, hallucination detection live outside OSS runtime. Common patterns use pre_model_hook with Lakera/Presidio/OpenAI moderation wired as callbacks.
Not first-party in core. llama-index-integrations ecosystem includes llama-index-guardrails on PyPI and Guardrails AI / NeMo Guardrails integrations. Available but not shipped in core.

Built-in processors under packages/core/src/processors/processors/: moderation, pii-detector, prompt-injection-detector, cost-guard, regex-filter, language-detector, unicode-normalizer, system-prompt-scrubber. Each can ctx.abort with retry. Best-in-class first-party coverage.

Information-flow control via IntegrityLabel/ConfidentialityLabel/ContentLabel and LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware / PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware (ADR 0024). Purview integration package for Microsoft compliance labels. PII redaction remains BYO via middleware.

Best guardrail surface in the comparison: @input_guardrail, @output_guardrail, @tool_input_guardrail, @tool_output_guardrail with allow/reject_content/raise_exception tri-state. Tripwire mechanism halts runs. No shipped PII / prompt-injection detector — only the framework hooks.

First-class: InputGuardrail, OutputGuardrail, ToolInputGuardrail, ToolOutputGuardrail, HandoffEnabledPredicate. All produce tripwireTriggered halts. No first-party PII / prompt-injection detector — BYO via LlmGuard/Lakera.

First-party hooks (before_model_request, after_tool_execute, wrap_output_validate) let you plug detectors in. No bundled PII / injection detector. Third-party pydantic-ai-backend provides DockerSandbox.
Not provided. No built-in PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination check. Pure BYO.

Bedrock Guardrails are first-class for the Bedrock provider: GuardrailConfig wired through, with redactContent chunks rewriting messages. Provider-specific only — for other providers it is BYO via hooks.
BedrockGuardrailConfig native plus a generic interventions subsystem with proceed/deny/guide/confirm/transform policy actions. GuardContentBlock support. PII / prompt-injection detection remains BYO.
Not provided. PII, prompt-injection, hallucination detection are BYO via LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams or prepareStep. No shipped detectors.

No allow/deny list, no canUseTool hook. tool.FilterToolset removes tools from the LLM's view but tools that ARE in the toolset run as plain Go calls without sandbox. RequireConfirmation flag offers HITL gating only.

@tool(requires_confirmation=True) per-tool HITL gate, tool_hooks server-side deny, skills frontmatter allowed-tools, path-traversal protections in skill loaders, plus JWT-scope RBAC at the HTTP layer. Layered and composable.

AgentHooks::on_tool_call returning Abort gates per call. WasmRuntime executes tools in a wasmtime sandbox, and CodeActAgent runs TypeScript via Deno AST + rquickjs. No declarative per-tool allowlist data structure.

SandboxSettings (macOS sandbox-exec / Linux seccomp) with network allow/deny, excluded commands, ignore-violations, nested-sandbox. permission_mode default/acceptEdits/plan/bypassPermissions/dontAsk/auto plus can_use_tool callback. Most comprehensive permission surface in the comparison.

Section calls it "excellent": canUseTool callback, PreToolUse hook with allow/deny/defer, PermissionMode (six modes), PermissionRequest hook, persisted PermissionUpdate rules, per-MCP-server tool ACL, disallowedTools, tools: [] disable. The richest permission model.

Construction-time tools=[...] allow list, per-tool max_usage_count cap, before_tool_call hook returning False blocks, MCP ToolFilter. RBAC is AMP-only. No declarative per-tool ACL with role/group/scope rules in OSS.

Allow/deny via BeforeAgent middleware filtering runCtx.Tools is BYO. WrapInvokableToolCall returning an error denies a call. Per-tool ACL is also BYO. No built-in execution sandbox; tools run with the process's OS permissions.

ToolApproval middleware with AllowedTools allowlist interrupts on un-allowed tools requiring RestartWith approval. Filesystem middleware uses os.Root sandbox to block path escape via .. / abs paths / symlinks with size caps. Two real primitives but bash etc. unmanaged.
wrap_tool_call is the per-tool ACL hook returning a ToolMessage to deny. No declarative allow_tools=[...] list; engineers wire policy in the wrapper. Functional but everything is wrapper logic.
No canUseTool hook. Permission enforced only by what tools you put in tools=[...] at construction. Inside a tool you can raise to refuse, but no declarative ACL.

activeTools per-call whitelist, requireApproval boolean / needsApprovalFn per tool, RBAC + FGA at the HTTP layer with agents:execute/read perms, processInputStep returning {activeTools} as canUseTool equivalent. No direct canUseTool callback.

approval_mode ("always_require" / "never_require") on FunctionTool / @tool decorator (ADR 0006). ToolApprovalAgent in .NET tracks standing-approval rules / state. ContextProvider filters tools; FunctionMiddleware can terminate disallowed calls.

function_tool(needs_approval=True | callable) HITL with ToolApprovalItem and RunState.approve/reject, MCP server-level require_approval, 4 tool-level guardrail decorators, is_enabled per tool. No declarative allow/deny list but building blocks compose to the same effect.

tool({needsApproval: true | predicate}) runtime approval gate, tool({isEnabled}) visibility filter, per-tool inputGuardrails/outputGuardrails block or mutate, agent.toolUseBehavior limits loops. Strong layered approach.

@agent.tool(requires_approval=True) plus HandleDeferredToolCalls capability for HITL approval. before_tool_execute hook returning SkipToolExecution(result) gates calls. PrepareTools capability for per-step ACL and ApprovalRequiredToolset for declarative per-tool ACL.

Entire permission model is the on_tool_call hook returning Skip{reason} or Terminate. No per-tool ACL, no structured permission verdicts, no default-deny mode. Filtering is opt-in via hook logic only.

Permission enforced via BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel_tool (True or string) plus the Interrupt mechanism for HITL approval. No declarative allow-list; caller is responsible for python_repl / shell sandboxing.
Permission via BeforeToolCallEvent.cancel or InterventionHandler.beforeToolCall returning deny(reason). No declarative allowed_tools list at the agent config layer — you write the policy.

toolApproval returns approved/denied/user-approval per tool or globally with structured tool-output-denied chunks. activeTools allowlist filter, tool.needsApproval per-tool flag. Strong runtime gating.
No E2B, Daytona, Modal, or code-interpreter integration. Gemini's native code_execution runs in Google's sandbox but is opaque to the caller.
E2B, Daytona, and Docker tools all run code in remote/isolated sandboxes under tools/e2b.py, tools/daytona.py, tools/docker.py. Three first-party adapters.
No integrations with E2B / Daytona / Modal. AutoAgents brings its own sandbox (wasmtime + rquickjs) — in-tree but no external provider integrations.
First-party bash sandbox via OS primitives only (macOS sandbox-exec, Linux seccomp). No E2B / Daytona / Modal adapters.

Built-in Linux sandbox via bubblewrap configured by Options.sandbox SandboxSettings with filesystem/network restriction, allowUnixSockets, failIfUnavailable. Linux-only. No E2B / Daytona / Modal integration.

E2B and Daytona are first-party in crewai-tools. E2BBaseTool with E2BExecTool, E2BFileTool, E2BPythonTool across three lifecycle modes (one-shot, persistent, attach). DaytonaSandboxTool with similar shape.

eino-ext ships filesystem.Backend implementations: adk/backend/agentkit/ is a Docker-shelled Python interpreter (filesystem analog of E2B/Daytona, but only for the filesystem middleware). No E2B / Daytona / Modal direct integration.
No E2B, Daytona, Modal, or code-interpreter plugin in go/. googlegenai/code_execution exposes Gemini's built-in code execution as a model feature, not a Genkit-level sandbox.
Not in this repo. Engineers wire E2B / Daytona / Modal as @tool-decorated wrappers around their SDKs.

llama-index-tools-code-interpreter (local, not sandboxed), llama-index-tools-azure-code-interpreter (Azure hosted sandbox), llama-index-tools-aws-bedrock-agentcore. E2B / Daytona / Modal: no first-party packages found.
Not first-party. You bring your own (E2B, Daytona, Modal) and wrap in a createTool.

Hyperlight (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hyperlight) hardware-isolated Wasm sandbox and DockerShellExecutor with ContainerUser / DockerNetworkMode / ShellPolicy for sandboxed shell execution. Strong first-party isolation choices.

Best in class: src/agents/extensions/sandbox/ ships blaxel, cloudflare, daytona, e2b, modal, runloop, vercel adapters. Each provider has mounts.py + sandbox.py exposing a BaseSandboxClient. Plus agents.computer.AsyncComputer for computer-use sandboxes.

Built-in UnixLocalSandboxClient (@openai/agents/sandbox/local) and OpenAI-hosted shell with container_auto. Third-party Docker / Blaxel / E2B-like providers referenced in CHANGELOG. Growing but smaller than Python sibling.
Third-party pydantic-ai-backend (Docker), various community packages. No E2B / Daytona / Modal integration in core.
Not provided. No E2B, Daytona, or Modal integration.
strands-agents-tools/code_interpreter/ ships sandbox bindings. Smaller surface than crewai/agno/openai-agents-python but present and first-party.
Not provided. The bash tool runs in-process; you sandbox at the OS / container level.

Experimental_Sandbox interface in @ai-sdk/provider-utils abstracts the runtime that hosts tool execution; tools receive options.experimental_sandbox. Concrete E2B / Daytona / Modal adapters are not first-party — you implement the interface.
Any tool placed on llmagent.Config.Tools or Toolsets is callable by the LLM. There is no policy layer to flip the posture.

Default-allow at tool registration (you ship the catalog), then deny via tool_hooks / guardrails / RBAC. JWT auth at the HTTP layer is deny-by-default when os_security_key or JWT is configured. Mixed posture.
AgentHooks::on_tool_call defaults to Continue. There is no central ACL — hook logic is the only gate.

permission_mode="default" prompts on dangerous tools; "dontAsk" is a true default-deny posture (only pre-approved tools run); bypassPermissions is default-allow. can_use_tool callback enables fine-grained control. Both postures available as first-class config.

permissionMode default prompts for dangerous operations from a CLI-defined exhaustive list. dontAsk flips to default-deny (only pre-approved tools run). Production typically uses acceptEdits or bypassPermissions with canUseTool gating. First-class posture toggle.

Tools are default-deny — an agent has only the tools you pass via tools=[...]. Skills default-deny similarly. MCP is default-allow (all server tools available unless ToolFilter set). Hooks default-allow. Mixed posture by subsystem.
All registered tools are visible to the LLM unless explicitly filtered. Skill middleware enumerates all skills by default. No allowTool gate before LLM can call it.
Default-allow for tools — everything registered is callable. ToolApproval middleware flips this to default-deny + explicit allowlist or approval, but it is opt-in per-call. No global toggle.
Default-allow. Whatever tools you pass to ToolNode / create_react_agent are dispatched. wrap_tool_call is opt-in for tightening — no built-in deny-first mode.
Default-allow. Whatever you pass to tools=[...] is callable. No deny-first posture toggle.
Default-deny for HTTP routes when server.auth is configured. Default-allow for tools unless requireApproval or activeTools whitelist is set. Mixed posture across layers.
Tools are default-allow (approval_mode defaults to "never_require"). Shell tools default to a ShellPolicy that denies unless explicitly allowed. Mixed posture per tool family.

Default-allow for tools — any tool in Agent(tools=[...]) is callable. Opt-in via needs_approval=True and guardrail decorators. Shell sandboxes ship explicit deny-network policies (ShellToolContainerNetworkPolicyAllowlist default-deny + allowlist). No global default-deny mode.
Tools default to isEnabled: true, needsApproval: false. The default is allow. Opt-in to deny via needsApproval predicate or isEnabled false.
Default-allow for declared tools, default-deny for unknown tools (model can only call registered ones). Approval is opt-in per tool via ApprovalRequiredToolset.
Default is allow-all-registered — every tool you .tool(...) is callable. Filtering is opt-in via hook logic. No default-deny mode.
Default-allow. python_repl and shell ship with confirmation prompts, but the SDK does not enforce an allow-list otherwise. Caller is responsible for tightening.
Default-allow. No tool requires explicit permission; the model can call any registered tool unless you intercept via hook.

Default-allow at tool dispatch — if toolApproval is not set, tools execute. Setting a global toolApproval: () => 'user-approval' cleanly flips the entire run to default-deny-pending-human. Easy one-line posture flip.

ADK Go ships OTel-native tracing with GenAI semantic conventions and spans for invoke_agent, generate_content, and execute_tool wired directly into the agent runtime. Setup is via telemetry.New(...) returning TracerProvider/LoggerProvider with OTLP HTTP exporters out of the box plus WithOtelToCloud for GCP Cloud Trace. The bundled REST server also exposes an in-memory DebugTelemetry for in-process inspection.

Agno wires OpenTelemetry through openinference-instrumentation-agno: setup_tracing(db=db) installs an AgnoInstrumentor that auto-traces agent runs, model calls, tool executions, team coordination, and workflow steps. A DatabaseSpanExporter persists spans to agno_traces/agno_spans tables and any standard OTLP exporter (Datadog, Honeycomb, Jaeger) can be added to the same TracerProvider. Extras for weave/openlit wire alternative backends.

AutoAgents ships a dedicated autoagents-telemetry crate with a TelemetryProvider trait, bundled OTLP (HTTP/gRPC) and Langfuse (feature-gated) implementations, and a Tracer that subscribes to a handle's event stream and converts events to spans. Redaction is built into the config. There is no first-party LangSmith adapter, but the OTel pipe covers the common case.

The Python SDK injects the caller's OpenTelemetry trace context (TRACEPARENT/TRACESTATE) into the bundled Claude CLI subprocess so CLI-emitted LLM/tool spans parent under your distributed trace. You install with the [otel] extra and let the CLI's own OTel emission do the heavy lifting. No first-party LangSmith/LangFuse/Datadog adapters — wiring is whatever your OTel collector accepts.

The TypeScript SDK forwards the caller's active OpenTelemetry trace context to the CLI subprocess (CHANGELOG: "trace context propagation") so CLI-emitted spans for LLM and tool calls parent under your trace. You combine that with @opentelemetry/api in your consumer code for top-level spans. There is no first-party LangSmith/Langfuse exporter — the design assumes you point an OTel collector at whatever backend.

CrewAI ships OpenTelemetry by default (OTLP HTTP exporter, disable via CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY) and exposes a 151-event event bus that backs a long list of documented first-party listener integrations including Datadog, Langfuse, Langtrace, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, MLflow, Maxim, Openlit, Opik, Patronus, Portkey, Weave, and the CrewAI AMP Prompt Tracing dashboard. Breadth here is unusually deep.

Eino ships three first-party tracing exporters in eino-ext (Langfuse with batched submission/masking/sampling, LangSmith with full hierarchical dotted_order trace assembly, and APMPlus OTel-native exporter) plus CozeLoop for ByteDance's internal platform. callbacks.AppendGlobalHandlers(handler) wires global tracing once and every Graph/ChatModel/Tool/Retriever/Indexer/Embedding/Lambda invocation is automatically traced.

Genkit Go is OTel-native: spans (generate, tool, plus custom flow steps via genkit.Run) are emitted with action name/type, latency, and error attributes, and tracing is on by default. The googlecloud plugin ships exporters for Google Cloud Trace, Metrics, and Logging with built-in attributes like feature_name, flow_name, model. LangSmith would require a custom OTel exporter.

LangGraph relies on LangChain's callback ecosystem with the paid hosted LangSmith as the first-party tracer (auto-tracing every Runnable when LANGSMITH_API_KEY is set) and community handlers for Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Weights & Biases, Opik (Comet). LangSmith ships an OTel exporter but native OTel emission is not built into the OSS. 25+ exporters via the broader LangChain callback ecosystem.

LlamaIndex ships a dedicated llama-index-instrumentation library (extracted from core in 2025) with an async-task and thread-safe dispatcher tree of event/span handlers and a first-party OTel exporter via llama-index-observability-otel that bridges spans to any OTel-compatible backend. The integrations package ships ~20+ callback/observability adapters (Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, Opik, OpenInference, PromptLayer, UpTrain, W&B, HoneyHive, AgentOps, Literal AI, Argilla, AIM).

Mastra runs three observability pipelines inside ObservabilityEntrypoint: stream chunks carry usage, a metrics bus emits with cost context, and an IModelSpanTracker emits per-call/per-tool/per-processor spans with Langfuse, OpenTelemetry, and custom storage exporters. MODEL_GENERATION spans are re-stamped on fallback so cost attribution stays correct, and the metric system has built-in cardinality protection (blocked labels, UUID detection).

Microsoft Agent Framework's enable_instrumentation() wires the OTel tracer/meter/logger using GenAI semantic conventions: invoke_agent, chat, execute_tool spans (plus compaction spans from CompactionTelemetry). It is compatible with Azure Monitor / Application Insights / Jaeger / any OTel collector and emits a gen_ai.client.token.usage histogram alongside per-span gen_ai.usage.* attributes.

The Python SDK has a built-in TraceProvider + BatchTraceProcessor, default BackendSpanExporter to OpenAI's hosted dashboard, and 13 span data types covering agents, generations, function tools, guardrails, handoffs, MCP, voice and turns. 19 documented partner exporters (Weights & Biases, Arize-Phoenix, Future AGI, MLflow, Braintrust, Pydantic Logfire, AgentOps, Scorecard, Respan, LangSmith, Maxim, Comet Opik, Langfuse, Langtrace, Okahu-Monocle, Galileo, Portkey, LangDB, Agenta). No native OTel exporter shipped.

The JS SDK has a first-party tracer with a BatchTraceProcessor, an OpenAI exporter that ships traces to the OpenAI Traces dashboard by default, and rich span types (AgentSpan, GenerationSpan, FunctionSpan, HandoffSpan, GuardrailSpan, MCPListToolsSpan, TranscriptionSpan, SpeechSpan). Community integrations (AgentOps, Respan, PromptLayer) adapt to the TracingProcessor interface, but no first-party LangSmith/Langfuse/OTel adapter ships.

Pydantic AI is OpenTelemetry-native via the Instrumentation capability which installs spans for the agent run, model requests and tool calls with GenAI-spec attribute names. Logfire is the first-party backend and any other OTel-compatible backend works without extra wiring. Cleanest spec-conformant implementation in the Python set.

Rig emits info_span! invoke_agent and execute_tool spans pre-stamped with GenAI semantic-convention fields (gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/output_tokens/cache_read/cache_creation/reasoning_tokens, gen_ai.tool.*) in both non-streaming and streaming loops. The telemetry module exposes ProviderRequestExt/ProviderResponseExt/SpanCombinator traits for providers to fill spans with native request/response data, and OTel export is via standard tracing-opentelemetry (example: agent_with_tools_otel.rs).

Strands Python's Tracer creates four span types (agent, event-loop-cycle, model-invoke, tool-call) using GenAI semantic conventions (gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.agent.id, gen_ai.usage.*). It exports via OTLP HTTP when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is set (otel extra installs opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http). Built-in, no extra glue required.

Strands TypeScript's setupTracer() configures a global OTel TracerProvider and the agent auto-emits agent.invoke, agent.loop.cycle.<N>, agent.model.invoke, and agent.tool.<name> spans. OTLP HTTP and console exporters plus anything else registered on the global OTel SDK. A lightweight in-memory AgentTrace tree is always collected (regardless of OTel config) and exposed on AgentResult.traces for local inspection.

Vercel AI SDK exposes a Telemetry interface with 12 callbacks (onStart, onStepStart, onLanguageModelCallStart/End, onToolExecutionStart/End, onStepFinish, onObjectStepStart/Finish, onEmbedStart/End, onRerankStart/End, onEnd, onError) plus an executeTool wrapper for nested-span propagation. @ai-sdk/otel ships the OpenTelemetry implementation that wires to Datadog/Honeycomb/Tempo/Signoz. Solid but no first-party LangSmith/Langfuse exporters.

Per-event usage_metadata captures PromptTokenCount, CandidatesTokenCount, TotalTokenCount, CachedContentTokenCount and ThoughtsTokenCount on every session.Event and persists to the DB row. USD cost is not provided — there is no per-model price table; you maintain one yourself and multiply. No first-party budget enforcement.

Agno reports tokens at five granularities (per-message MessageMetrics, per-run RunMetrics, per-session SessionMetrics, per-model ModelMetrics, streaming ModelRequestCompletedEvent) including input/output/total/cache_read/cache_write/reasoning. USD is first-party: BaseMetrics.cost is computed by model adapters using the pricing tables in agno.models.defaults.py and accumulated up via ModelMetrics.accumulate. RunMetrics.cost and SessionMetrics.cost roll up automatically.

StreamChunk::Usage carries prompt/completion/total tokens per LLM call from autoagents-llm and propagates into the Event stream. No first-party rollups for turn/session/tenant, no USD price-per-1k-tokens table, no $ conversion. Aggregation is left entirely to the OTel pipeline you build with autoagents-telemetry.

ResultMessage.total_cost_usd is computed by the bundled CLI and exposed per turn (including across model fallback) — the report calls this out as the only stack in the comparison with first-party USD cost on the result object. Tokens are surfaced per LLM call (AssistantMessage.usage), per turn (ResultMessage.usage), per sub-agent task (TaskUsage), and broken down per-model in ResultMessage.model_usage.

SDKResultMessage.total_cost_usd is built-in (computed by the CLI from its bundled pricing tables) and Options.maxBudgetUsd is a server-side enforced ceiling that emits subtype: 'error_max_budget_usd' on overrun. Tokens flow per LLM call (SDKAssistantMessage.message.usage), per turn (SDKResultMessage.usage), per model (SDKResultMessage.modelUsage) and per sub-agent (AgentOutput.usage). Strongest in the comparison alongside the Python sibling.

UsageMetrics tracks total/prompt/cached_prompt/completion/reasoning/cache_creation_tokens at per-call, per-task and per-kickoff levels via TokenCalcHandler subscribing to LiteLLM. LLM.completion_cost is declared but the report could find no code path that populates it from a per-token price table — effectively no first-party USD computation. AMP and Langfuse-style backends add cost rollups externally.

ResponseMeta.Usage on each assistant message exposes PromptTokens, CompletionTokens, TotalTokens, plus PromptTokenDetails.CachedTokens and CompletionTokensDetails.ReasoningTokens. USD is not provided — Eino reports tokens; conversion is a simple lookup since RunInfo.Type tells you the model adapter but you maintain the table. No turn/session/tenant rollups, only the per-call data.

GenerationUsage on ModelResponse.Usage is unusually detailed (InputTokens, OutputTokens, TotalTokens, CachedContentTokens, ThoughtsTokens, plus characters/images/audio/video for multi-modal). USD is not provided — no pricing.json, no cost_usd field, no getSpendReport. The final resp.Usage reflects the last call only; the addAutomaticTelemetry middleware emits per-call OTel metrics if you want aggregation.

AIMessage.usage_metadata is LangChain's standard with input/output/total tokens plus input_token_details (audio, cache_creation, cache_read) and output_token_details (audio, reasoning). USD is not provided in OSS — the report calls out that this is materially different from Claude Agent SDK (no built-in price table, no total_cost_usd, no max_budget_usd cap). Cost is offloaded to paid LangSmith which extends UsageMetadata server-side.

TokenCountingHandler accumulates prompt_llm_token_count and completion_llm_token_count across the run by reading ChatResponse.raw payloads (provider-dependent). USD is not provided — searching the whole core package for cost_usd/cost_in_dollars/usd returns nothing. You compute USD yourself from token counts times your provider price table.

note: 3 — rich tokens USD field is BYO
details: LanguageModelUsage tracks input/output/reasoning/cache_read/cache_write tokens at per-step (onStepFinish), per-turn (onFinish.totalUsage) and per-run (MastraModelOutput.totalUsage) levels with raw provider passthrough. USD is not computed by the SDK — CostContext.estimatedCost is just a field the caller or exporter fills in and there is no pricing.ts table in @mastra/core. BYO pricing logic in onStepFinish.

AgentResponse.usage_details / ChatResponse.usage_details / Message Content.from_usage all carry input_token_count, output_token_count, total_token_count plus arbitrary extra integer fields, and observability.py emits OTel attributes gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/output_tokens and a gen_ai.client.token.usage histogram. INNER_ACCUMULATED_USAGE accumulates across inner chat-client calls of an agent run. USD is not built-in — tokens only, you compute cost in a downstream processor.

Usage carries requests/input_tokens/output_tokens/total_tokens plus InputTokensDetails (cached_tokens) and OutputTokensDetails (reasoning_tokens) and request_usage_entries preserves per-API-call breakdown after aggregation. Usage.add(other) aggregates per-call into per-turn into per-session via task_usage_to_span_data. USD is not provided; the report shows a 14-line compute_cost helper that the host has to maintain.

RequestUsage entries (Usage.requestUsageEntries) preserve per-API-call breakdown and aggregated Usage is on RunContext.usage / RunResult.state._context.usage with inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens, inputTokensDetails, outputTokensDetails. USD is not provided — the SDK only reports tokens; you compute cost from your own pricing table. No tenant aggregation.

RunUsage on AgentRunResult.usage and live RunContext.usage track requests, tool_calls, input_tokens, cache_write_tokens, cache_read_tokens, output_tokens plus a details dict. USD is computable first-party via the genai-prices package (Pydantic-maintained, used internally by RequestUsage.extract — usage.py:147-178) — calc_price(model, provider, usage) returns total_usd. One of only three first-party USD stacks alongside the two Claude SDKs and Agno.

Rig's Usage struct (completion/request.rs:394-409) carries input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens, cached_input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, reasoning_tokens on CompletionResponse, PromptResponse (with += aggregation across turns in agent.prompt) and MultiTurnStreamItem::FinalResponse, plus on every chat span via GenAI attribute fields. USD is not provided; you compute it from your own cost table.

Per-assistant-message message[metadata][usage] gives inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens plus cacheReadInputTokens and cacheWriteInputTokens, and agent.event_loop_metrics.accumulated_usage accumulates totals across the session. BeforeModelCallEvent exposes projected_input_tokens. USD is not provided — tokens only, no per-model price table, no cost_usd field.

Message.metadata.usage on every assistant message and result.metrics.accumulatedUsage on AgentResult carry inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens, cacheReadInputTokens, cacheWriteInputTokens. AgentMetrics also exposes cycleCount, agentInvocations[], toolMetrics call/success/error counts, projectedContextSize, totalDuration. USD is not provided; the SDK only counts tokens.

note: 3 — thorough tokens USD only via Gateway
details: LanguageModelUsage is unusually thorough with cache read/write, no-cache, text and reasoning sub-token detail at per-call, per-step (StepResult.usage) and per-run (GenerateTextResult.totalUsage) levels. USD is not computed by the SDK and there are no pricing tables, no costUSD field, no tokenCost helper. USD only surfaces via the Vercel AI Gateway REST API (GatewaySpendReportRow.totalCost/marketCost) — direct provider calls bypass that.

No first-party rollup helpers — the report lists per-tenant as ❌ DIY (stuff tenant_id into state, roll up at query time) and per-conversation as ⚠️ DIY (sum events with the same InvocationID). USD itself is BYO as well, so per-tenant cost stacks two layers of host code: tag with tenant, maintain pricing table, aggregate via plugin OnEventCallback or downstream tracing backend.

RunOutput.metrics.cost is available per run so per-conversation cost is mostly free (sum cost across runs on a session), but per-tenant is BYO — tag sessions with tenant_id in metadata and aggregate via your own DB query against agno_sessions / agno_metrics. No tenant primitive ships.

There is no tenant field in the framework; any tenant-tagged cost is computed by your own code from the Usage events. USD is also BYO, so this is doubly host-built. Telemetry attributes via the OTel provider are the only handle.

total_cost_usd is per turn — for per-tenant or per-conversation aggregation you accumulate that yourself keyed by your tenant id. The SessionKey.project_key is documented as the natural tagging key but the SDK does not roll up. Solid base because USD is first-party, but no rollup primitive.

total_cost_usd is per SDKResultMessage and SessionStore is explicitly not an aggregation point (entries are opaque pass-through). Per-tenant/per-conversation requires summing by session_id and your own tenantId mapping. modelUsage and AgentOutput.usage help with model and sub-agent splits but the SDK does not roll usage up for you.

Not provided. Pattern is a BaseEventListener that handles LLMCallCompletedEvent and tags by tenant, but listeners attach to a global bus so the handler fires for every crew in the process and you must filter on source.id. AMP's Traces dashboard offers org-wide cost views with org-as-tenant semantics. Awkward but workable.

First-party rollup absent. BYO via metadata-tagged tracing: every callbacks.Handler.OnStart sees the ctx (which can hold tenantId via WithSessionValues), and you emit metrics tagged by tenant from a custom handler. No tenant primitive ships.

Not provided. The googlecloud plugin exports OTel metrics with built-in feature_name/flow_name/model/error attributes but there is no built-in tenant_id; you add it via a custom OTel SpanProcessor or WrapGenerate middleware. USD is also BYO.

Not provided in OSS — BYO via metadata-tagged tracing. The recommended pattern is stamping metadata[tenant_id] on every run and a BaseCallbackHandler that joins tenant_id + model_name + usage_metadata and emits OTel metrics or a DB insert. LangSmith does this server-side if you pay for it.

BYO via metadata-tagged spans. The instrument_tags(...) context manager (llama-index-instrumentation dispatcher) is the recommended mechanism for per-tenant tagging — your downstream OTel/Datadog/etc. backend then aggregates. No native rollup primitive.

Per-tenant is not natively scoped. You attach it via the observability metrics path — keep your pricing table, hook onStepFinish to compute tokens * rate, emit a metric with costContext.estimatedCost. The metrics bus and MetricsConfig support labels but tenant tagging is BYO.

BYO. Add a tenant_id attribute on the span via a ChatMiddleware (the report shows a TenantTagger example) or enable_instrumentation configuration, then aggregate downstream in a trace backend (Azure Monitor, etc.). Per-agent-run accumulation is built in but tenant aggregation is not.

BYO via metadata-tagged tracing: RunConfig.trace_metadata={tenant_id: ...} and RunConfig.group_id tie multiple runs into one trace group. The first-party tracing pipeline carries these through trace_metadata so per-tenant rollups happen in the trace backend rather than in-process. No first-party in-process aggregator.

Per-session / per-tenant are not provided by the SDK; you aggregate yourself in a custom Session impl or after each run, tagging with your tenantId, and then in a TracingProcessor read span.metadata?.tenantId and emit per-tenant Datadog metrics. The first-party tracer makes this workable.

Not first-party in-process — you use a before_run/after_run hook to fold result.usage into your billing store keyed by metadata[tenant_id]. However Pydantic AI Gateway adds per-project/per-user/per-key USD caps with daily/weekly/monthly windows out of the box (docs/gateway.md:24) — the only stack in this set besides Vercel AI Gateway with a hosted spend-control primitive.

Not provided. There is no tenant-aware aggregator and per-conversation aggregation is not done by Rig — you sum PromptResponse.usage across all agent.prompt(...) calls sharing the same conversation_id yourself. Built on top of the tracing or Usage data via the metrics crate.

BYO. Subscribe to AfterModelCallEvent, multiply event.stop_response.message[metadata][usage] by your price table, aggregate by tenant from event.invocation_state.tenant_id. The report shows a small CostSink hook example that does exactly this for Datadog.

Per-tenant rollup not built in. You tag traces with agent.traceAttributes = { tenantId } (agent.ts:198) and aggregate downstream in your OTel collector. The light usage example uses an AfterModelCallEvent hook to push tokens per tenant to a metric client.

Via AI Gateway: gateway.getSpendReport({ groupBy: 'user' | 'tag' | ..., tags, userId, model, provider, credentialType }) returns USD totalCost / marketCost per group with tokens broken out. You tag each call with runtimeContext.tenantId via providerOptions.gateway.tags or metadata and group by tag. Without AI Gateway it falls back to BYO from LanguageModelUsage in onFinish.

The event stream effectively is the audit log: every session.Event carries Author, Timestamp, Content, Actions and persists to DB with no UPDATE paths in session/database/service.go (append-only by design). Suitable for forensic review but not tamper-evident (no hash chain). For out-of-band sinks register a plugin.OnEventCallback (plugin/plugin.go:31,167).

No first-class audit log distinct from tracing. The combination of JWT auth filling request.state.user_id, per-resource RBAC via require_resource_access, persisted traces (agno_traces/agno_spans), persisted runs (with user_id, agent_id, timestamps) and an agno_approvals table for HITL audit trail gives an audit-friendly footprint, but the framework doesn't ship a dedicated audit hook event stream abstraction.
BYO via the event stream. Events carry sub_id, actor_id, actor_name; timestamps are added on receive. No tamper-evident or sequence-numbered audit log built in.

Indirect but rich. The SessionStore mirror is your audit log — every transcript line (tool calls, tool results, prompts, mode changes) flows through SessionStore.append(). Combined with include_hook_events=True (added 0.1.74) you get a hook-execution audit stream with HookEventMessage carrying hook_event_name, subtype hook_started/hook_response, exit codes, outcomes. No tamper-evident chain (no signatures or hashes).

The on-disk JSONL transcript is the closest thing to a first-class audit log: every action of the loop (tool calls, decisions, permission denials, model responses) is in there, append-only on local disk, with optional SessionStore mirror for a tamper-resistant copy. For a true audit log you hook PostToolUse / PermissionDenied / PermissionRequest and push to your sink. No signed/append-only ledger.

Not first-class. The event bus emits structured events with timestamps and emission_sequence: int sequence numbers and parent IDs which you persist via a custom listener. The event_record is part of every checkpoint so post-hoc reconstruction of one run is straightforward. No tamper-evidence (no hash chain, no signatures).

Not first-class as separate from tracing. You write a callbacks.Handler (or use agent-level WithCallbacks) that emits structured audit events to your sink. Tamper-evident logging (hash chain, signed events) is not provided.

Not provided as a distinct primitive. All you get is tracing — there is no audit log interface (like Anthropic's) that you can swap to a separate tamper-evident sink. BYO via a WrapTool hook that logs to a write-once store.
Not provided as a tamper-evident audit stream. Engineers BYO by hooking on_chain_start/on_chain_end/on_tool_start/on_tool_end and shipping to an immutable log sink (S3, BigQuery, ClickHouse).
Not first-class. The instrumentation event stream + your own sink (Postgres / S3) is the recommended approach. Not tamper-evident out of the box.

Spans and metrics are the primary audit signal and storage/domains/observability/ persists all spans/metrics for query. RBAC + FGA route guards log denials at the middleware layer (more than most stacks for compliance). No first-party tamper-evident audit log — you'd ship spans to an append-only sink.

Trace data is the audit substrate; no separate tamper-evident audit log. The security.py LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware (security.py:793) records which labelled content flowed through which tools — useful for prompt-injection audit but not a general audit log. Most stacks in this set are at the same "trace is audit" level.
Not first-class. Tracing serves a similar role but is not tamper-evident. For audit hook into RunHooks.on_tool_start/on_tool_end and ship to your own append-only log.

Tracing spans (with traceIncludeSensitiveData: true) capture LLM inputs/outputs and tool inputs/outputs (docs/src/content/docs/guides/tracing.mdx:100-107). For tamper-evident logging you build your own append-only sink and call addTraceProcessor to mirror — the first-party tracer makes the mirror straightforward.

note: 2 — OTel spans Logfire treats as audit
details: Via OTel spans — Logfire treats every agent/model/tool span as an audit record. No tamper-evident store in-tree; for that you ship spans to a write-once backend. Strong only because the OTel emission is spec-conformant and Logfire is a first-party backend that explicitly positions itself as audit.

Not provided as a distinct facility. Tracing spans contain message-level data (gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages — mod.rs:451-452) — use them as your audit log by routing to your exporter of choice. No append-only or tamper-evident primitive.
Not first-class. Tracing serves double duty; for tamper-evident audit BYO sink subscribing to MessageAddedEvent + BeforeToolCallEvent + AfterToolCallEvent. No hash chain or signed ledger primitive.

Not a separate primitive but the hook event stream is the natural audit-log source — register a hook on every relevant event, serialize via event.toJSON() (designed for wire transport), pipe to your sink. The new interventions subsystem (strands-ts/src/interventions/registry.ts) is closer to "tamper-evident policy log" but no signed/append-only ledger is shipped.
Not provided — BYO. Use the Telemetry interface + your structured logger. The SDK does not ship tamper-evident audit log primitives.

note: 2 — no typed run ctx; state delta only
details: Run accepts userID/sessionID/appName plus WithStateDelta(map[string]any). No typed Context field; tenant lives in app:-prefixed Session.State by convention. RunConfig only has StreamingMode and SaveInputBlobsAsArtifacts.

Agent.run() exposes user_id, session_id, session_state, dependencies dict, metadata dict, plus knowledge_filters. dependencies/metadata land on RunContext and are the canonical per-call channel. No typed schema.

Task struct exposes only prompt, image, system_prompt, submission_id. No tenant/user/locale/metadata fields; the only workaround is stuffing data into system_prompt or capturing it at agent construction time.

ClaudeAgentOptions has ~50 fields (user, cwd, env, session_id) but no opaque user-context field to pass into hooks/tools. Tenant info is wired via closures, env vars, or SessionKey.project_key for the store.

Options has ~80 fields including sessionId, cwd, env, sessionStore, but no first-class tenantId or opaque user-context. Tenant is carried via closures in canUseTool/hooks plus env and SessionKey.projectKey.

No single run-loop input struct; each entrypoint differs. Tenant can only live in Crew.config/Agent.config/execution_context or OTel baggage. None of these are validated or designed for per-request tenant injection.
Runner.Run takes context.Context + WithSessionValues(map[string]any). Recommended idiom for tenant/user/locale; no typed Spec T or first-class struct, but covers the use case via ctx values.

No first-class tenantId field on GenerateActionOptions. Tenant flows via context.Context + ContextProvider (auto-populated from HTTP headers in genkit.Handler). Untyped ActionContext = map[string]any.

StateGraph(context_schema=Context) declares a typed dataclass; Runtime[ContextT] is the canonical run-deps channel. Frozen for the run, propagated everywhere. Strongest typed run-loop context in the benchmark.

note: 2 — kwargs into ctx.store; no typed ctx
details: No first-class context field on AgentWorkflowStartEvent. Tenant info goes via initial_state into ctx.store (untyped KV) or **kwargs captured in start event. No typed run-loop context.

RequestContext<T> is a typed Map with reserved keys (resourceId, threadId, versions, authToken). HTTP layer merges body context with server context, preserving reserved keys server-side for security. Designed for multi-tenant servers.

Python: function_invocation_kwargs Mapping[str,Any] is the per-call channel; .NET: AgentRunOptions.AdditionalProperties + AgentRunContext async-local. Untyped bags; no first-class tenant/user field on the run options.
Runner.run(context: TContext) carries a typed dataclass. Wrapped into RunContextWrapper[TContext] and propagated to instructions, guardrails, tools. Clean and idiomatic for tenant_id/user_id passing.
run(agent, input, { context: TContext }) wraps into RunContext<TContext> propagated to every tool, hook, guardrail, handoff. Type-safe per-call context, mirroring the Python SDK.

agent.run(deps=TenantDeps, metadata=..., spec=...) — deps is a typed dataclass; metadata is a dict or callable for OTel tagging; RunContext exposes 17 fields including deps, run_id, conversation_id, metadata.
PromptRequest has no tenant/user/locale fields. Tenant must be embedded in per-tool closures at AgentBuilder time or stuffed into preamble/conversation_id.
Agent.stream_async(prompt, invocation_state=dict) is the per-call channel; threaded into ToolContext and hooks. No typed schema, no first-class tenant field, but reliably propagated.
stream(args, { invocationState }) per-call escape hatch — Record<string, unknown>. Threaded by reference into every hook event and ToolContext. No typed schema.

ToolLoopAgent<CALL_OPTIONS, TOOLS, RUNTIME_CONTEXT> has typed generics. runtimeContext is per-call and feeds prepareStep/telemetry; toolsContext is per-tool typed context validated against contextSchema.
ToolContext exposes UserID(), AppName(), SessionID(), State(), Artifacts(), SearchMemory(). State() carries app:tenant_id by convention. Comprehensive runtime info reaches every tool.

FunctionCall._build_entrypoint_args inspects signature and injects run_context: RunContext when the tool declares it. RunContext exposes dependencies, user_id, session_state, messages. Idiomatic, well-typed.
ToolRuntime::execute takes only serde_json::Value args. No Context parameter; the tool sees no caller info. Per-tenant state must be captured as &self fields at construction.
SDK MCP @tool handler signature is Callable[[dict], Awaitable[dict]]. No ToolContext, no RunContext, no tenant id. Tenant must be closure-captured at server construction time.
tool() handler is (args, extra) — extra is the MCP request meta, not a harness RunContext. No first-class context propagation. Closure capture or PreToolUse hook is the workaround.
BaseTool._run(*args, **kwargs) receives only LLM-generated arguments. No context object. Workarounds: tool __init__ closure capture, or before_tool_call hook (global).
tool.InvokableRun(ctx, argumentsInJSON, opts...) gets context.Context; recommended path is context.WithValue + GetSessionValue. Also tool.Option for impl-specific config.
Tool function receives *ai.ToolContext that embeds context.Context. core.FromContext(ctx) returns ActionContext map populated by ContextProvider from HTTP headers.
ToolRuntime[ContextT, StateT] is a typed dataclass injected into tool signatures with state, context, config, store, tool_call_id. Parameter is stripped from LLM-facing JSON schema.
Tool may declare ctx: Context; workflow auto-injects the live Context. ctx.store.get('state') yields tenant from initial_state. Context param is excluded from LLM-visible schema.
Every tool's execute(args, ctx) gets ToolExecutionContext.requestContext (the typed Map). Tool can declare requestContextSchema (Zod) for validation. Workspace, browser, agent, writer also exposed.

Python @tool function may declare ctx: FunctionInvocationContext; _discover_injected_parameters auto-finds it. Exposes function, arguments, session, metadata, kwargs, result. .NET equivalent via FunctionInvokingChatClient.CurrentContext.
FunctionTool.on_invoke_tool(ctx, input) — ctx is ToolContext(RunContextWrapper) with typed .context: TContext plus tool_call_id, tool_name, agent, run_config. Idiomatic per-tenant tool authoring.
tool({ execute: (args, runContext) => runContext.context.tenantId }) — same RunContext instance threaded through entire run. Type-safe via generics.
Tool function takes ctx: RunContext[DepsT] as first arg; RunContext exposes deps, messages, usage, retry, tool_call_id, run_id, metadata, model_settings (17 fields). Excluded from LLM schema.
Tool trait's call(&self, args: Self::Args) receives no context. State must live on &self. Tool dispatch in prompt_request shows no ctx threading.
Class-based AgentTool.stream(tool_use, invocation_state) gets the per-call bag; decorated tools with context=True get ToolContext with .invocation_state and .agent.
Tool callback receives (input, context: ToolContext) — context exposes toolUse, agent, invocationState (shared by-reference). Hook mutations are observable in later tool callbacks.
tool.execute(input, options) — options.context is validated against tool.contextSchema (Zod), passed via toolsContext[name]. runtimeContext is NOT directly propagated to execute (gap).

BeforeToolCallback receives mutable args map[string]any; mutation in place forces server-side override. Per-call not per-tool-declaration; LLM still sees the field in the schema (leaky). No declarative InjectedToolArg.
tool_hooks list wraps every tool call as middleware; hook(function_name, next, args) can mutate args before calling next_func(**args). Has access to run_context. Not typed, but reliable mechanism.
on_tool_call takes &ToolCall by shared reference; cannot mutate args. Only HookOutcome::Continue/Abort. Forced args requires building one agent per tenant with tenant baked into the tool struct.

Two first-class mechanisms: PreToolUse hook returns {updatedInput} that the CLI uses instead of LLM input; can_use_tool returns PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=...). Both out-of-band via control protocol; LLM cannot bypass.
PermissionResult { behavior: 'allow', updatedInput } and PreToolUseHookSpecificOutput.updatedInput — CLI dispatches with the updated input. Canonical multi-tenant pattern. LLM cannot override.
ToolCallHookContext.tool_input is mutable in place. Global registration only — no per-crew/per-tenant scoping. Hook fires for every crew in the process; ContextVar workaround required.

ToolsNodeConfig.ToolArgumentsHandler(ctx, name, arguments string) returns rewritten JSON; or compose.ToolMiddleware.Invokable wraps the endpoint. Both BYO; LLM still sees the field unless scrubbed at info generation.
ai.Hooks.WrapTool receives ToolParams{Request, Tool}; middleware can mutate params.Request.Input map before next(). BYO — no built-in middleware ships.

_inject_tool_args strips LLM-supplied values for injected keys and replaces with harness values. Declarative InjectedState/InjectedStore/ToolRuntime; field excluded from LLM-facing JSON schema. The cleanest mechanism in the benchmark.
FunctionTool.partial_params merges as default but **kwargs from LLM win. Real force requires closure-wrapping or reading tenant from Context inside the tool. Convention not enforcement.

No dedicated PreToolUse hook returning updatedInput. Canonical answer is to keep tenantId out of the LLM-visible inputSchema and read it from requestContext inside execute. processInputStep can rebuild toolsets with closures.
FunctionMiddleware.process can mutate ctx.arguments before call_next(). BYO; no declarative pinned_args. Documented pattern in examples.
No first-class mutate-args hook. on_tool_start is read-only. Standard pattern is to keep tenant out of the schema and read from ctx.context.tenant_id. tool_input_guardrail can reject but not rewrite.
No PreToolUse mutate hook. Standard pattern is ignore LLM's arg and substitute from runContext.context inside execute. callModelInputFilter operates on messages, not on pending tool args.

@hooks.on.before_tool_validate(tools=['topic_search']) returns {**args, 'tenant_id': ctx.deps.tenant_id}; takes precedence over LLM args. Also args_validator and reading from ctx.deps. Three documented mechanisms.

on_tool_call receives args as &str — read-only. ToolCallHookAction is only Continue/Skip/Terminate. Force tenant pattern is to capture it as a tool struct field, requiring per-tenant agent construction.
_can_write whitelist includes 'tool_use'; hook mutates tool_use['input'] before executor re-reads it. Equivalent to Claude Agent SDK's PreToolUse updatedInput.
Hooks may mutate event.toolUse.input to overwrite any field the model generated. Documented as the canonical mechanism. interventions transform() provides typed equivalent.

experimental_refineToolInput[name](input) => input' runs before dispatch; refined input is what tools/callbacks/telemetry see. Per-tool. Cleaner pattern is to keep tenantId out of inputSchema and pass via toolsContext.
Toolset.Tools(ctx) called per request; predicate reads ReadonlyState. Static agent.Tools slice is NOT filtered per request — only Toolsets. Per-tenant requires wrapping into Toolset.

agent.tools can be Callable[..., List] receiving run_context, session_state; cache_callables=False re-runs per request. Same pattern works for knowledge, members, instructions. Per-turn requires re-invocation.
#[agent(tools=[...])] derive macro fixes the toolset at compile time. No activeTools, allowed_tools, or prepareStep. Per-tenant filter requires building a different agent per tenant.
